title: PolicyIK: High-Precision Inverse Kinematics for Robot Arms with Reinforcement Learning
authors: Yuhan Liu,Xinqi Liu,Zixuan Dong,Keith W. Ross,Shenji Wan
abstract: Inverse kinematics (IK) converts end-effector pose commands into joint motion, and many vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely on it to act on a given arm and to transfer across embodiments. Precise IK remains laborious: redundancy and singularities complicate the inverse mapping, execution depends on hand-tuned controllers, and training data on physical robots are costly to collect. We present PolicyIK, a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning policy for high-precision IK. It updates joint-position references from pose feedback and observes its accumulated reference relative to the measured joints, so it can retain the offset that the position controller needs at rest. Two-scale pose errors with an error-dependent action gain resolve millimeter residuals while preserving large motions. Progress and dwell rewards teach it to both reach the tolerance and stay within it. In simulation, a single attempt by the trained PPO policy keeps the mean errors over the final second within 1 mm and 0.2∘0.2^{\circ} on 93.5% of held-out tasks, and a deployment protocol raises success to 98.9%. When trained directly on a physical arm with an off-policy RL learner, PolicyIK achieves higher reaching and holding success than all four classical IK controllers under the same time budgets. In simulated pick-and-place, PolicyIK executes the end-effector commands of the π0.5\pi_{0.5} VLA policy with 95.7% success. These results show that reinforcement learning can provide high-precision inverse kinematics for robot arms. Code is available at https://github.com/Tinaliu0123/PolicyIK.
introduction:
Many learned manipulation policies act on a robot arm through inverse
kinematics (IK), which turns end-effector pose commands into joint motion.
Vision-language-action (VLA) and generalist policies often predict
end-effector poses or pose increments and leave the conversion to joint
commands to an IK or operational-space controller
(Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al., 2024; Octo Model Team et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2024). Because this interface is shared across
arms, the same policy can run on different robots
(Chi et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024; Lepert et al., 2024; Ha et al., 2024). Such transfer delegates the
feasibility and accuracy of every command to the target robot’s IK. Transfer
methods assume controllers that reach commanded poses within a few millimeters
(Chen et al., 2024), yet transfer fails at joint limits and on motions the arm cannot follow (Chi et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2023). IK accuracy thus
carries over to every policy that acts through it.

Developing and deploying a precise pose controller raises three challenges. First, the inverse
mapping itself is difficult. A redundant arm can reach a pose with many joint configurations (Burdick, 1989), and near singularities small pose corrections demand large joint motions, so numerical solvers trade accuracy for robustness and can fail even on reachable poses (Buss, 2009; Deo and Walker, 1995; Beeson and Ames, 2015).
Second, the realized pose depends on robot-specific execution. Finite gains,
gravity, and joint limits shift where a position-controlled arm comes to rest. Controller dynamics also affect
how action errors propagate during policy execution (Bronars et al., 2026).
The controllers that compensate for these effects rely on damping factors, task
weights, and gains that experts tune for each robot
(Lynch and Park, 2017; Charbonneau et al., 2018; Buss and Kim, 2005; Lee et al., 2026). Third, collecting
training data on physical robots is costly, as each trial requires robot
execution and a reset.

We investigate reinforcement learning (RL) for this setting. An RL policy learns the
mapping from pose error to joint commands through interaction with the robot’s
dynamics. Sampling goals from reachable configurations yields feasible goals
across the workspace, and the designed reward targets the required tolerance. Prior RL controllers have reached position goals with
fixed-base arms and tracked full poses with legged manipulators, with errors
from several millimeters to a few centimeters
(Kumar et al., 2021; Aljalbout et al., 2024; Portela et al., 2025; He et al., 2026), and a hybrid reaches
sub-millimeter accuracy in kinematic simulation by pairing the policy with
damped least squares, which supplies the final correction (Yu and Tan, 2025).
Reaching millimeter-level full-pose accuracy with the policy alone calls for a
formulation designed around terminal precision.

We present PolicyIK, a goal-conditioned RL formulation that learns
high-precision IK for robot arms through a joint-position interface
(Figure 2). Like closed-loop IK (Siciliano, 1990), the
policy updates a joint reference from pose feedback, but learns this update
from interaction. The formulation addresses three properties of precise
regulation. First, the policy accumulates its actions in the reference and
observes the reference relative to the measured joints, so it can retain the
offset that the position controller needs at rest. Second, pose errors enter
the observation at coarse and fine scales, and an error-dependent gain shrinks
actions near the goal, which resolves small residuals while preserving large
motions. Third, the reward credits progress beyond the best error so far and time within tolerance, so it trains both reaching and holding.
We train with PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) in parallel simulation
(Mittal et al., 2023) and with FlashSAC (Kim et al., 2026) on physical arms.
Since every hardware transition costs robot time, a reverse curriculum and
near-goal sampling focus training on the terminal phase, while a
latent-alignment critic handles large-rotation detours.

We evaluate PolicyIK in simulation and on a physical arm (Figure 1). On a
simulated 7-DoF arm, PolicyIK reaches median errors of 0.25 mm and
0.04∘0.04^{\circ} and meets the 1 mm and 0.2∘0.2^{\circ} tolerance on 93.5% of held-out
tasks in one attempt and on 98.9% with a deployment protocol. Removing
any design component lowers single-attempt success by 1.8–9.2 points.
Direct hardware training demonstrates the value of learning to maintain a pose
after reaching it. PolicyIK achieves higher reaching and holding success than all four
classical IK controllers under the same time budgets. In simulated pick-and-place, it executes the
end-effector commands of π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Physical Intelligence and others, 2025) with 95.7% success
across ten adapted LIBERO-Object tasks (Liu et al., 2023), without pick-and-place data in its training.
These capabilities come with a low inference cost: an actor forward pass takes
0.035 ms on CPU, well below the 33 ms control period.
Our contributions are as follows:

We show that goal-conditioned RL formulates inverse kinematics for robot arms and can train a policy to reach and hold millimeter-level full-pose
precision through a joint-position interface.

We identify three design choices behind this precision: observing the
joint reference relative to the measured joints, sensing pose errors at
centimeter and sub-millimeter scales with smaller steps near the goal, and
rewarding each new best error and every step within tolerance. Ablations show
they affect reaching and holding separately.

We train PolicyIK directly on two physical arms (OpenArm and xArm7) with
FlashSAC (Kim et al., 2026), hindsight goal relabeling
(Andrychowicz et al., 2017), and a curriculum from near-goal starts
(Florensa et al., 2017) to large rotations. It holds reached poses
within 1 mm and 0.2∘0.2^{\circ} more reliably than classical IK controllers, and executes a
VLA policy’s commands in simulated pick-and-place with 95.7% success.

1. We show that goal-conditioned RL formulates inverse kinematics for robot arms and can train a policy to reach and hold millimeter-level full-pose
precision through a joint-position interface.

2. We identify three design choices behind this precision: observing the
joint reference relative to the measured joints, sensing pose errors at
centimeter and sub-millimeter scales with smaller steps near the goal, and
rewarding each new best error and every step within tolerance. Ablations show
they affect reaching and holding separately.

3. We train PolicyIK directly on two physical arms (OpenArm and xArm7) with
FlashSAC (Kim et al., 2026), hindsight goal relabeling
(Andrychowicz et al., 2017), and a curriculum from near-goal starts
(Florensa et al., 2017) to large rotations. It holds reached poses
within 1 mm and 0.2∘0.2^{\circ} more reliably than classical IK controllers, and executes a
VLA policy’s commands in simulated pick-and-place with 95.7% success.

title: GUILD: Guided Iterative Data Collection for Imitation Learning
authors: Shivin Dass,Kevin Nguyen,Rohan Yelandur,Junhong Xu,Roberto Martín-Martín
abstract:
Imitation learning policies in robotics are trained on datasets collected through costly real-world teleoperation. Often, the data-collection process is unguided, relying on the teleoperator’s intuition, resulting in data that contributes little to overall policy performance. Recent work has shown that curating such unguided datasets can substantially improve policy performance, but these approaches operate by filtering existing datasets after collection and therefore do not prevent the acquisition of uninformative data. In this work, we propose GUILD, a novel Guided Data Collection (GDC) method that actively reasons about which data should be collected to maximize downstream policy performance. We introduce an iterative framework that alternates between 1) task proposal and data collection and 2) data evaluation to close the loop. For task proposal, we leverage semantic priors from vision–language models to identify relevant environments, object configurations, and goals for data collection. However, since semantic relevance does not imply policy improvement, we perform data evaluation. By leveraging predictive data attribution we approximate how the collected trajectories influence policy performance on a target deployment setting. This signal is then used as feedback to guide subsequent data collection, closing the data collection loop.
We evaluate our approach in simulation and real robot settings, demonstrating that guided data collection substantially improves sample efficiency and deployment performance compared to passive data collection strategies, multiple baselines and experienced roboticists.
More info at our website.
introduction:
Imitation learning (IL) has demonstrated a powerful paradigm for enabling robots to perform a wide range of manipulation tasks [1, 2, 3, 4].
However, successfully deploying robotic systems often requires strong performance under specific real-world conditions, where task-relevant training data may be scarce and additional data collection may be impractical or infeasible.
Consider a robot operating in an end-user home, hospital, or warehouse: although these environments represent the ultimate deployment targets, collecting large-scale demonstrations directly within them is often constrained by privacy, safety, cost, or limited accessibility.
In many practical settings, however, robots have access to separate training environments where interaction data is easier to acquire.
For instance, while collecting demonstrations in the end-user’s home may be difficult, humans can often gather data by teleoperating robots in other apartments, mock setups, or laboratory spaces.
These auxiliary environments provide scalable sources of interaction, but they remain imperfectly aligned with the target domain.
As a result, the central challenge is not simply collecting more data, but deciding what data should be collected so that it transfers most effectively under distribution shift.

A common strategy in robot learning is to collect data broadly across diverse tasks and environments [5, 6, 7], under the assumption that scale alone will produce robust policies.
However, recent work in machine learning [8, 9, 10] and robotics [11, 12, 13] has shown that carefully curated datasets can substantially outperform much larger unfiltered ones when targeting specific downstream domains.
These findings suggest that not all demonstrations contribute equally to policy learning.
Existing approaches to data curation, however, primarily operate as a post-hoc filtering mechanism: they identify useful subsets only after large datasets have already been collected [11, 13, 14].
This process is inherently inefficient, since the cost of collecting discarded data has already been incurred.
In contrast, expert roboticists often rely on intuition to decide what interactions are most valuable to collect for improving downstream performance.
Yet such intuition is difficult to formalize, expensive to acquire, and not always reliable.
Reducing the burden of robot data collection therefore requires automated methods capable of guiding humans toward collecting the most informative demonstrations for downstream policy learning.

In this work, we study the problem of Guided Data Collection (GDC) [15]: rather than collecting data indiscriminately and filtering it afterward, GDC methods actively reason about what data to collect, where to collect it, and which interactions to prioritize in order to maximize downstream deployment performance.
We focus on the practical setting where direct access to the deployment environment is unavailable, but data collection remains possible in related auxiliary environments.

To address this challenge, we formulate guided data collection as an iterative optimization problem over the data-generation process itself.
We introduce GUILD (Guided Iterative Imitation Learning Data Collection), a framework that tightly couples task proposal, data collection, and data evaluation within a closed feedback loop.
Given the large combinatorial space of possible environments, object configurations, and manipulation tasks, GUILD leverages semantic priors from vision–language models to define a structured proposal distribution over candidate data-collection tasks.
However, semantic relevance alone does not imply downstream improvement.
To address this, GUILD uses data attribution [16, 17, 18] to estimate how individual data points influence deployment-time performance on a small set of target-domain demonstrations, and uses this signal to iteratively reallocate the collection budget toward increasingly beneficial interactions.
By continuously refining the data-collection process based on utility, GUILD closes the loop between data collection and downstream policy evaluation.
We evaluate GUILD in both simulation and real-world robotic settings, demonstrating substantial improvements in sample efficiency and downstream policy performance compared to several baselines, passive data collection strategies and even expert roboticists.

title: PyRUA-DataFarm: LLM Agent as a Cost-Efficient Teleoperator for Real-Ready Robot Data
authors: Kewei Zhang,Juncheng Ma,Guodong Lv,Duomin Wang,Feixiang Ruan,Ruiyang Si,Chuanrui Zhang,Yuxuan Chen,Hao Chen,Yichen Liu,Yintianrun Zhang,Yufan Deng,Enze Xie,Daquan Zhou
comment: . Project page:this https URLCode:this https URL
abstract:
Teleoperation remains the default way to collect robot demonstrations, but every
episode costs robot and operator time, and every new task starts from scratch. We ask
whether a coding agent can take over the teleoperator’s job. In our DataFarm,
the agent receives a data request and one calibration episode of the robot in the target
scene and rebuilds the task in simulation: it writes the scene, an expert controller, and
a success judge. The simulator supplies exact actions, and a video model conditioned on
real images renders each rollout as photographic video, generating all camera views
together consistently. The output is real-ready data:
synchronized camera views labelled with the robot’s actions, on
which a policy can be trained directly and deployed on the real robot. Independent judges
certify the expert and every rendered episode before admission. On five real-robot tasks, policies trained only
on farm data match policies trained on as many teleoperated episodes (93 vs. 84
successes in 100 trials), and under an unseen tablecloth and coloured light they keep
87 successes where the teleoperation-trained policies fall to 46. Adapting a task is
fully automatic and costs $21 of API usage on average, paid once per task, plus $5 for a
render contract; every further episode costs $0.80 on average for simulation, rendering, and
review, with no robot or operator.
One hour of three-view data for a task costs $107 on average, these costs included,
slightly below a quote of $117 for teleoperation in China and below $290
in labour alone in North America.
introduction:
Teleoperation remains the primary source of training data for robot
policies [25, 2, 3]. Its appeal is that the
data are faithful by construction: every recorded action was executed by the robot,
and every image shows the scene in which the policy will be deployed. Its weakness
is cost. Each episode requires a robot, an operator, and resets after failures, so
the cost grows with the amount of data and starts over with every new task, scene,
or viewpoint.

Synthetic data promises to break this scaling, yet existing pipelines trade the cost
of collection for two other costs. The first is human engineering: whether
demonstrations are multiplied from a few seeds [34, 49]
or tasks are written by language models [46, 6], a
person still has to assemble and debug the scene, the expert, and the success check
for every new task. The second is the visual gap between simulation and reality.
Real-to-sim-to-real methods narrow it by reconstructing the
scene [44, 16, 37], but whatever is hard
to reconstruct, such as deformable cloth or a lit display, still looks synthetic,
while video generation models that synthesize the motion themselves can no longer
provide exact action labels [22]. Producing real-ready robot data, exact enough to train on and realistic
enough to deploy on the real robot without any real demonstrations, cheaply for every
new task therefore remains an open problem.

We address this problem with DataFarm, an agentic data farm in which a coding agent
takes over the teleoperator’s role, a simulator supplies the actions, and a video
model supplies the appearance (Figure 2). Given a data request and a
single calibration episode, a short recording of the robot in the target scene, the
agent compiles the task into simulation as an engineer would: it reconstructs the
scene and cameras from the calibration episode, verifies that the simulator can
reproduce the required skills, and writes an expert controller together with a
success judge. The simulator then executes the expert from many initial states to
produce trajectories with exact actions and states, and a video model conditioned on
real frames renders each trajectory, all camera views in one generation, in the
appearance of the target scene, where new
appearances such as a different tablecloth or lighting are specified in text. The
output is real-ready: synchronized, mutually consistent photographic camera views with the robot’s own
action labels, which a policy consumes exactly as it would consume teleoperated
data.
Because the agent harness is decoupled from individual tasks, a new task requires no
task-specific engineering by a person, and once a task is compiled, every further episode is
produced without a robot, an operator, or a reset.

Delegating data production to an agent, however, raises a question that
teleoperation never faces: who verifies the data? An agent that writes both the
expert and its success checks may approve its own mistakes, and a video model asked
to look realistic may copy the layout of its references, hallucinate objects, or
drift from the simulated motion. DataFarm therefore separates certification from
production. The expert is developed against a judge it cannot inspect and admitted
only on held-out initial states, the renderer may alter appearance but not geometry,
objects, or timing, and every rendered episode is compared with its simulated state
by machine checks and an independent reviewer before it enters the dataset.

Experiments on five bimanual tasks covering rigid, articulated, deformable, and
display-bearing objects show that this design yields real-ready data at low cost:
policies are trained on it directly and deployed on the real robot
(Figure 1). Policies trained only on farm data
match those trained on the same number of teleoperated episodes in the original scene
(93 vs. 84 successes in 100 trials) and remain robust under a tablecloth and coloured
light absent from both training sets (87 vs. 46), which we attribute to the
appearance variation the farm adds around fixed, exact trajectories. Rendering with
real images is essential to this transfer: the same trajectories rendered with
conventional domain randomization yield only 26 and 21 successes
(Section 6.1). Every camera view of a farm episode both follows the
simulation and looks real: image statistics place farm episodes more than twice as close
to real camera frames as the simulator’s own renderings, and the farm’s renderer keeps
all views faithful to the simulated motion, whereas calling the video model directly does
not (Section 6.4). The farm also operates without human
intervention: adapting a task costs $21 of API usage on average, paid once per task, a render
contract adds $5, and every further episode costs $0.80 on average for simulation, rendering,
re-rendering, and review, in the
original scene or under new appearance, so 100 episodes of a task cost $1.06 per
episode on average, and one hour of synchronized three-view data for a task costs $107,
these costs included, slightly below a quote of $117 for teleoperation in China and below
$290 in labour alone in North America (Section 6.2).

In summary, our contributions are threefold:

We introduce DataFarm, an agentic data farm that turns a data request and one
calibration episode into verified, real-ready robot data without human intervention.
The simulator determines actions and states, a real-image-conditioned video model
determines appearance, and certification is kept separate from production, all under
an agent harness that is independent of individual tasks.

We show that the farm produces action-labelled, multi-view data that closely
matches real camera recordings, at a lower cost than teleoperation.

We show on a real robot that policies trained solely on farm data match
teleoperated data in the original scene, generalize substantially better to unseen
appearance, and far outperform a conventional real-to-sim-to-real baseline.

1. We introduce DataFarm, an agentic data farm that turns a data request and one
calibration episode into verified, real-ready robot data without human intervention.
The simulator determines actions and states, a real-image-conditioned video model
determines appearance, and certification is kept separate from production, all under
an agent harness that is independent of individual tasks.

2. We show that the farm produces action-labelled, multi-view data that closely
matches real camera recordings, at a lower cost than teleoperation.

3. We show on a real robot that policies trained solely on farm data match
teleoperated data in the original scene, generalize substantially better to unseen
appearance, and far outperform a conventional real-to-sim-to-real baseline.

title: PACT: Pose-Robust Actuation Co-Design for Tendon-Driven Robotic Hands
authors: Prashant Kumar,Rachael Granberry,Taylor Niehues,Andrew A. Stanley,Gabe Pirie
abstract:
Humanoid robotic hands must provide sufficient force, speed and backdrivability within a human-scale envelope. Tendon-driven transmissions address this challenge by relocating actuators to the palm and forearm, but routing paths, moment arms, and capstan dimensions jointly determine both force capability and joint speed, so selecting them sequentially satisfies one requirement at the expense of the other. This paper presents a pose-robust actuation co-design for tendon-driven robot hands (PACT) framework that optimizes tendon routing, moment arms, and capstan dimensions under pose-dependent force requirements and drivetrain-bandwidth constraints. A feasible-force formulation enforces actuator bounds and equilibrium at all joints, while a max–min objective maximizes task-force coverage at the weakest pose. Applied to a four-degree-of-freedom finger, the framework produces an asymmetric N+1N+1 tendon topology using quasi-direct-drive actuators. Across eight poses, the design achieves task-force coverage of 0.880.88–1.001.00 and a predicted 5​Hz5\,\mathrm{Hz} minimum isolated-joint flexion/extension bandwidth within a 70th-percentile human-size envelope. Prototype measurements
deviate from predictions by up to 24.5%24.5\%, primarily due to unmodeled transmission losses. These results indicate that co-designing routing with the drivetrain can meet pose-dependent force requirements without relaxing the bandwidth constraint, paving the way for human-sized robotic hands with human-level performance.
introduction:
Dexterous robotic hands require substantial force capability, rapid response,
and mechanical backdrivability within a compact form factor. Quasi-direct-drive (QDD) actuators
come closest to closing this gap by combining torque density, bandwidth, and
low reflected impedance through relatively low transmission ratios
[1, 2]. Human-hand anthropometry severely limits the space available at the finger
joints [3, 4]. For the actuator considered here, applying
this dimensional constraint limits the estimated output torque to approximately
0.09​N​m0.09\,\mathrm{N\,m}. This is substantially below the joint torque estimated
from representative human fingertip-force measurements
[5, 6]. Sizing a QDD actuator for the maximum load at every joint
exceeds the packaging, mass, and thermal budgets of a human-scale hand. This
tradeoff forces robotic hands either to exceed the dimensions of a human hand or to accept force and bandwidth penalties. Tendon-driven transmissions alleviate
this constraint by relocating actuators proximally, reducing distal mass and
enabling compact fingers without sacrificing useful grasping forces
[7, 8, 9].

The performance of a tendon-driven finger depends on strongly coupled routing
and drivetrain choices. Tendon topology and moment arms map tendon forces to
joint torques, whereas motor selection, gearing, and capstan dimensions
determine tendon-force capacity, motor-speed requirements, and reflected
inertia. For example, reducing the capstan radius increases the available tendon force but proportionally lowers the joint speed obtainable from a given motor speed. Such couplings motivate optimizing the routing and drivetrain parameters jointly, rather than independently, for optimal performance.

While achieving sufficient fingertip force is important, the objective is not necessarily to maximize
the total force-set volume, but to orient and shape the feasible set toward the
required task-force region. Tendon coupling can be exploited to concentrate fingertip-force
capability in task-relevant directions to avoid allocating actuation capacity
to directions that contribute little to the intended manipulation tasks.

Existing force-set optimization frameworks [10] generally consider a single pose
and therefore do not guarantee that task requirements are met throughout the
required workspace. Because the manipulator Jacobian varies with joint
configuration, a routing and transmission optimized at one pose may perform
poorly at another. Although prior studies have examined tendon routing,
asymmetric actuation, force-polytope shaping, and actuator distribution
[11, 10, 12, 13], the joint optimization
of tendon topology, heterogeneous actuator allocation, transmission geometry,
force capability, and bandwidth across multiple poses remains insufficiently
explored.

This paper presents a pose-robust actuation co-design for tendon-driven robot hands (PACT) framework that selects tendon
routing and drivetrain parameters simultaneously. Given a library of poses
with associated force and motion requirements, the framework optimizes tendon
topology, signed moment arms, capstan radii, and actuator allocation.
Fingertip-force capability is evaluated using an exact feasible-force set that
enforces all joint-equilibrium equations. Dynamic feasibility is assessed
using a drivetrain model incorporating continuous motor torque, speed limits,
gear ratios, capstan radii, and reflected rotor inertia. A max–min objective
selects the shared physical design that maximizes performance at its weakest
pose.

We apply the framework as shown in Figure 1 to a four-degree-of-freedom (DoF) finger with three
flexion/extension (F/E) joints and one MCP abduction/adduction (A/A) DoF.
The resulting design uses an asymmetric N+1N+1 tendon arrangement. A
wrist-mounted, high-torque QDD actuator drives a shared, force-dominant flexion
tendon, while three smaller palm-mounted QDD actuators drive differential
tendons that regulate posture and shape the force set. A separate
bidirectional actuator controls abduction/adduction. This heterogeneous
allocation avoids uniformly oversizing the actuators and limits the number of
high-force tendons crossing the wrist.

In summary, this paper contributes:

Integrated routing and drivetrain design. A mixed
discrete–continuous optimization selects routing signs, moment arm
magnitudes and capstan radii.

Integrated routing and drivetrain design. A mixed
discrete–continuous optimization selects routing signs, moment arm
magnitudes and capstan radii.

Worst-pose performance optimization. A max–min objective
selects one shared physical design by explicitly maximizing performance at
the weakest pose in a prescribed pose library.

Exact feasible-force evaluation. Admissible fingertip
forces are defined as the preimage of the bounded actuator-generated
joint-torque set under the transposed fingertip Jacobian. Unlike
pseudoinverse projections, this formulation admits only forces that
satisfy every joint-equilibrium equation.

Experimental validation. A four-DoF
tendon-driven finger demonstrates the proposed framework experimentally.

title: GSBR: Geometric Support Behavior Regularization for Online RL
authors: Charles Xu,Jacob Berg,Liyiming Ke,Sergey Levine
abstract:
Regularizing online reinforcement learning (RL) toward a pretrained base policy can improve sample efficiency and learning stability, but regularization that is too restrictive limits how much the policy can improve. Base policies – typically diffusion or flow-matching models trained by imitation learning on large, diverse datasets – capture many behaviors that are reasonable but suboptimal. Existing regularizers using such base policies are too restrictive in one of two ways: behavioral cloning regularizers pull the actor toward the full base-policy distribution, penalizing it for discarding suboptimal modes, while hard support constraints forbid improvements that lie just outside the base policy’s support. We propose Geometric Support Behavior Regularization (GSBR), which penalizes actions by their distance from the base policy’s support. Actions within the support incur no penalty, so the actor can concentrate on high-value modes; outside the support, where value estimates are less reliable, the penalty grows smoothly with distance while still permitting improvement when the value gained outweighs the penalty. GSBR estimates this distance from a finite set of base-policy samples, so it requires only sample access to the base policy.
Across 19 tasks on four robotic benchmarks, GSBR raises the average
success rate from 33% for the base policy to 95%, achieving the highest
average success rate and throughput among all compared methods, with
about 23% higher normalized throughput than the next-best RL method.
Project website and open-source code: https://charlesxu0124.github.io/gsbr/.
introduction:
Online reinforcement learning (RL) can be costly when every interaction happens on a physical system, so practical methods often rely on a behavior prior that focuses exploration on plausible actions. In robotics, such priors are now available at scale: vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) learn diverse behaviors from large demonstration datasets (Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2026), but often lack the robustness and throughput required for reliable deployment (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026).
RL fine-tuning can close this gap by updating a policy that is regularized toward the pretrained base model.
This raises a general question for RL: how should a behavior regularizer preserve the base policy’s guidance while giving the actor enough freedom to improve on it?

Improving upon base policies typically has two requirements: mode selection and local refinement. Consider a scene with two objects and the task is to grasp a specified target. Foundation models trained on large-scale data often produce diverse behaviors - and such base policies might have two action modes, one to grasp each object. The actor should be updated to discard the mode that reaches for the wrong object; we call this mode selection.
However, existing behavior constraints can hinder one of the requirements and restrict policy improvement.
Action regression (Fujimoto and Gu, 2021; Park et al., 2025b) and distribution-matching regularizers (Li and Levine, 2026; Fang et al., 2025) tie the actor to the base policy’s full action distribution, penalizing the actor even for discarding poor modes (Figure 1(a)).
Support constraints (Kumar et al., 2019; Wagenmaker et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025) remove this penalty and permit mode selection, but can be too restrictive and often exclude optimal actions outside the base policy’s support (Figure 1(b)).

Our key insight is to allow both mode selection and local refinement by introducing a geometric relaxation of the support constraint.
We introduce Geometric Support Behavior Regularization (GSBR), an RL algorithm that estimates the support of the base policy using finite samples, and regularizes actions differently based on whether they are inside or outside the support.
Actions inside the estimated support incur no penalty, allowing the actor to discard poor modes and concentrate on better ones without preserving their relative frequencies. Outside the support, GSBR replaces the infinite penalty of a hard constraint with a finite one that grows with distance, reflecting that value estimates become less reliable far from the base policy. Because the support of a learned base policy is intractable to compute, we approximate it by the union of neighborhoods around actions sampled from the base policy, with a radius that adapts to the observed samples’ distances from each other. GSBR provides a practical sample-based geometric support regularizer fitting for the diverse distribution of large-scale robot foundation policies.

Our contributions are (1) a geometric behavior regularizer that permits both mode selection and local refinement in RL finetuning, (2) a sample-based approximation of multi-modal action distribution with an adaptive radius, with error bounds and a guarantee that the error vanishes as the number of reference samples grows, (3) an evaluation across 19 tasks drawn from four benchmarks where GSBR raises the average
success rate from 33% for the base policy to 95%, achieving the highest
average success rate and throughput among all compared methods, with
about 23% higher normalized throughput than the next-best RL method.
Further analysis shows that our approximation closely matches the true support region and examines the effects of sample count and support radius.

title: Should the Action Expert Train the VLM? Action-Token Supervision and Gradient Routing in Mixture-of-Transformer VLAs
authors: Asher James Hancock,Boyi Li,Yuxiao Chen,Shuhan Tan,Wenhao Ding,Thomas Tian,Yan Wang,Boris Ivanovic,Marco Pavone
abstract: Vision–language–action (VLA) models increasingly pair a pre-trained vision–language model (VLM) with a flow-matching expert that conditions its action predictions on the VLM’s key–value representations. Those representations must carry information useful for control, yet the VLM was never trained for the action expert’s flow-matching objective. Two signals can address this: gradients backpropagated from the expert’s loss (coupling), or VLM supervision to predict discrete tokens encoding the same target actions. Prominent training recipes forgo the first, blocking expert-to-VLM gradients (insulation) to protect the VLM’s existing capabilities, while also supervising it on vision–language data and action tokens. Because vision–language co-training also aims to preserve those capabilities, the additional protection provided by insulation is unclear. At the same time, insulation removes a direct signal about which features continuous action prediction requires. On the other hand, action-token supervision offers an alternative way to learn action-relevant representations, which may explain why insulation succeeds in practice. We disentangle these factors in autonomous driving and manipulation by independently varying action-token supervision and whether the expert’s loss updates the VLM. In open-loop driving, insulation is competitive with coupling when action tokens are supervised; without them, coupling reduces trajectory-prediction error by roughly 25%. When both components are trained jointly from the outset, coupling increases closed-loop driving route progress by approximately 17% with action-token supervision and 40% without it, and similarly improves robot manipulation performance under both settings. These findings show that the value of gradient insulation depends on the VLM’s action supervision and the evaluation setting, challenging insulation as a default VLA training recipe.
introduction:
Pretrained vision–language models (VLMs) bring broad perceptual, semantic, and reasoning capabilities to embodied control. Robotic control, however, requires precise continuous outputs at frequencies poorly suited to autoregressive decoding with large VLMs. Many recent vision–language–action (VLA) models therefore use Mixture-of-Transformers-style architectures [23], pairing an autoregressive VLM with a smaller diffusion or flow-matching action expert [2]. The VLM processes visual observations and language instructions, while the expert efficiently generates continuous action chunks conditioned on the VLM’s per-layer key–value (K/V) representations [34].

This architecture leaves open a consequential training decision: should the continuous-action loss train only the expert, or also the VLM that produces its conditioning K/V cache? Allowing expert gradients to update the VLM (coupling) enables co-adaptation and can teach the backbone which information its representations must preserve for precise control. Yet it also exposes pretrained visual and linguistic features to gradients from a newly introduced, often randomly initialized expert, which may degrade the VLM’s semantic and world understanding.

Popular approaches therefore block the action expert’s gradients from entering the VLM (insulation), either through stop-gradient or frozen-backbone training [34, 6]. However, full-parameter fine-tuning on a narrow robot training distribution can degrade pretrained capabilities regardless of gradient routing [11]. When vision–language co-training is also used to mitigate forgetting, it is unclear whether insulation provides additional protection.

Insulation is also rarely evaluated in isolation. Blocking expert gradients removes one source of action-relevant learning signal, but such systems typically supply another: they train the VLM to predict discrete action tokens [33], which directly supervise the behavior the expert models. Co-training on general vision–question-answering (VQA) and chain-of-thought examples may preserve the VLM’s semantic capabilities, but it does not explicitly encourage representations relevant to control. In the absence of action-token supervision, insulation may therefore eliminate the only objective that directly adapts the VLM for trajectory prediction. Crucially, defining an analogous discrete proxy for continuous prediction targets is a domain-dependent design choice whose effectiveness must be established empirically. It is therefore unclear whether the reported benefits of insulation arise from gradient blocking itself or depend on this auxiliary supervision.

Prior work has not isolated this interaction. Knowledge Insulation reports benefits from insulated training while supervising the VLM with FAST action tokens and vision–language objectives, but does not evaluate insulation without FAST supervision [6, 33]. In contrast, Wall-OSS-0.5 reports stronger action performance from coupled training even when discrete-action and multimodal objectives are retained [39]. Because these systems also differ in training recipes, initialization, data, and optimization, their seemingly opposing results cannot isolate the contributions of action-token supervision and expert-to-VLM gradient flow in downstream control or determine how the two mechanisms interact.

Contributions.
In this work, we study how a VLA’s representations are made action-relevant, and whether the two available signals—the expert’s gradient and discrete action-token supervision—substitute for one another. We cross action-token supervision with expert-to-VLM gradient flow in autonomous driving and robot manipulation, under both joint training and training schedules in which one component is adapted first. Within each training schedule and action-token setting, routing comparisons hold data, architecture, optimization, and semantic co-training fixed. In open-loop driving evaluations, the two routing choices are nearly indistinguishable with action-token supervision; without it, coupling reduces trajectory-prediction error by roughly 25%. This pattern holds across training schedules and in both in- and out-of-distribution evaluations. Under joint training, coupling improves closed-loop performance regardless of supervision: driving route progress increases by approximately 17% with action tokens and 40% without them, while manipulation task progress improves under both settings. Together, these results identify action-token supervision as a factor previously entangled with gradient routing and show that VLM insulation is a conditional choice, not a default training recipe for training VLAs.

title: Reality and Perceptual Gaps in Expressive Swarm Robotics
authors: Ali Imran,Abdalwhab Bakheet Mohammed Abdalwhab,Rafael Gomes Braga,Hélène Duval,Audrey Rochette,Vivek Shankar Varadhajan,Yann Bouteiller,Jean Mazerolle,Giovanni Beltrame,David St-Onge
abstract: Moving robot swarms from simulation into the physical world can be difficult because small discrepancies in hardware, timing and communication can cascade across interacting robots and alter group behaviour. This challenge is known as the reality gap. When swarms operate in human environments, a second challenge emerges: a perceptual gap between what the swarm physically does and what human onlookers actually perceive. This study examines the same decentralised coordination code deployed across three robotic swarms—tabletop, aerial and human-scale mobile manipulators—during live artistic performances. We find that while the underlying algorithms executed reliably on all three platforms, physical embodiment drastically altered visible motion—distorting execution timescales by more than a factor of three and reshaping trajectory geometry. More importantly, audience surveys revealed that human interpretation does not mirror technical success: how observers attribute meaning (perceived purpose) and how they react emotionally (comfort versus threat) depend heavily on physical form. Meaning attribution and emotional responses did not vary together. Our results demonstrate that successfully transferring swarm software to physical hardware is insufficient for real-world deployment. Addressing the reality gap does not guarantee that the resulting collective motion will be readily interpreted by human observers. Swarms destined for human environments must be engineered not only for decentralised stability but also for the expressive physical dynamics through which humans interpret collective motion.
introduction:
Over the past decades, swarm robotics has moved from predominantly simulation-driven studies toward increasingly capable physical multi-robot systems. Software frameworks such as ROS2swarm [1], CrazyChoir [2], Crazyswarm2 [3], and Aerostack2 [4] have made collective behaviours more modular across specific hardware ecosystems, while large field demonstrations have shown that multi-robot coordination can persist in unstructured environments [5]. For swarms, however, transferring a controller from simulation to hardware is more than a conventional sim-to-real problem repeated across many robots. Collective behaviour emerges from repeated local interactions, so small discrepancies in sensing, localisation, communication timing, actuation, or update frequency can propagate through the network and alter group-level dynamics, even when the same decentralised program executes correctly on every agent. The transfer target is therefore not only an agent-level controller but also the interaction process from which the collective regime emerges. A behaviour may therefore survive deployment at the code level while changing in period, spatial organisation, convergence, or interaction structure at the collective level. Existing work has addressed these effects through simulator-in-the-loop refinement [6, 7], Real2Sim2Real transfer of emergent behaviours [8], mixed-reality validation over physical communication networks [9], and quantitative robustness and deployment metrics [10, 11, 12]. Across much of this work, transfer is assessed from the behaviour of the robotic system itself: whether the physical swarm realises the collective organisation specified by its controller.

Two years of deploying heterogeneous swarms in public performances exposed a complementary problem: a collective behaviour can be physically realised as specified and still remain difficult for a human observer to interpret. We refer to the discrepancy between the collective organisation physically realised by the swarm and the organisation inferred by an observer as the perceptual gap. This challenge becomes increasingly relevant as robot collectives move into spaces shared with non-expert humans, where motion must support anticipation, prediction, and appropriate trust [13, 14, 15].

As illustrated in Fig. 1, the perceptual gap follows the reality gap rather than replacing it. A designer specifies collective dynamics, which robots physically realise through interactions shaped by sensing, timing, and embodiment. This realised motion then becomes the stimulus from which human observers interpret the collective. The two gaps are therefore distinct but sequentially coupled: discrepancies introduced during physical realisation shape what becomes available to perception, while preserving the specified collective organisation does not guarantee how it will be interpreted. This distinction motivates characterising the collective motion realised across robotic embodiments before examining audience interpretations.

The perceptual gap in a swarm is not simply the legibility problem of a single robot multiplied by the number of agents. Classical legibility concerns inference of an intended goal from observed motion [16, 17]. Recent work on multi-robot systems extends this notion to coordination objectives—what the group is doing relative to itself—as well as spatial goals [18]. For expressive swarms, however, the perceptual question is broader: collective behaviours need not be goal-directed, and observers may construct meaning from their organisation without inferring a predefined objective. In a decentralised swarm, the organisation of interest often exists primarily in the relations among agents. Individual robots execute local rules and exchange information that remains invisible to an external observer; the collective can therefore be read through changes in density, alignment, synchrony, spatial distribution, transitions between behavioural regimes, and the evolving relations among agents. Embodiment and context further shape this reading through scale, morphology, sound, appearance, and spatial framing. Existing work already indicates that collective-behaviour cues can be more informative than trajectory-level cues for swarm legibility in goal-oriented tasks [19], and that spatial distribution and density influence perceived agency in embodied swarms [20]. Human–swarm transparency research has mainly addressed operators interacting through dedicated interfaces [21, 22], whereas public-facing observers must make sense of the collective from its behaviour alone. In parallel, expressive-motion approaches based on Laban analysis [23], animation pipelines [24], or generative models [25] have largely focused on individual robots. How expressive intent can be observed, composed, and iteratively refined at the level of a decentralised collective therefore remains comparatively unexplored, particularly outside artistic research-creation settings [26, 27].

To investigate these two gaps together, we draw on DESSAIM, an interdisciplinary research-creation project bringing together artists and roboticists to develop and stage expressive collective behaviours. The project brought together three robotic swarms spanning markedly different physical scales: tabletop Sushis, aerial CrazyCognies, and human-scale mobile manipulators, the Doodies (Sec. 4.1.1). Across these systems, the same Buzz behavioural code [28] was deployed through PyBuzz, a software stack that confines platform-specific sensing and actuation to adapter layers (Sec. 4.1.2). This common representation enabled comparison of how the same collective behaviours were physically realised across embodiments, while exposing a limitation of platform abstraction: parameters expressed in controller steps may retain their numerical values without preserving their physical timescales.

On the perceptual side, DESSAIM adopted an iterative research-creation process combining behaviour composition, transitions between swarm states, Movement Observation–Analysis (MOA) [29], embodiment, scenography, sound, and repeated public presentations and surveys. These elements were co-designed rather than manipulated as independent experimental factors, forming a coupled expressive design space through which artists and roboticists could observe how collective motion was interpreted and guide subsequent revisions. Audience questionnaires and open-ended responses collected across successive performances provide complementary evidence of how meaning, affect, agency, and collective organisation were attributed differently to the three embodiments. In particular, the results indicate that meaning attribution and affect need not vary together: collective motion may be interpreted as meaningful while simultaneously eliciting feelings of discomfort or threat.

The purpose of this work is therefore narrower than a general report on field
deployment, but broader than the validation of a software framework. PyBuzz,
localisation, communication, and cross-platform behavioural analysis are used
here as engineering instruments for exposing the simulation-to-deployment gap
rather than as the subject of a standalone software contribution. Conversely,
the artistic practices are not treated as an art-theoretical endpoint, but as
methods for interrogating how collective robotic motion is composed, observed,
and interpreted. Public performance provides an ecological testbed in which
these concerns meet: the swarm must remain technically coherent under changing
physical conditions while also remaining available to human perception and
interpretation.

Taken together, the study combines a quantitative cross-platform
characterisation of shared swarm behaviours, localisation results under
performance constraints, and audience-perception data with a two-axis
methodology for working on the reality and perceptual gaps. The central argument
is not that either gap has been closed, but that human-facing swarm robotics
must make both observable and actionable. Robust deployment infrastructure is
required to preserve collective organisation across embodiments; an expressive
toolkit is required to understand and shape how that organisation is perceived
and interpreted once it reaches the physical world.

authors: Seungyong Lee,Suhyeok Jang,Minyoung Kim,Jinwoo Shin

abstract:
Robot foundation models have shown remarkable performance in robot control, yet adapting them to a new task still relies heavily on teleoperated demonstrations.
Egocentric human videos offer a scalable substitute, but overlaying rendered robots on human videos or retargeting human poses into robot actions leaves significant visual or action gaps for high-DoF robot embodiments.
To address this limitation, we propose RoboTryOn, which treats human-to-robot translation as virtual try-on: try-on keeps the person and swaps the garment, RoboTryOn keeps the demonstrated motion and swaps the human for the robot.
Specifically, RoboTryOn converts a human video into a video of the target robot specified by a reference image, while preserving the original task, objects, and background. To maintain visual consistency, we translate selected keyframes autoregressively and use them to guide video synthesis with motion conditioned on the human hand skeleton.
Additionally, we use an inverse dynamics model (IDM) that incorporates depth features to infer action labels from synthesized videos for policy learning.
Our experiments across multiple humanoid embodiments show that policies trained with our synthetic data improve the average success rate on novel tasks, including challenging bimanual manipulation, from 2% to 60%, without any real robot demonstration of those tasks.
Moreover, training with our synthetic data matches the performance of policies trained solely on teleoperated demonstrations at approximately a third of the collection cost, demonstrating the cost efficiency of our approach.
introduction:
Robot foundation models trained on large-scale demonstrations have made
substantial progress toward general-purpose robot control
(Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024; Octo Model Team et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025a; NVIDIA et al., 2025; Black et al., 2025),
while extending them to new tasks and environments still requires additional
robot demonstrations
(Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024; Khazatsky et al., 2024; Bu et al., 2025). Collecting such
demonstrations through teleoperation requires robot hardware, a
teleoperation system, and substantial operator effort
(Zhao et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024; Chi et al., 2024; Khazatsky et al., 2024). The
burden is heaviest for dexterous hands, where operators must
coordinate many degrees of freedom and fine-grained contacts through
retargeting interfaces that are challenging to develop and operate
(Handa et al., 2020; Qin et al., 2023; Cheng et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025).

Alternatively, human videos offer another way to demonstrate a new task.
In particular, egocentric recordings of human object manipulation already exist at internet scale and far outnumber the demonstrations teleoperation can produce, ranging from in-the-wild collections to manually annotated corpora recorded for robot learning (Goyal et al., 2017; Shan et al., 2020; Damen et al., 2022; Grauman et al., 2022; Grauman et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2022; Hoque et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Punamiya et al., 2026).
They capture how people grasp and manipulate objects, including coordinated bimanual interaction, without a robot during collection. Recent works use these videos to learn transferable visual and behavioral knowledge (Nair et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025; Dyna Robotics, 2026), or convert them into robot data through retargeting (Kareer et al., 2025), rendering (Lepert et al., 2025b; Lepert et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026), or generative translation (Song et al., 2025; Ci et al., 2025).

However, a human video is separated from a robot demonstration by a
visual gap and an action gap, and both are severe for dexterous hands
(Liu et al., 2025b; Punamiya et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026).
In terms of appearance, human videos show a human arm and hand, whereas the policy observes a robot at deployment. Prior work narrows this gap by masking the human arm or
overlaying a rendered robot, and must apply the same edit to the
robot’s camera stream during both training and deployment
(Kareer et al., 2025; Lepert et al., 2025b; Lepert et al., 2025a).
In terms of action, the reconstructed hand pose is itself imprecise, and no exact retargeting map takes it to robot joint commands, since human and robot hands differ in morphology and kinematics (Handa et al., 2020; Qin et al., 2023; Kong et al., 2026).
Even a perfect mapping would reproduce only the shape of the hand, not how firmly the robot must grip the object (Chen et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026).

Our approach.
We address these gaps by treating human-to-robot transfer as virtual
try-on, which keeps the motion and changes the embodiment. RoboTryOn converts a human manipulation video into a paired robot demonstration
with action labels. To this end, we first generate a target robot video
performing the same task in the source scene and then predict the
corresponding joint-space actions with an inverse dynamics model (IDM),
rather than deriving robot actions directly from reconstructed hand
motion. As in keyframe-based video virtual try-on (Zuo et al., 2025), we
autoregressively translate selected human frames into robot keyframes,
and synthesize the motion between consecutive keyframes under the
guidance of the human hand skeleton flow.
Our generative models learn this translation from robot videos through a shared arm mask and hand skeleton interface, allowing the same conditions to be extracted from human videos at inference without paired human and robot demonstrations. We then train a policy on the synthesized robot demonstrations, enabling the robot to learn new tasks with few or no teleoperated demonstrations.

Our experiments show that RoboTryOn consistently improves policy
performance when task-specific robot demonstrations are limited or
unavailable. In particular, averaged over two robot embodiments, RoboTryOn increases the success rate from 2.1% to 60.0% on out-of-domain tasks with goals, skills, and objects unseen in real robot
demonstrations. It also achieves 45.9% on challenging bimanual tasks
despite all teleoperated demonstrations containing only single-arm
manipulation. Finally, training with
demonstrations derived from human video matches the performance of
training on teleoperated demonstrations alone while requiring approximately a third
of the collection cost (see Figure 6).

We summarize our main contributions below:

We introduce RoboTryOn, which turns an egocentric human video into a
robot demonstration the way virtual try-on swaps a garment, with
generative models trained on robot data alone.

We show that our synthetic data bridge the visual and
action gaps in human videos, removing the need for test-time visual editing and generating better action labels than retargeted actions.

Through experiments on two real robots with dexterous hands over diverse out-of-domain tasks, we demonstrate that our synthesized demonstrations enable learning tasks without teleoperated demonstrations and reduce data collection costs relative to teleoperation.

1. We introduce RoboTryOn, which turns an egocentric human video into a
robot demonstration the way virtual try-on swaps a garment, with
generative models trained on robot data alone.

2. We show that our synthetic data bridge the visual and
action gaps in human videos, removing the need for test-time visual editing and generating better action labels than retargeted actions.

3. Through experiments on two real robots with dexterous hands over diverse out-of-domain tasks, we demonstrate that our synthesized demonstrations enable learning tasks without teleoperated demonstrations and reduce data collection costs relative to teleoperation.

title: Asynchronous Robot Policies
authors: Sombit Dey,Luc Van Gool,Danda Pani Paudel
comment: For code, checkpoints and more results, check outthis https URL
abstract:
Scaling vision-language foundation models has significantly advanced generalist robot manipulation, but the increased model scale introduces computational latency that degrades real-time physical reactivity.
Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures execute high-level semantic reasoning and action execution sequentially within the primary control loop, creating a fundamental tension between semantic-reasoning capability and robot agility.
To address this, we propose Asynchronous Robot Policy (ARP), an architectural framework that decouples semantic reasoning from low-level action generation using asynchronous processes operating at independent frequencies.
In ARP, a high-capacity Vision-Language Model (VLM) asynchronously updates a semantic memory at low frequency, while a lightweight Vision-Action Expert, conditioned on this semantic memory, generates robot actions at a much higher control frequency.
Such a formulation, enables having a fast perception-action loop without compromising on the semantic capability.
To overcome asynchronous memory staleness, ARP trains the vision-action expert on the semantic staleness and execution delay, with temporally mismatched observation across processes.
introduction:
Scaling has become the dominant paradigm of modern artificial intelligence (Kaplan et al., 2020).
However, scaling model size incurs a fundamental trade-off: increased capability at the cost of higher computational latency and degrading real-time responsiveness.
While higher latency may be tolerable in static or text-based applications, it presents a critical failure mode in robotics.
Physical robotics requires tight perception-action loops to handle real-time contact dynamics and sudden environmental shifts, such as grasping falling objects or absorbing unexpected bumps.

Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) (Brohan et al., 2022; Zitkovich et al., 2023) models fall victim to this bottleneck, creating a persistent tension between model capability, computational overhead, and closed-loop reactivity.
Consequently, scaling the vision-language backbone improves high-level reasoning at the expense of motor agility, yielding a system that is semantically rich but physically lag-bound and depends on open-loop deployment.
To resolve this friction, we propose Asynchronous Robot Policies (ARP). As illustrated in Fig. 1(b), ARP breaks the reactivity-capability trade-off, enabling the seamless integration of significantly larger foundational models into robot pipelines without significantly compromising dynamic reactivity or real-time performance.

Existing generalist VLA policies execute the vision-language foundation model and the action expert sequentially within the primary control loop. Their latencies therefore add up, giving a total perception-to-action latency of tVLM+tAEt_{\text{VLM}}+t_{\text{AE}}, as shown in Fig. 1(a). In contrast, ARP decouples VLM and action expert into asynchronous processes running at different frequencies. The VLM operates at a lower frequency f1f_{1} for high-level semantic reasoning, while a compact vision-action expert operates at a higher frequency f2≫f1f_{2}\gg f_{1}.
Under ARP, the effective perception-action loop latency is strictly reduced to the expert execution time (tVA-Et_{\text{VA-E}}), so that control reactivity no longer grows linearly with the VLM scale. Importantly, this decoupling allows ARP to benefit from larger, more capable VLMs while maintaining reactivity, as shown in Fig. 1 (b).

Making robot policies asynchronous, however, introduces several new challenges. The fast action expert must continuously act on a compact semantic memory produced by a slower VLM, while the robot state evolves during both VLM and action expert inference. This creates two sources of mismatch: the semantic memory may be stale relative to the current observation, and newly predicted actions may arrive after execution has already progressed. Performing the two loops asynchronously can therefore lead to outdated conditioning, delayed actions, and discontinuities across replanning cycles. ARP addresses these challenges by compressing rich VLM activations into fixed-width asynchronous memory, explicitly conditioning the action expert on semantic staleness and execution delay, and training with temporally mismatched memories and action-prefix conditioning to support smooth continuous replanning.

Asynchronous paradigms have been explored in prior work, mainly for cloud-to-edge VLA deployment, extending the action expert’s contextual history, or smoothing execution through asynchronous action chunking (Hirose et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026; Tang et al., 2025; Black et al., 2025).
However, these approaches still retain dependencies on the main model pipeline.
To our knowledge, ARP is the first truly asynchronous robotic control framework, where one can vary the rate of two processes, featuring an autonomous Vision-Action Expert. This expert is capable of executing high-frequency reactive motor commands independently while continuously synthesizing semantic updates from the asynchronous VLM.

Evaluated on quasi-static Franka robot manipulation tasks, ARP achieves an 18% higher success rate while taking 20% less time than conventional VLA baselines.
In dynamic environments, ARP achieves 3-5×\times the performance of the baseline, successfully handling target perturbations where synchronous policies fail.
Furthermore, ARP reduces computational demand by running the VLM at 10×\times lower frequency with no significant loss in performance owing to the asynchronous nature of ARP.
These results indicate that ARP offers a viable blueprint for bridging the gap between large-scale semantic reasoning and agile physical control.

title: WayTrace: A Map-to-Language-to-Trace Hierarchy for Embodied Urban Navigation
authors: Manthan Patel,Jonas Frey,Pascal Roth,Marco Hutter,Cesar Cadena
comment: Under Review
abstract:
Web services provide walking directions for nearly every city, but following them reliably over long routes remains
challenging for autonomous robots. Point-goal navigation policies rely heavily on accurate GNSS, while most vision-language
navigation models struggle to execute even short instructions outdoors. We present WayTrace, a hierarchical system that connects
web-map directions to robot motion through language. An off-the-shelf orchestrator vision-language model reads the
turn-by-turn directions, a satellite map and recent camera images, and issues one atomic language command at a time, such as
“cross the road to the left”. An onboard trace predictor, trained on over one million automatically labelled samples from street-level images, draws the path for this command in the image, and a reinforcement learning policy tracks it. In long-range
simulated missions, WayTrace remains robust to GNSS noise and rarely leaves crosswalks or sidewalks, while point-goal
baselines degrade sharply with about ten times more violations. Deployed on a wheeled-legged robot, WayTrace completes
real-world missions of up to 1.37 km at about 1.1 m/s through a busy city centre, rural trails and a university
campus, handling crosswalks, staircases and construction sites.
Project page: https://way-trace.github.io
introduction:
Humans navigate unfamiliar cities with little effort. Given a destination, a person consults a web map
and follows its turn-by-turn directions, such as continuing along a sidewalk, turning onto a crosswalk or taking the stairs. Neither a metric goal nor precise position is required. The map indicates the next manoeuvre and its
approximate location, while vision resolves where the crosswalk begins and when a turn has been completed.
Since web maps provide such directions for nearly every place where people walk, a robot that follows them in the same manner
could be deployed in any city given only a destination and without a prior mapping run, enabling applications such as
last-mile delivery, urban inspection and guidance of visually impaired people.

Existing learned navigation methods fall short of this goal over long routes.
Point-goal methods [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] receive the route as a sequence of GNSS waypoints, and their performance is therefore bounded by the accuracy of the position estimate.
In cities, GNSS errors of several metres are common [6], enough to place a waypoint on the road or on the opposite side of the street, and over routes of several hundred metres such errors inevitably lead to failures.
Waypoints also carry no notion of the social norms, such as staying on the sidewalk and crossing at crosswalks, so a policy that reaches every waypoint may still violate them and pose a safety risk in urban traffic.

Vision-language navigation (VLN) replaces coordinates with natural-language instructions,
but it has been studied predominantly in simulated indoor environments [7, 8] and on street-view panoramas [9].
Recent models bring vision-language navigation to real
robots [10, 11, 12, 13], but they are typically demonstrated on single instructions over short distances.
We find that these models are brittle even at the level of a single atomic
instruction (Section V-D), which makes it infeasible to follow a kilometre-long route by chaining such instructions.

In this work, we simplify the problem. Web-map directions already decompose a route into a sequence of atomic instructions, each describing a single manoeuvre such as “cross the road” that can be grounded in the camera image.
Long-range navigation thus separates into deciding which atomic instruction applies at the current moment and executing that instruction reliably.
The first problem requires the map and contextual reasoning but only a coarse position, since GNSS is needed only to identify the current step of the route rather than the exact position of the robot.
The second problem requires only the camera and a short observation history.
Language is a suitable interface between the two
levels, since it is what web maps produce and what vision-language models (VLMs) reason in.
Based on this observation, we propose WayTrace, a map-to-language-to-trace hierarchy ().
An off-the-shelf orchestrator VLM reads the web-map directions, a satellite map of the surroundings and the recent camera images, and issues the next atomic
command. An onboard trace predictor draws the path for this command in image space, and a reinforcement learning (RL) policy tracks the path lifted to 3D.

We evaluate WayTrace on ten long-range missions in a simulated Zurich old town and in real-world deployments. With
perfect GNSS, WayTrace completes 83 % of the missions. It achieves the highest success rate at every level of GNSS
error, and its success rate decreases gradually to 63 % with a drifting GNSS error of 7 m RMS, whereas that of point-goal
baselines drops below 25 % and they leave the crosswalk or the sidewalk about ten times as often. Vision-language baselines complete
at most 7 % of the missions, even with language commands from a tuned oracle. In the real world, WayTrace completed
three missions of up to 426 m through a busy city centre fully autonomously, and a 1.37 km mission along rural trails
and through a university campus with two short operator interventions. The main contributions of this work are as
follows.

WayTrace, a hierarchical navigation framework that translates web-map directions into atomic language commands
and executes them as image-space traces.

A language-conditioned trace predictor together with an automatic labelling pipeline that produces most of its
training data from unlabelled street-level image sequences.

An extensive evaluation against point-goal and vision-language navigation baselines in simulation, an analysis of each
component and real-world deployments on a wheeled-legged robot.

1. WayTrace, a hierarchical navigation framework that translates web-map directions into atomic language commands
and executes them as image-space traces.

2. A language-conditioned trace predictor together with an automatic labelling pipeline that produces most of its
training data from unlabelled street-level image sequences.

3. An extensive evaluation against point-goal and vision-language navigation baselines in simulation, an analysis of each
component and real-world deployments on a wheeled-legged robot.

title: DexHOT: Learning Hand-Object Configuration Transfer for Dexterous Manipulation
authors: Zhewei Gui,Anthony Bolton,Jiyao Zhang,Zeyuan Chen,Qiyang Yan,Tianyu Wang,Hao Dong
abstract:
Dexterous manipulation involves not only moving objects, but also arranging the hand around them to maintain useful contacts and enable subsequent actions. Yet many learning-based systems specify goals primarily through object poses or trajectories, leaving hand–object configurations to emerge implicitly. We introduce DexHOT, which formulates dexterous manipulation as hand–object configuration transfer: moving between feasible configurations that jointly specify hand articulation and object pose relative to the wrist. DexHOT learns a reusable relation-conditioned transfer primitive from synthetic feasible configuration pairs, without human reference motions, and composes long-horizon behaviors through closed-loop tracking of configuration subgoals. On DexHOTBench with 120 objects, a single policy achieves 80.5% transfer success on seen objects and 69.4% on unseen objects; on a real dexterous hand, it achieves 61.5% success over 200 real-robot transfers and 90% task success across six demonstration-guided tasks. These results show that explicit hand–object goals provide an expressive and composable interface for dexterous manipulation.
More details and videos are available at https://dex-hot.github.io/.
introduction:
Dexterous manipulation depends on both object motion and hand arrangement.
A mug held by its rim, handle, or body can have the same pose, yet differ in stability, functionality, and subsequent manipulation options.
Object-state goals cannot express these differences.

Recent learned systems span increasingly complex capabilities, from dexterous grasping [1, 2, 3] and task-specific in-hand reorientation [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10] to tool manipulation [11] and more general dexterous skills [12, 13, 14], together with robust sim-to-real transfer under challenging contact dynamics [15, 16, 17, 18, 19].
Many use target object orientations or pose trajectories.
These compact goals make learning tractable but leave the hand–object relation implicit: hand configurations reaching the same object goal can differ substantially in usefulness for subsequent interaction.

This limitation becomes particularly important in long-horizon manipulation.
Regrasping, tool use, and functional interaction often require intermediate hand–object configurations that enable the next phase of the task [20, 21, 22, 23].
Contact-switching behaviors such as finger gaiting [24] can emerge in object-goal systems [4, 7, 18], but the goal does not explicitly prescribe the resulting hand configuration, and discovering these behaviors through exploration remains challenging [25].

We therefore formulate dexterous manipulation as hand–object configuration transfer.
A configuration specifies the hand articulation together with the object pose relative to the wrist, and a transfer seeks to move from one feasible configuration to another.
This changes the unit of goal-conditioned control from an object state to a hand–object relation, allowing both object motion and the resulting hand configuration to be specified explicitly.

Based on this formulation, we present DexHOT, a framework for learning reusable hand–object configuration transfer (Fig. ).
DexHOT is built on the idea that long-range in-hand transfers can be composed from short, locally reachable transfers.
We synthesize diverse pools of physically feasible configurations, train a single relation-conditioned controller using local-goal sampling and population-based reinforcement learning (RL), and reuse it through hierarchical chaining of configuration subgoals.
The resulting controller exhibits dexterous skills such as finger gaiting and finger pivoting without planner-guided rollouts, an explicit exploration manifold, or skill-specific supervision during training.

To evaluate configuration transfer directly, we introduce DexHOTBench, comprising 120 objects with physically validated configuration pools and fixed transfer pairs spanning different distances.
The 80 held-out objects contain 40 unseen objects from training categories and 40 objects from unseen categories.
A single policy achieves 73.1% success averaged over close and far transfers of all 120 objects, with 80.5% on seen and 69.4% on held-out objects, and 61.5% success over 200 real-robot transfers spanning seen and unseen objects.

Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce Hand–Object Configuration Transfer (HOT), a dexterous manipulation formulation in which goals explicitly specify both hand articulation and the relative hand–object pose.

We develop DexHOT, which learns a reusable configuration-transfer controller across objects from local feasible transfers and composes it into long-range and long-horizon dexterous behaviors. DexHOT exhibits emergent finger gaiting and finger pivoting and outperforms prior methods on demonstration-guided tasks.

We introduce DexHOTBench, a 120-object benchmark for configuration transfer, and demonstrate generalization to held-out objects together with zero-shot transfer to real-robot manipulation.

1. We introduce Hand–Object Configuration Transfer (HOT), a dexterous manipulation formulation in which goals explicitly specify both hand articulation and the relative hand–object pose.

2. We develop DexHOT, which learns a reusable configuration-transfer controller across objects from local feasible transfers and composes it into long-range and long-horizon dexterous behaviors. DexHOT exhibits emergent finger gaiting and finger pivoting and outperforms prior methods on demonstration-guided tasks.

3. We introduce DexHOTBench, a 120-object benchmark for configuration transfer, and demonstrate generalization to held-out objects together with zero-shot transfer to real-robot manipulation.
