title: Physics-Based Plausibility Assessment of AI-Predicted Vehicle Parameters for Automotive Radar in Pre-Crash Scenarios
authors: Rainer Engert,Patrick Zaumseil,Thomas Brandmeier
abstract:
Automotive radar is a key sensing modality for safety-critical vehicle functions due to its robustness under adverse weather and lighting conditions. Recent advances in  ai (ai)-based radar perception enable the direct estimation of object parameters from a single radar measurement cycle. However, the internal decision process of data-driven models is typically not explicitly linked to the underlying radar sensing physics. Consequently, object estimates may achieve high statistical accuracy while remaining physically inconsistent with the measured radar signature, particularly in previously unseen scenarios. Such inconsistencies are especially critical for heading estimation, as they directly affect trajectory prediction and collision assessment in pre-crash scenarios.
This paper presents a physics-based consistency assessment framework for validating ai-derived vehicle hypotheses in automotive radar perception. The proposed approach generates an expected radar signature from ai-estimated object parameters using a physics-based reference model that incorporates occlusion-dependent edge visibility, aspect- and angle-dependent  rcs (rcs) modeling, and characteristic wheel-induced  md (md) signatures. The expected signature is compared with the observed radar point cloud using a Wasserstein-distance-based consistency metric computed from three complementary features: the spatial distribution of detections along object edges, the local detection count, and the radar reflection intensity. In this way, physically implausible object hypotheses can be identified and corrected independently of the underlying neural network architecture and without model retraining or architectural modifications. The proposed consistency module is integrated as a cascaded post-processing stage for vehicle heading estimation. Experimental evaluation on 11921192 real automotive radar frames demonstrates a statistically significant improvement of approximately 𝟏𝟗 %19\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} in heading accuracy compared to the ai-only baseline. The results indicate that physics-based consistency assessment of ai-derived object hypotheses can effectively reduce large heading errors and improve the reliability and robustness of radar perception systems in safety-critical automotive applications.
introduction:
The ongoing integration of driver assistance and automated driving functions is expected to contribute to an increasingly heterogeneous traffic environment. As a result, vehicles with different levels of automation will operate alongside manually driven vehicles and other traffic participants, leading to more complex interaction patterns and dynamic traffic situations [1]. Consequently, vehicle safety systems increasingly depend on a reliable perception of surrounding traffic participants and their motion patterns. This is particularly important for traffic safety and pre-crash applications, which impose stringent end-to-end latency requirements while requiring highly dependable prediction and decision-making capabilities [2, 3, 4]. Errors in perception can propagate to downstream prediction and planning modules, ultimately degrading the safety performance of the overall driving systems [5] and can compromise collision assessment and the activation of pre-crash occupant restraint systems [6]

Among the sensing modalities used in automotive applications, radar has gained prominence due to its robustness in adverse weather and lighting conditions and its ability to provide direct measurements of object distance and relative radial velocity [7, 8, 9]. In particular, radar measurements can contain distinctive md signatures that capture object-specific motion patterns and provide additional information beyond object-related parameters such as position, velocity, orientation, and spatial extent [10, 11]. Among these parameters, the heading angle is particularly important, as it describes the object’s orientation and forms part of the vehicle state representations used for state estimation and trajectory planning [12, 13]. An erroneous heading estimate can adversely affect subsequent trajectory prediction and collision assessment algorithms, thereby impairing the performance of downstream pre-crash vehicle safety systems [14, 15]. Consequently, automated driving functions rely on continuously available and reliable object information, making accurate object state estimation safety-critical [16].

To fully exploit the rich information provided by high-resolution radar sensors, recent research has increasingly focused on data-driven radar perception approaches. Deep learning methods have demonstrated promising performance for tasks such as object detection, classification, and oriented bounding box prediction directly from radar data [17, 18]. In contrast to conventional model-based signal processing pipelines, these approaches learn task-specific feature representations from data and can capture complex relationships that are difficult to model
analytically. Their growing adoption in automotive perception pipelines, however, raises important questions regarding interpretability and functional safety [19, 20].

One major challenge is the substantial variability and complexity of real-world traffic scenarios, including rare and previously unseen situations, which cannot be exhaustively captured during development and validation [21]. Even with comprehensive training data, previously unseen variations in sensing conditions, environmental conditions, and traffic scenarios may arise during deployment, potentially degrading model performance in ways not captured by offline evaluation metrics [22, 23]. This issue is particularly relevant for radar sensing, where measurements are generated through electromagnetic wave propagation and are influenced by a variety of physical effects, including multipath propagation [24], target-dependent reflection behavior [25], coherent interference effects [26], partial occlusions, and overlapping object responses. As a result, the measured radar response of the same target may vary considerably with small changes in aspect angle, target distance, and other influencing factors, posing challenges for robust radar perception [7, 27]. This motivates an additional assessment of whether ai-estimated object parameters, particularly the heading angle, are physically consistent with the radar response generated by the corresponding object.

To address this, the present work introduces a physics-based plausibility module implemented as a post-processing stage downstream of the object estimation network. The module interprets ai-derived object parameters as physical hypotheses and validates them against radar-specific characteristics of the measured point cloud, providing an additional supervisory layer for data-driven perception systems. Physically inconsistent estimates are identified and corrected before they propagate to downstream processing stages, thereby enhancing the reliability of subsequent vehicle safety functions and improving the robustness of ai-based radar estimation in safety-critical automotive scenarios.

The proposed method evaluates whether ai-estimated object parameters are physically consistent with the observed radar response. This requires both a model of how object properties are reflected in radar measurements and a framework for assessing the resulting signatures for plausibility. The following section reviews related work from physics-based radar signature modeling and ai model validation and discusses why existing approaches do not directly address the problem of runtime plausibility assessment.

Automotive radar simulation models differ substantially in their level of abstraction, computational complexity, and electromagnetic fidelity, ranging from simplified object-level sensor models to high-fidelity ray-tracing and full electromagnetic propagation models. Magosi et al. [28] provide a systematic classification of automotive radar sensor models and show that different validation tasks require different levels of model abstraction.

Early approaches approximate vehicle geometries using virtual scattering centers extracted from ray-tracing simulations [29], thereby enabling efficient approximation of their scattering characteristics. The virtual scattering centers are generated by clustering ray-tracing-derived scattering centers using a greedy algorithm rather than by explicitly modeling individual vehicle components.

Semi-physical models extend this by incorporating sensor-specific effects such as range, velocity, angle, detection probability, and rcs-dependent reflection behavior. Guo et al. [30]
and Li et al. [31] combine geometric object representations with sensor-specific uncertainty models, while Magosi and Eichberger [32] propose a modular, component-based model with dedicated wheel components to increase simulation realism.

High-fidelity approaches further increase physical realism through ray tracing,  sbr (sbr) techniques, or full-scene propagation models. Chipengo et al. [33, 34] generate synthetic radar responses of complete traffic scenes using sbr, explicitly distinguishing their approach from simplified point-scatterer models that inadequately capture wave propagation and multipath interactions. Thieling et al. [35] propose a scalable GPU-based ray-tracing architecture for dynamic 33D scenes, while Schüßler [36]
demonstrates an sbr-based simulator for high-resolution automotive MIMO radars. Haider et al. [37] present a ray-tracing-based  fmcw (fmcw) radar sensor model that incorporates  mimo (mimo) signal processing and sensor-specific non-idealities, such as phase noise and mixer nonlinearity. More generally, Magosi [38] emphasizes that the architecture and capabilities of radar sensor models should be selected according to the respective development phase.

Several studies specifically investigate md signatures arising from rotating wheels and moving vehicle components, demonstrating that radar observations are determined not only by object position and extent but also by aspect angle, component visibility, scattering characteristics, and motion-induced Doppler effects [39, 40, 41, 10, 42]. In the automotive context, component-oriented sensor models incorporate dedicated wheel models with associated md signatures to reproduce wheel-specific radar phenomena [32].

However, most existing radar simulation approaches are designed for sensor validation, synthetic data generation, or target classification, and they generate radar measurements from known simulated scenes rather than evaluating predicted object hypotheses against observed data. This distinction motivates the second research area reviewed below.

Despite the growing deployment of ai-based perception in autonomous systems, runtime monitoring and safety assurance of  dnn (dnn)-based perception remain active challenges [43]. Due to their black-box nature, dnn often lack transparency, raising concerns regarding reliability, trustworthiness, and safety, particularly in safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving [44]. Prior research has examined the vulnerability of deep learning models to adversarially perturbed inputs [45, 46], and robustness benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate neural networks under realistic corruptions and perturbations [47].

In radar-based perception, adverse weather conditions, multipath reflections, and ghost objects can significantly degrade data quality and reduce the  snr (snr) [48, 24], while fluctuations in rcs may further destabilize object detection. These sensor-specific effects motivate the use of  xai (xai) methods to improve the interpretability of deep learning models and to better understand the decision-making process and validate model predictions [49, 50, 51].

Beyond performance-based evaluation, recent research emphasizes the importance of validating machine learning models against physical principles and domain knowledge. Furthermore, physics-informed machine learning models incorporate physical constraints and prior knowledge into the learning process to promote physically consistent, plausible, and trustworthy model predictions [52, 53, 54]. In autonomous driving, recent work has shown that conventional accuracy metrics alone are insufficient to assess trajectory prediction quality, as learning-based models may generate physically infeasible trajectories. Consequently, physically infeasible metrics have been introduced as a complementary evaluation criterion to account for physically infeasible outputs from learning-based models [55].

More recently, runtime monitoring and validation of ai-based perception systems have emerged as an active research direction. Rahman et al. [56] survey runtime monitoring approaches for machine learning in robotic perception, arguing that design-time verification alone is insufficient for unknown deployment environments and that continuous runtime assessment of reliability is necessary. Keser et al. [57] propose an interpretable, model-agnostic plausibility verification framework for 22D object detectors based on domain-invariant concept bottleneck models, enabling operation-time plausibility checks without requiring access to the detector’s internal representations. Aslam et al. [58] propose a function monitor for the runtime validation of camera- and LiDAR-based ai perception, addressing the lack of complete requirements specifications assumed by ISO 26 26226\,262 and ISO 21 44821\,448.

Existing validation approaches, however, are predominantly applied offline against labeled datasets and do not enable frame-level plausibility evaluation of individual object hypotheses at runtime. The present work addresses this gap by using physics-based radar modeling as a hypothesis-conditioned reference. The ai-predicted object position, dimensions, and heading are used to generate an expected radar signature, which is then compared with the observed radar point cloud via Wasserstein distances to assess the physical consistency of the prediction at runtime. Unlike existing simulation approaches, which generate measurements from known scenes, the proposed method inverts this process: it evaluates how well a predicted object hypothesis explains the observed sensor data.

The works discussed above demonstrate that physics-based radar modeling and md signature simulation have been extensively studied for radar sensor validation, data augmentation, and target classification. However, several key distinctions separate the proposed approach from existing methods.

Existing radar simulation approaches generate radar measurements from known, fully specified scenes and are designed for sensor validation, synthetic data generation, or target classification. None of the reviewed approaches use a predicted object hypothesis to construct an expected radar signature and evaluate it against an observed point cloud at runtime. The direction of inference is inverted in the proposed method: rather than simulating what a sensor would measure given a known scene, the proposed framework assesses how well an ai-predicted object hypothesis explains the observed radar data.

Existing ai validation approaches in radar perception are predominantly applied offline, relying on labeled datasets and statistical performance metrics such as  iou (iou), precision, and recall, evaluated against ground-truth annotations. While these metrics provide a global assessment of model quality, they do not support frame-level plausibility evaluation of individual object hypotheses at runtime and are not applicable in deployment scenarios without ground truth.

Physics-informed machine learning and xai methods address model transparency and physical plausibility at the level of model internals, using gradients, feature activations, or physical constraints during training. These approaches operate at the model level and do not perform signal-level consistency checks between predicted object parameters and observed radar measurements during inference.

The proposed method addresses all three gaps simultaneously. An expected radar signature is constructed directly from the ai-predicted object hypothesis, including position, dimensions, and heading angle, using a physics-based reference model that accounts for occlusion-dependent edge visibility, aspect- and angle-dependent rcs variations, characteristic wheel-induced md signatures, and the resulting spatial distribution, intensity, and density of radar detections. The expected signature is then compared with the observed radar point cloud using a Wasserstein-distance-based score to perform a frame-level physical-consistency assessment, independently of the ai model’s internal structure and without requiring retraining or architectural modifications.

The primary objective of this work is therefore to introduce a physics-based consistency assessment framework for validating ai-derived vehicle hypotheses in automotive radar perception. Its main contributions are:

A physics-based radar signature generation model that constructs expected radar signatures from ai-derived vehicle object parameters, thereby enabling the physical validation of individual object hypotheses from a single radar observation. The model combines geometric visibility constraints, aspect-dependent scattering characteristics, velocity-dependent Doppler effects, and detection-density modeling to represent the expected spatial, intensity, velocity, and detection-count distributions of radar observations.

A neural-network-independent physical consistency assessment that compares expected and observed radar signatures using a Wasserstein-distance-based metric. In contrast to conventional prediction confidence measures, the proposed method evaluates whether ai-derived object hypotheses are physically supported by the measured radar response and identifies physically implausible object estimates.

A cascaded post-processing framework for radar-based vehicle estimation that refines ai-derived heading estimates without retraining the model or modifying the architecture. Experimental evaluation on real automotive radar data demonstrates a statistically significant improvement of approximately 19 %19\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} compared to the ai-only baseline.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section II describes the two-stage radar-based object detection pipeline, covering the radar signal processing chain and the adopted ComplexYOLO detector. Section III presents the physics-based assessment framework, including the geometric data association, the physical model, and the rotation-based heading correction. Section IV describes the experimental setup, including the radar sensor configuration, the empirical model parameters, and the validation and test datasets used for evaluation. Section V reports the quantitative and qualitative evaluation of the proposed approach on both validation and test data. Section VI interprets the results in the broader context of radar-based vehicle perception and discusses the identified limitations. Finally, Section VII summarizes the key findings and outlines directions for future work.

1. A physics-based radar signature generation model that constructs expected radar signatures from ai-derived vehicle object parameters, thereby enabling the physical validation of individual object hypotheses from a single radar observation. The model combines geometric visibility constraints, aspect-dependent scattering characteristics, velocity-dependent Doppler effects, and detection-density modeling to represent the expected spatial, intensity, velocity, and detection-count distributions of radar observations.

2. A neural-network-independent physical consistency assessment that compares expected and observed radar signatures using a Wasserstein-distance-based metric. In contrast to conventional prediction confidence measures, the proposed method evaluates whether ai-derived object hypotheses are physically supported by the measured radar response and identifies physically implausible object estimates.

3. A cascaded post-processing framework for radar-based vehicle estimation that refines ai-derived heading estimates without retraining the model or modifying the architecture. Experimental evaluation on real automotive radar data demonstrates a statistically significant improvement of approximately 19 %19\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} compared to the ai-only baseline.

title: PrimeSim: A Generalist World Model Simulator from Large-Scale Cross-Embodiment Demonstrations
authors: Travis Davies,Wentao Ma,Lihao Guo,Tengfei Ma,Xiaowen Chang,Jiafeng Xu,Shilong Wang,Yiqi Deng,Shaowen He,Xiaoqi Li,Qian Zhu,Ran Cheng,Hao Dong
abstract:
A robot world model that serves as a simulator must do more than generate plausible videos: it must faithfully follow commanded actions, maintain consistency across camera views, and sustain coherent long-horizon rollouts.
We present PrimeSim, an action-conditioned, multiview world model simulator that addresses these challenges through progressive midtraining and posttraining.
Starting from a pretrained video generator, we midtrain on 30,110 hours of robot demonstrations spanning 22 platforms.
To improve action following, we introduce a unified cross-embodiment action representation and frame-aligned dual-path conditioning to strengthen action–frame correspondence.
To maintain multiview consistency, we develop view-aware interleaved attention with explicit camera identities, enabling cross-view information exchange while preserving view-specific representations.
We further introduce a fast-video, slow-memory posttraining framework that transforms the bidirectional video generator into an efficient autoregressive simulator.
By combining fast causal generation, self-rollout training, and hierarchical temporal memory, PrimeSim mitigates error accumulation from self-generated histories and supports coherent long-horizon simulation.
PrimeSim runs at 10.1 FPS, remains stable over long-horizon rollouts on rigid and deformable manipulation tasks, and transfers to held-out platforms within 100 to 200 gradient steps where the pretrained backbone does not.
Against five open-source action-conditioned world models it leads four of the five WorldSimProbe suites and posts the best overall EWMBench score, while fine-grained local calibration still trails the field; its rollouts are faithful enough to support GRPO-based policy optimization.
We release the model weights, inference code, and training code.
introduction:
A world model that renders the consequences of a policy’s actions can serve as a
simulator: rollouts become parallel, repeatable, and free of the risk of damaging
hardware. This sidesteps both the danger and the sample cost of online training
on real hardware [43, 64, 65, 61], and avoids the sim-to-real
gap [34, 19] and the per-environment engineering that
hand-built physics simulators demand. The idea runs from model-based
reinforcement learning, where agents learn from imagined rollouts alone
[30, 31, 32, 79], through interactive video generation
for games and open-ended worlds [4, 7, 23, 73, 55, 66, 20], to action-conditioned robot world models
[29, 25, 50, 26]. What such a model
must do is narrower than generating plausible video: it must adhere to the actions

title: Coordinating Humanoid Loco-Manipulation through Action-Conditioned Latent Foresight
authors: Ju Dong,Xinyu Xiao,Yiming Zhou,Tianshuo Yang,Xuerong Liu,Lei Zhang,Jian Chen,Haocheng Zhao,Yu Fu,Yujie Wei,Diwen Zheng,Alois Christian Knoll,Angela P. Schoellig,Ping Luo,Jianwei Zhang
comment: including supplementary material
abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated body motion and hand interaction over time, and a plausible-looking command sequence can still drop a held object or leave an interaction incomplete. We present action-conditioned latent foresight, a latent world–action model (WAM) that evaluates proposed command sequences before execution. An action generator proposes joint motion–hand command sequences from vision, language, and the robot state. An action-conditioned endpoint predictor estimates the visual features each sequence prefix reaches and measures progress toward a demonstration-derived subgoal, while a joint temporal prior scores temporal consistency given the robot state and preceding commands. The robot executes the first commands of the best-scoring sequence and replans from the next observation. During training, action consistency regularization reconstructs the first demonstrated command from observed and predicted feature changes, encouraging the predictor to retain action-relevant information. On ten tasks in the humanoid loco-manipulation simulation benchmark SIMPLE, our method achieves 89.7% average success, compared with 73.7% for Ψ0\Psi_{0} and 82.0% for DiT4DiT. On seven real-robot tasks, it achieves 85.7% under standard conditions and 65.7% under unseen object configurations, while GR00T N1.7 achieves 70.0% and 48.6%, respectively. Project page: https://ju6276.github.io/Action-Grounded-Foresight/.
introduction:
Everyday humanoid tasks require coordinated actions over time. To place a basket on a table, the robot must raise and position the basket while maintaining its grasp until the table supports it. To load a washer, it must open the door, carry a T-shirt to the drum without dropping it, and release it only once it is inside. These tasks connect whole-body motion with hand interaction: an execution decision concerns both the scene a command sequence will reach and the relationships among commands along the way.

Vision-language-action (VLA) policies generate commands from images and language instructions [1, 2, 3], while humanoid models incorporate human motion and predictive representations [4, 5, 6, 7]. When an action generator proposes several sequences, the robot must decide which one to execute. Latent world models provide predictions for goal-directed planning [8, 9]. Most world–action models use future prediction to improve command generation [10, 11, 12] rather than to compare sampled sequences before execution. Existing verifiers use VLM judgments [13, 14], while DreamTrajectory combines predicted trajectory agreement with action smoothness [15]. Two signals are relevant for evaluating proposed humanoid actions: predicted visual progress evaluates the endpoint relative to a task goal, while temporal consistency evaluates relationships among commands within the sequence.

We introduce action-conditioned latent foresight, a latent world–action model (WAM) that uses both signals for humanoid loco-manipulation (Fig. 1). An action generator proposes joint motion–hand command sequences; an action-conditioned endpoint predictor scores their visual progress toward a demonstration-derived subgoal, and a joint temporal prior scores their temporal consistency. The robot executes the first commands of the best-scoring sequence and replans from the next observation.

Our contributions are threefold:

We propose action-conditioned latent foresight, which scores generated motion–hand sequences before execution using predicted visual progress and a learned joint temporal prior.

We develop action consistency regularization for latent prediction. A training-only inverse action decoder reconstructs the first demonstrated command from both observed and predicted feature changes, encouraging the predicted features to retain information about the executed action.

We evaluate ten SIMPLE [16] simulation tasks and seven real-robot tasks, including unseen object configurations. Our method exceeds the evaluated baselines in average success; closed-loop ablations show gains from action consistency regularization and joint temporal scoring.

1. We propose action-conditioned latent foresight, which scores generated motion–hand sequences before execution using predicted visual progress and a learned joint temporal prior.

2. We develop action consistency regularization for latent prediction. A training-only inverse action decoder reconstructs the first demonstrated command from both observed and predicted feature changes, encouraging the predicted features to retain information about the executed action.

3. We evaluate ten SIMPLE [16] simulation tasks and seven real-robot tasks, including unseen object configurations. Our method exceeds the evaluated baselines in average success; closed-loop ablations show gains from action consistency regularization and joint temporal scoring.

title: CLARA: A Cognitively-Driven Clarification Framework for Grounding Ambiguous Requests
authors: Dimitrios Bekris,Marios Glytsos,Panagiotis P. Filntisis,Niki Efthymiou,George Retsinas,Petros Maragos
comment: Work conducted in early 2025
abstract: Robotics and AI systems are increasingly deploying large vision-language models (LVLMs) to follow high-level instructions, from routine household chores to more complex organizational tasks. Yet, broad directives like “clean the room” or “organize the desk” frequently omit crucial details about user preferences and specific arrangement of objects that influence the desired outcome. Without any further guidance, such models tend to overestimate their grasp of ambiguous instructions and frequently assume they have sufficient understanding despite missing important details. In this paper, we propose CLARA (Conversational cLArification for Robotic Arrangement), a cognitively-driven clarification framework that proactively elicits key information from users, in a similar fashion as humans’ clarification seeking behavior. Through targeted questioning, CLARA refines ambiguous requests into structured, detailed instructions describing precisely how objects should be organized or rearranged, according to the user’s preferences. These clarifications then guide a diffusion-based image generation pipeline, producing realistic visual renderings of the final, desired scene. This final rendering also serves as a visual confirmation of the system’s understanding from the user. Experimental results and user studies demonstrate that CLARA leads to more accurate and consistent outcomes compared to another State-of-the-Art LVLM system, highlighting the importance of interactive clarification for bridging the gap between vague directives and fully grounded task specifications.
introduction:
Robotics and intelligent systems/agents increasingly rely on large vision-language models (LVLMs) [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] to interpret and execute human instructions, in an effort to simplify tasks ranging from household chores to complex workflows[6, 7, 8, 9]. Crucial to their effectiveness is accurately grounding ambiguous high-level commands, such as “clean the room” into precise visual outcomes according to the desires of the instructor, since this can mean drastically different things based on an individual’s expectations, cultural norms, or personal preferences. Unlike structured tasks in controlled environments, everyday scenarios often involve vague instructions and considerable variation in how individuals imagine the outcomes, making the task of LVLMs more difficult to reliably translate user intent from limited textual input alone.

From a cognitive standpoint, clarification-seeking behavior is recognized as a fundamental part of how humans manage ambiguous information. Conversation is viewed as a cooperative, joint activity in which speakers and listeners work together to ensure mutual understanding (i.e., establishing “common ground”). Developmentally also, adults often scaffold children’s understanding by prompting them to explain or by clarifying instructions (since initially children tend to overestimate their understanding of an ambiguous message), which over time teaches children how to resolve ambiguities through conversation. Interestingly, LVLMs as well tend to in many cases overestimate their understanding of the user’s query, and do not engage in dialogue to refine their understanding. In this paper, inspired by such clarification-seeking behavior, we aim to equip LVLM-powered robotic agents with a proactive questioning mechanism designed to clarify the user’s intent.

Most existing grounding methods for vision-language models depend on single-turn, prompt-based interactions, assuming initial instructions fully represent user intentions [10, 11]. While those methods are effective for simple direction, they frequently struggle with high level ambiguous requests. For instance, an instruction like ”clean the room” can lead to diverse visual interpretations based on different individual expectations regarding organization or aesthetics. Although recent diffusion-based image generation models [12, 11] have significantly improved prompt to image translation, they rely on explicitly detailed prompts therefore limiting the applicability where user intentions remain underspecified. More adaptive approaches incorporate conversational grounding, allowing users iterative clarification through dialogue [13, 14, 15]. Yet, current methods mostly allow small, step by step improvements without actively asking users for important clarifications, making them less useful in real situations.

To overcome these limitations, in this paper, we propose a framework that enables robotic agents to actively ask targeted questions, effectively grounding and clarifying abstract user goals like “clean this room”, converting them into specific, visually coherent outcomes. More specifically, we propose a chatbot-based framework designed to ground ambiguous user goals through targeted questioning and iterative interaction. Our approach initiates a guided dialogue, proactively asking clarifying questions in an effort to capture the user’s precise visual intent. Leveraging these input clarifications, our system generates a visualization of the final scene, in order to verify with the user that it correctly understood their intentions.

In summary, our key contributions are:

A conversational grounding framework inspired by human clarification-seeking behavior, that proactively engages users through targeted clarifying questions to accurately determine visual intent.

Integration of the interactive dialogue with image editing and diffusion-based image generation to better align the user’s intentions(goals) with the system’s “understanding”, and verify the system’s clear understanding of the instruction.

A comparative user study with a a state-of-the-art LVLM-based system (Gemini 2.0), which shows that LVLMs augmented with such clarification seeking behavior are significantly preferred by the users in terms of their effectiveness for task completion.

1. A conversational grounding framework inspired by human clarification-seeking behavior, that proactively engages users through targeted clarifying questions to accurately determine visual intent.

2. Integration of the interactive dialogue with image editing and diffusion-based image generation to better align the user’s intentions(goals) with the system’s “understanding”, and verify the system’s clear understanding of the instruction.

3. A comparative user study with a a state-of-the-art LVLM-based system (Gemini 2.0), which shows that LVLMs augmented with such clarification seeking behavior are significantly preferred by the users in terms of their effectiveness for task completion.

title: Action Intent as a Bridge: Transferring Manipulation Knowledge from Human-Centric Videos to Robots
authors: Zhiqian Xia,Lianyang Ma,Haifeng Xia,Siyu Xia,Wei Wang,Xiaochun Cao
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved promising performance for generalized robotic manipulation, yet their reliance on expensive real-robot data remains a fundamental bottleneck. A scalable alternative is to transfer knowledge from off-the-shelf human-centric videos. However, existing methods extract latent action representations that are entangled with scene-specific noise, diluting the transferred knowledge. Motivated by this limitation, we propose Action-Intent Transfer (AIT), a two-stage method that transfers knowledge through a clean action representation shared across humans and robots. In the first stage, AIT extracts explicit action intents and disentangles the implicit action intent from manipulation videos. In the second stage, AIT aligns the human and robot domains within this shared intent space and decodes the intent into executable robot actions. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world environments demonstrate that AIT transfers human knowledge more effectively and consistently outperforms prior baselines.

title: LLM-Assisted Planning with Distributed Onboard Behaviour Tree Execution for Multi-AUV Missions
authors: Ehsan Khorrambakht,Cristiano Caissutti,Andrea Munafo,Andrea Caiti
abstract: Coordinating autonomous underwater vehicles requires translating operator intent into feasible assignments while preserving autonomous execution when communication is limited. We present a hierarchical framework that couples Large Language Model (LLM) interpretation of natural-language mission instructions with Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) and distributed Behaviour Tree (BT) execution. The LLM extracts assignment and ordering constraints, which the MILP optimizer combines with vehicle capabilities and temporal requirements. A BT–LLM Bridge distributes the resulting allocations to onboard BT Mission Managers. Per-vehicle Robotic Agents assess local faults and request selective replanning, allowing unaffected vehicles to continue their assigned tasks. Evaluation in a ROS-based AUV simulator compares Qwen-3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B on constraint extraction and tests recovery from sensor degradation and critical vehicle faults. Qwen-3-8B provides more accurate constraint extraction, and all tasks are completed in the tested failure scenarios. These simulation results support the feasibility of combining language-based mission specification with structured allocation and distributed execution.
introduction:
In recent years, the growing deployment of autonomous vehicles in maritime environments has emphasized the need for trustworthy autonomy frameworks that enhance human supervision and ensure reliable mission execution. These environments are dynamic, uncertain, and characterized by bandwidth-limited communication, causing single vehicles to struggle due to limited endurance, sensing range, and communication capabilities. Cooperative fleets of Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) can mitigate these limitations, yet coordinating multiple vehicles remains challenging under intermittent acoustic connectivity (Stojanovic and Preisig, 2009).

Large Language Models (LLMs) offer new capabilities for interpreting natural-language (NL) mission specifications and generating structured plans. However, they introduce risks for safety-critical underwater operations, including infeasible outputs, limited grounding in robot capabilities, and inference latency incompatible with real-time control (Liang et al., 2022; Ahn et al., 2022). Behaviour Trees (BTs), by contrast, provide deterministic, modular, and interpretable mission execution (Sprague et al., 2018). Recent efforts have explored LLM-assisted BT generation (Izzo et al., 2024), but these approaches focus on single robots and assume reliable communication.

Despite progress in LLM-based planning, BT execution, and multi-AUV coordination, three challenges remain. First, existing systems do not support NL interfaces for multi-robot task allocation involving heterogeneous capabilities and task dependencies, still relying on structured mission files (Wang and others, 2023). Second, distributed failure handling under intermittent acoustic communication is limited. Third, current LLM–BT integrations lack mechanisms to align high-level LLM reasoning with the deterministic execution required across multiple vehicles.

This work addresses these gaps through a hierarchical architecture that integrates LLM-assisted planning with distributed BT execution for robust multi-AUV missions. The main contributions are as follows:

An LLM-assisted Planner which extracts operator constraints and embeds them in a Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP) for capability-aware task allocation.

Distributed Robotic Agents (RAs) enabling autonomous failure assessment and selective replanning, reducing communication demands.

A BT Mission Manager on each vehicle enabling deterministic, modular, and reactive onboard execution of navigation and survey tasks using pre-defined BT subtrees.

A topside–seaside separation in which all semantic interpretation and multi-robot reasoning occur topside, while onboard autonomy relies solely on deterministic BT control.

The remainder of the paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 presents the system architecture. Section 4 describes the experimental setup and results. Section 5 concludes the paper.

title: Physical Diffusion Policy via MPM-Guided 3D Gaussian Simulation
authors: Can Wang,Qiyuan Qiao,Lei Liu,Ge Yuan,Xinhui Liu,Dong Xu
abstract: Learning robust manipulation policies for diverse everyday objects remains challenging because objects with different materials exhibit distinct deformation and contact dynamics. While diffusion policies provide a powerful framework for modeling multimodal manipulation behaviors, they typically lack explicit physical reasoning and may produce averaged actions when facing heterogeneous objects. We present a physics-aware diffusion policy that augments visual imitation learning with object physical understanding. Our framework recovers material properties from visual demonstrations by coupling 3D Gaussian Splatting with differentiable Material Point Method simulation, where video guidance and particle-level constraints enable accurate physical parameter estimation. The estimated physics conditions are further integrated into a material-aware Mixture-of-Experts diffusion policy, allowing adaptive behavior generation across different physical regimes. For practical deployment, we introduce a physics memory bank that provides efficient physical retrieval without requiring online simulation optimization. Experiments on a wide range of simulated and real-world objects demonstrate improved manipulation success and generalization over existing diffusion-based approaches. These results show that incorporating physical knowledge is critical for scalable robot manipulation in diverse environments.
introduction:
Robot manipulation in unstructured environments requires the ability to interact with objects that exhibit diverse physical properties. While humans can effortlessly adapt their behaviors by reasoning about material characteristics such as stiffness, deformability, and compliance, robots typically rely on visual observations and previously collected demonstrations to infer appropriate actions. This gap becomes particularly challenging when manipulating everyday objects, where even visually similar objects may require fundamentally different interaction strategies due to variations in their underlying physical dynamics.

Diffusion policies [1] have recently emerged as a powerful framework for robot manipulation by learning expressive action distributions from human demonstrations. Recent efforts have further improved diffusion policies by incorporating richer geometric representations, such as 3D point clouds and multi-view spatial features, to enhance scene understanding and manipulation precision [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. Nevertheless, existing diffusion policies primarily treat objects as visual entities and lack explicit awareness of their physical properties. This limitation becomes particularly pronounced in real-world manipulation, where objects with different materials can exhibit substantially different deformation and contact behaviors. Without physical understanding, a single policy may average incompatible interaction patterns, resulting in suboptimal behaviors when encountering heterogeneous objects.

A natural solution is to provide manipulation policies with explicit physical knowledge of objects. However, obtaining accurate physical properties from visual observations remains challenging. Traditional system identification approaches typically require carefully designed interactions, force measurements, or object-specific simulators, which are difficult to scale to diverse real-world objects [10, 11, 12]. Recent advances in differentiable simulation [13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18] provide an opportunity to infer physical parameters by optimizing simulation outcomes against observations.
Nevertheless, existing methods are primarily designed for physical parameter estimation or sim-to-real transfer, rather than enabling robots to explicitly reason about object physics during policy learning. As a result, the challenge of incorporating physical understanding into general-purpose robot manipulation remains largely unresolved.

In this work, we propose a physics-aware manipulation framework that bridges visual observations, differentiable physical simulation, and diffusion-based control. Given multi-view observations of an object, we construct a unified 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [19] and Material Point Method (MPM) [20, 21, 22] representation, enabling differentiable simulation and rendering. By optimizing the simulated dynamics against demonstration videos with particle-level physical constraints, our framework estimates object-specific physical parameters, including elasticity, plasticity, and viscosity-related properties. These physical properties are then used as conditions for a physics-aware diffusion policy. To better handle diverse material behaviors, we introduce a material-aware Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, where a learned router dynamically selects material-specific experts to generate physics-consistent manipulation trajectories. Furthermore, we develop a physics memory bank that stores previously estimated physical properties, allowing efficient deployment without expensive online simulation optimization.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce a physics-aware manipulation framework that integrates differentiable physical simulation with diffusion policies, enabling robot manipulation conditioned on estimated object physical properties.

We propose a differentiable 3DGS-MPM representation with video-guided optimization and particle-level constraints to recover material properties from visual observations.

We design a material-aware MoE diffusion policy that adaptively selects specialized experts for different physical regimes, improving manipulation generalization across heterogeneous objects.

We construct a physics memory bank for efficient deployment, avoiding costly online physical optimization while preserving physics-consistent manipulation performance.

1. We introduce a physics-aware manipulation framework that integrates differentiable physical simulation with diffusion policies, enabling robot manipulation conditioned on estimated object physical properties.

2. We propose a differentiable 3DGS-MPM representation with video-guided optimization and particle-level constraints to recover material properties from visual observations.

3. We design a material-aware MoE diffusion policy that adaptively selects specialized experts for different physical regimes, improving manipulation generalization across heterogeneous objects.

4. We construct a physics memory bank for efficient deployment, avoiding costly online physical optimization while preserving physics-consistent manipulation performance.

title: All-For-One: Distilling Visual Foundation Models to a Fast, Memory-Efficient Visuomotor Policy
authors: Byungkun Lee,Minho Park,Hojoon Lee,Dongyoon Hwang,Donghu Kim,Hyunseung Kim,Kyungmin Lee,Yunho Kim,Jaegul Choo
abstract:
Visual Foundation Models (VFMs) provide semantic cues such as depth and segmentation useful for robotic manipulation, but directly deploying them in closed-loop control is impractical due to high computational cost, temporal inconsistency, and distribution shift between static internet images and egocentric robot observations.
We propose All-For-One (AFO), a two-stage distillation framework that leverages VFMs strictly as privileged information during training, using downstream robotic data.
Following the privileged learning paradigm, AFO decouples semantic representation learning from inference-time policy execution.
In the All stage, a teacher policy fuses RGB observations with outputs from multiple VFMs to learn a semantically enriched representation.
In the For-One stage, this knowledge is distilled in-distribution into a lightweight RGB-only student policy.
Evaluated on two Adroit tasks and five MetaWorld tasks in simulation, as well as three real-world manipulation tasks, AFO outperforms prior foundation-model-based approaches while using
over 30×\times fewer parameters than VFM-based encoders and 50×\times lower latency than its own teacher in simulation benchmarks,
providing an efficient pathway for transferring foundation-model knowledge to robotic control.
introduction:
Robust visual perception is a prerequisite for robotic manipulation in unstructured environments.
To interact effectively with the physical world, a robot must infer rich semantic and spatial information from visual observations, including the location of task-relevant objects, their boundaries, and depth.
Such information directly influences downstream control [12, 27, 2, 53, 4, 14].
However, robotic learning systems typically operate under severe data constraints: collecting real-world demonstrations is expensive, time-consuming, and task-specific.
This data scarcity has motivated extensive interest in leveraging general-purpose vision foundation models (VFMs) that can transfer across tasks and environments.

To leverage vision foundation models (VFMs), one line of work directly adopts off-the-shelf foundation encoders such as DINOv2 [39] or CLIP [42] as frozen perception backbones, or propose robot-centric pretraining [43, 37, 35] and distillation methods [50] from large-scale data [11, 16].
However, such pretrained encoders are typically large [18, 13], incurring an unfavorable compute–performance tradeoff (Figure 1).
Moreover, since they are often pre-trained on general web-crawled images (e.g., ImageNet [11]), a substantial distribution shift arises between static, exocentric web imagery and egocentric, task-driven robot observations.
As a result, these representations usually yield only marginal gains over small models trained from scratch, or even degrade performance [17, 35].

Recently, VFMs have advanced beyond generic vision encoders.
For example, Molmo [10] localizes objects via pointing from free-form natural language, SAM [26, 46, 7] produces fine-grained segmentation masks from a point prompt, and DAM [57, 58, 32] predicts reasonable depth maps from RGB images alone.
In principle, these capabilities could help overcome the data limitations of robotic learning.
In practice, however, their tremendous computational and memory footprints preclude real-time, on-device inference in closed-loop control, rendering their predictions available only as privileged signals at training time.
In this paper, we explore a distillation method that transfers this privileged knowledge from VFMs into compact models suitable for real-time control.

To this end, we propose All-For-One (AFO), a two-stage distillation framework that leverages visual foundation models (VFMs) strictly as privileged information during training.
In the All stage, a teacher policy is trained on downstream robotic data, fusing RGB observations with depth and segmentation outputs from multiple large-scale VFMs to learn a semantically enriched representation.
In the For-One stage, this VFMs’ privileged knowledge is distilled into a lightweight, RGB-only student policy using only robotic data.
The student is trained end-to-end from raw RGB observations by imitating expert actions while aligning its internal representation with the teacher’s VFM-derived features, thereby transferring privileged visual knowledge without requiring VFMs at inference time.

We evaluate AFO on seven tasks across two simulation benchmarks [44, 59], as well as three real-world manipulation tasks on a 6-DoF Indy7 robotic arm.
As shown in Figure 1, AFO successfully transfers privileged VFM knowledge into a compact RGB-only policy.
Notably, the end-to-end trained student surpasses not only the baselines but also its heavy VFM-based teacher, as it adapts its representation to the target domain while bypassing the VFMs’ occasional prediction errors that we analyze in detail.
Overall, AFO offers a practical and efficient pathway for transferring foundation knowledge to robotic policies while preserving real-world deployability.
Our contributions are threefold:

We propose All-For-One (AFO), a two-stage framework that treats multiple VFMs as privileged information at training time and distills their depth and segmentation knowledge into a lightweight, RGB-only policy that requires no VFMs at inference.

We show that the end-to-end distilled student not only matches but surpasses its VFM-based teacher, by adapting VFM-derived representations to the target domain while avoiding the teacher’s reliance on error-prone, costly VFM inference in the loop.

We validate AFO on seven simulated tasks across two benchmarks and three real-world tasks on a 6-DoF Indy7 arm, demonstrating strong performance and robustness to visual distribution shifts at a fraction of the teacher’s computational cost.

title: Spectrally Routed Diffusion Policy for Multi-Task Robotic Manipulation
authors: Mingcong Li,Yihan Zhou,Jiayu Qu,Xueyang Guo,Yilin Mo
comment: . Accepted for publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
abstract:
Diffusion-based policies have achieved strong performance on single-task robotic manipulation.
However, a single model trained jointly on multiple tasks consistently underperforms the per-task specialists trained on the same demonstrations.
We focus on two challenges.
First, the convolutional encoders commonly used in diffusion-based policies produce visual conditions that are not discriminative enough.
Second, gradients from incompatible action modes update the shared denoiser’s dense parameters along the same directions, causing destructive interference during joint training.
To address both, we propose SR-DP (Spectrally Routed Diffusion Policy).
A frozen VGGT encoder with a spatial-compression adapter produces compact multi-scale semantic-geometric tokens, a task-discriminative visual condition for tasks that share a workspace.
We first train the denoiser as a standard diffusion policy, then decompose selected linear layers by SVD into a frozen basis of orthogonal rank-one experts, adapted through spectral routing and Householder input rotations.
On six RoboTwin tasks, SR-DP averages a 68.4%68.4\% success rate, surpassing multi-task VO-DP by 21.821.8 points and the strongest per-task baseline by 3.83.8 points.
On four real-world bimanual tasks, Stage 2 reaches a 43.0%43.0\% average success rate and improves over Stage 1 by 19.019.0 points.
introduction:
Diffusion Policy [1] has emerged as a dominant paradigm for visuomotor imitation learning, achieving strong results on single-task benchmarks.
However, this success does not extend to the multi-task setting.
Joint training across diverse tasks challenges a shared policy’s ability to model task-specific action distributions [2, 3].
Enlarging the backbone or collecting more demonstrations only partially closes this gap, while the underlying cause remains poorly understood.

We attribute this degradation to two structural limitations.
On the perception side, the convolutional encoders commonly used in diffusion-based policies [1] apply global pooling that compresses each observation into a single vector, discarding the spatial layout that distinguishes tasks within a shared workspace.
Conversely, vision-language-action (VLA) methods preserve this detail but rely on large vision-language backbones with full token attention [4, 5].
Compact conditions that keep multi-scale spatial structure remain uncommon.
On the action side, different tasks induce distinct conditional action distributions.
Their gradients update the same weight directions of the shared denoiser in conflicting ways [6, 7], causing joint training to converge to a compromise that fits no single task.
Most existing approaches distribute capacity across multiple subnetworks via Mixture-of-Experts or action-distribution decomposition [3, 8, 2].
However, these modules are themselves newly added, unconstrained dense parameters, leaving capacity duplication and inter-task gradient interference unresolved.

Rather than introducing separate dense modules for different tasks, we constrain task adaptation to the structure encoded by the shared denoiser.
For a linear weight 𝑾\bm{W}, the SVD 𝑾=𝑼​diag​(𝝈)​𝑽⊤=∑d=1Dσd​𝒖d​𝒗d⊤\bm{W}=\bm{U}\,\mathrm{diag}(\bm{\sigma})\,\bm{V}^{\top}=\sum_{d=1}^{D}\sigma_{d}\bm{u}_{d}\bm{v}_{d}^{\top} expresses the layer as a set of orthogonal rank-one components.
We freeze the base factors 𝑼\bm{U}, 𝑽\bm{V}, and 𝝈\bm{\sigma}; a compact router modulates their effective spectral coefficients 𝝈^\hat{\bm{\sigma}}, while Householder reflections rotate the input directions under an orthogonality constraint.
Because the output directions 𝒖d\bm{u}_{d} remain fixed and orthogonal, changes in σ^d\hat{\sigma}_{d} act along separated output directions before nonlinear mixing, constraining task-specific adaptation without unrestricted dense-weight updates.

Building on this idea, we propose SR-DP (Fig. 1), a multi-task diffusion policy that pairs a visual encoder with a spectrally routed denoiser.
The visual encoder uses a frozen VGGT backbone [9], whose alternating frame-wise and global self-attention blocks capture both object identity and spatial arrangement that distinguish tasks sharing a workspace.
A spatial-compression adapter condenses VGGT’s dense per-view tokens into a compact multi-scale condition for the denoiser, while an auxiliary task-prediction head encourages the resulting condition to stay task-discriminative.
The denoiser is an AdaLN-Zero DiT [10] trained in two stages.
Stage 1 jointly trains the denoiser without task conditioning, yielding a shared base policy.
Stage 2 decomposes selected linear layers as above and adds a Householder rotation and a router conditioned on task identity, token state, and diffusion step.
This conversion preserves the base policy’s learned mapping at initialization.

We evaluate SR-DP as a multi-task model on six RoboTwin tasks [11] and on four real-world tasks collected on a teleoperated bimanual platform.
A single SR-DP model reaches 68.4%68.4\% average success on the six jointly trained RoboTwin tasks, exceeding the per-task VO-DP baseline by 3.83.8 points and the multi-task VO-DP baseline by 21.821.8; on our four real-world tasks designed with similar scenes but distinct action distributions, the Stage 2 model achieves 43.0%43.0\% average success, improving over Stage 1 by 19.019.0 points.

Contributions: This work advances multi-task diffusion policies through: (1) A spectral-routing adaptation for diffusion policies that combines Householder input rotations with routing conditioned on task identity, token state, and diffusion step, keeping the base SVD factors frozen while limiting inter-task interference and training fewer than 5%5\% of policy-head parameters in Stage 2; (2) A compact, task-discriminative visual condition built from a frozen VGGT encoder, a spatial-compression adapter, and a task-prediction head, enabling a DP-scale denoiser to serve multiple tasks that share a workspace; and (3) Experiments on RoboTwin and a real bimanual platform showing that a single multi-task model matches or exceeds the per-task baselines, with an analysis associating the gain with less opposition among spectral-coordinate loss sensitivities.

title: ReflexArc: Bottom-Up Integration of Instantaneous Tactile Reflexes into Whole-Body Humanoid Control
authors: Mingyu Wang,Si Li,Ziqing Chen,He Wang,Li Yi
abstract: Humanoid robots operating in cluttered environments must react to unexpected contacts before the first impact peak, which arrives within tens of milliseconds. Learned whole-body policies running at 50 Hz50\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} introduce a policy-cycle delay and may suppress a protective withdrawal as a tracking error. To address these challenges, we propose ARC (Ascending Reflex Control), a bottom-up framework that integrates instantaneous tactile reflexes with learned whole-body control. ARC consists of two components: an instantaneous reflex pathway and bottom-up reflex integration. The reflex pathway detects hazardous contacts from full-body tactile sensing, solves a whole-body withdrawal pose, and delivers it directly to the motors within 10 ms10\text{\,}\mathrm{ms}. Bottom-up reflex integration combines reflex-in-the-loop policy learning, reflex-transparent policy alignment, and reflex-informed policy adaptation to sustain the withdrawal, maintain balance, and complete longer-horizon recovery. We deploy ARC on a Unitree G1 and evaluate three categories of hazardous contact. Compared with an otherwise identical reflex delayed by 20 ms20\text{\,}\mathrm{ms}, ARC reduces the first force peak by 34.1 %34.1\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} and reduces the contact impulse from 0.2632 N s0.2632\text{\,}\mathrm{N}\text{\,}\mathrm{s} to 0.1225 N s0.1225\text{\,}\mathrm{N}\text{\,}\mathrm{s} (a 2.15×2.15\times ratio). We further demonstrate protected motion tracking, teleoperation, and vision-free obstacle traversal guided by foot tactile sensing.
introduction:
Humanoid robots increasingly operate in cluttered real-world environments, including teleoperated data collection [1, 2, 3, 4], traversal over complex terrain [5, 6, 7], and operation alongside people [8, 9, 10]. Unexpected contacts in these settings can damage the robot, its surroundings, or nearby people, and can cause falls. Reducing collision severity requires shortening contact before the first impact peak. Prior work [11, 12] shows that a compliant layer can delay this peak to a few tens of milliseconds after contact, consistent with observations of human impacts [13, 14]. This creates a brief window for protective withdrawal.

Existing learned whole-body controllers face two challenges in using this window. First, their top-down control flow introduces latency: a tactile event routed through a 50 Hz50\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} policy can wait up to 20 ms20\text{\,}\mathrm{ms} before the next policy update. Second, motion-tracking policies are trained to suppress deviations from a smooth reference, including those caused by a protective reflex. Distributed tactile sensing can trigger a reflex that bypasses policy inference and reaches the motors within milliseconds. However, bypassing inference alone does not resolve the interference between this bottom-up reflex and the top-down policy.

Unlike a manipulator, whose low-level controller can take over during a reflex [15, 16], a humanoid depends on its whole-body policy to maintain balance throughout withdrawal. The ongoing task should also continue whenever possible. The two controllers cannot simply be assigned different joints: torso and knee reflexes directly affect balance, and even a hand withdrawal can require coordinated motion of the rest of the body. Both pathways must therefore act on the same joints at the same time. Domain randomization [17, 18] further complicates this interaction by training the policy to reject abrupt disturbances, including the displacement produced by a reflex.

To address these challenges, we propose ARC (Ascending Reflex Control), which combines an instantaneous reflex pathway with bottom-up reflex integration (Fig. 2). The reflex pathway detects hazardous contacts on the first tactile frame and uses a model-based solver to compute a whole-body withdrawal pose, delivering the command directly to the motors within 10 ms10\text{\,}\mathrm{ms}. Bottom-up reflex integration then coordinates the reflex and policy through three designs. Reflex-in-the-Loop Policy Learning exposes the policy to reflex-induced states during training. Reflex-Transparent Policy Alignment shifts observations and actions and uses counterfactual supervision to prevent the policy from cancelling the reflex. Reflex-Informed Policy Adaptation uses contact information and a human motion prior to complete longer-horizon recovery beyond the immediate withdrawal.

We deploy ARC on a Unitree G1 and evaluate protected motion tracking, teleoperation, and vision-free obstacle traversal. In a controlled impact experiment, adding 20 ms20\text{\,}\mathrm{ms} to the same reflex increases the contact impulse by 2.15×2.15\times, highlighting the importance of direct motor access. Ablations assess the contribution of each integration design.

Our contributions are threefold:

Instantaneous tactile reflexes. A tactile startle detector and a model-based whole-body solver deliver protective commands to the motors within 10 ms10\text{\,}\mathrm{ms}, before the first impact peak.

Bottom-up reflex integration. Three complementary designs allow the reflex and a learned whole-body policy to act simultaneously, sustaining withdrawal while maintaining balance and enabling longer-horizon recovery.

Real-world validation. Experiments on Unitree G1 cover three categories of hazardous contact, quantify the effect of reflex latency, and demonstrate protected tracking, teleoperation, and tactile-guided traversal without vision.

1. Instantaneous tactile reflexes. A tactile startle detector and a model-based whole-body solver deliver protective commands to the motors within 10 ms10\text{\,}\mathrm{ms}, before the first impact peak.

2. Bottom-up reflex integration. Three complementary designs allow the reflex and a learned whole-body policy to act simultaneously, sustaining withdrawal while maintaining balance and enabling longer-horizon recovery.

3. Real-world validation. Experiments on Unitree G1 cover three categories of hazardous contact, quantify the effect of reflex latency, and demonstrate protected tracking, teleoperation, and tactile-guided traversal without vision.

title: RAFT: Reasoning-Aligned Fine-Tuning Improves Robustness of VLA Post-Training
authors: Shresth Grover,Andrey Kolobov,Dhruv Shah
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Adapting a generalist vision-language-action (VLA) policy to a target task with limited demonstrations can improve nominal task success while reducing robustness to variations in appearance, objects, and instructions. We introduce reasoning-aligned fine-tuning (RAFT), a two-stage post-training procedure: RAFT first trains low-rank adapters on task-relevant reasoning annotations, then freezes them while fine-tuning the policy on action demonstrations. On a physical DROID robot, RAFT achieves 75.0%75.0\% out-of-distribution success, compared with 27.9%27.9\% for plain fine-tuning; on a multi-stage bimanual YAM task, it reaches 70.0%70.0\% mean success, compared with 36.0%36.0\% for the strongest baseline. RAFT also improves success under visual, object, and instruction shifts in simulated pick-and-place and open-drawer tasks. Compared with plain fine-tuning, RAFT policies place more attention on annotated task regions and yield higher linear-probe accuracy for object identity in later layers. A broader reasoning-data mixture further improves downstream success across demonstration budgets.
introduction:
Generalist vision-language-action (VLA) policies, built on pretrained vision-language models and large robot datasets [1, 7, 22, 24, 3, 2], typically still require adaptation to reach the success rates needed to deploy the policy on a real-world target task [4, 23]. Because collecting task-specific demonstrations is expensive, this post-training often relies on a small dataset collected in a narrow set of environments. Fine-tuning can improve nominal success while reducing robustness to visual and semantic variations absent from those demonstrations [12, 43, 35, 37, 21, 38]. Existing approaches address this problem through parameter merging, as in RETAIN [39], or regularization during adaptation [20, 17]. We study a complementary approach, aligning a pretrained policy with task-relevant reasoning supervision before adapting it to the target actions.

Reasoning supervision can teach policies to identify task-relevant objects, spatial relations, and motion structure [41, 10, 42, 26]. We study how reasoning capabilities in pretrained VLMs can support low-data adaptation of generalist VLAs to a target skill. We introduce reasoning-aligned fine-tuning (RAFT), a two-stage adaptation procedure. Stage I learns low-rank adapters in the language and vision modules from task-relevant reasoning annotations while keeping pretrained parameters fixed. Stage II freezes these adapters and fine-tunes the language model, action expert, and projection layers on action demonstrations. Action gradients therefore do not directly update the reasoning-adapter weights. We find that how reasoning supervision is incorporated matters: jointly co-training reasoning and actions underperforms plain fine-tuning (63.2%63.2\% vs. 79.6%79.6\% mean success on simulated pick and place), and updating the reasoning adapter during action learning falls below Plain FT (74.0%74.0\% vs. 79.6%79.6\%) (Secs. 8.3 and 8.2). Staging the two, with the adapter frozen, yields these robustness gains. RAFT policies also place more attention on annotated task regions and yield higher linear-probe accuracy for object identity and episode-time position than plainly fine-tuned policies (Sec. 4.3).

We evaluate RAFT on two simulated tasks and two physical platforms: the single-arm DROID setup [22] and the bimanual YAM setup [10]. Evaluations test visual, object, instruction, and geometric variations of the adapted tasks. RAFT achieves the highest mean success on simulated pick and place and improves open-drawer success, with the largest gains on the physical robots: success on 75%75\% of out-of-distribution DROID trials versus 28%28\% for plain fine-tuning, and 70%70\% mean success on the multi-stage YAM task versus 36%36\% for the strongest baseline. Our contributions are threefold: (1) We propose RAFT a post training recipt that separates task relevant reasoning supervision from action fine tuning (2) We show improved downstream performace and robustness in simulation and on two physical robot platforms; and (3) We analyze why RAFT helps generalist policy adapt to a target by analyzing the features learned by RAFT.

title: RAIPAL: A Powerful and Agile Humanoid Arm for Human Tasks
authors: Donggeon Kim,Hyungho Chris Choi,Donghyuk Choi,Jeongsoo Park,Choongin Lee,Chan Park,Jemin Hwangbo
comment: Published in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L), 2026. Supplementary video:this https URL
abstract:
This paper presents humanoid manipulator hardware designed specifically for human-level performance throughout its broad domain of tasks, from heavy payloads to highly dynamic motions.
Unlike conventional designs targeting uniform workspace capability, the proposed approach derives
force, speed, and endurance targets from published measurements of task-relevant human upper-limb performance.
These targets guide the actuator, mechanism, and thermal design toward torque transparency and sustained operation.
The platform integrates force-oriented upper-arm components, speed-oriented forearm components, and a posture-dependent elbow mechanism that shifts its torque-speed behavior.
These components are driven by planetary actuators and compact actuator-embedded electronics.
Experimental results validate broad task capability, demonstrating a peak payload of 20 kg (2.25×\times its own mass), an endpoint speed of 20.6 m/s, and continued operation under repeated hammering impacts.
Thermal analysis further confirms that the robot’s sustained operation capability exceeds
the published human load–duration boundary
across nearly the entire load spectrum.
These findings show that
hardware targets derived from human-task measurements narrow
the human-to-humanoid capability gap.
A supplementary video is available at https://youtu.be/xVUWFICD5G0
introduction:
Advances in permanent-magnet motors and specialized robotic actuators let modern humanoids surpass average human benchmarks in isolated capabilities [1, 2].
However, payload and fast motion typically reflect different hardware priorities on different platforms, as shown in Table I.
General-purpose humanoids emphasize payload and runtime, whereas speed-oriented systems remain specialized and impractical for basic payload requirements.
Characteristics of human upper-limb tasks instead reveal a coordinated capability envelope spanning heavy-duty manipulation, rapid distal motion, compliant interaction, and load-dependent
endurance [3].
The direct use of these task priors and quantitative boundaries as hardware-design targets, however, remains largely unexplored.

Conventional manipulator sizing projects worst-case task-space forces into joint-space torque requirements, enforcing payload capability across broad workspace regions [4].
These guarantees suit fixed-base industrial manipulators but poorly match human tasks realized through coordinated, posture-dependent motion.
At the actuator level, the same bias is reinforced by conventional transmission choices: high-reduction precision drives favor compact torque generation but penalize speed, reflected inertia, and torque transparency, whereas low-reduction quasi-direct-drive actuators favor backdrivability and dynamic interaction but require larger motors for heavy-duty tasks proportional to human arms [5].
As a result, conventional sizing and actuator tradeoffs tend to push humanoid arms toward either strong and slow or fast and weak designs, rather than broad human-task capability.

This paper proposes a 7-DoF humanoid manipulator built for the wide domain of practical human tasks.
Instead of enforcing uniform workspace-wide capability, the proposed approach
extracts engineering targets from published measurements and analyses of task-relevant human upper-limb force, speed, posture, and endurance.
The resulting prototype, shown in Fig. 1, is validated through real-world experiments and analysis.
The key contributions of this work are as follows:

A source-grounded method for deriving robot force, speed, endurance, and mass-distribution requirements from measurements of human upper-limb tasks.

A top-down methodology that maps those task-derived parameters into force-, speed-, and posture-specialized hardware components.

Experimental validation through high-payload, high-speed, endurance, and high-impact demonstrations.

1. A source-grounded method for deriving robot force, speed, endurance, and mass-distribution requirements from measurements of human upper-limb tasks.

2. A top-down methodology that maps those task-derived parameters into force-, speed-, and posture-specialized hardware components.

3. Experimental validation through high-payload, high-speed, endurance, and high-impact demonstrations.
