title: ActOR: Ambient AI-Based Agentic Orchestration for Humanoid Autonomy in Operating Rooms
authors: Han Zhang,Sicheng Lu,Aleks Santari,Jeffrey K. Jopling,Masaru Ishii,Mathias Unberath
abstract: Purpose: Operating rooms (ORs) increasingly contain ambient sensing infrastructure in hopes that AI-based scene understanding would enable teams to optimize workflows and utilization. We pursue an alternative path: using ambient AI to orchestrate and inform robot action to benefit usage optimization. Deploying robots, such as humanoids, in the OR without ambient AI is severely limited by cumbersome de novo orientation and planning due to partial onboard observations. We posit that this can be achieved by coupling an ambient AI-based agentic orchestrator with the humanoid robotic actor, providing shared perception and execution feedback for humanoid autonomy in the OR.
introduction:
Operating rooms (ORs) face a growing shortage of perioperative nursing and support staff Xie et al. (2024). Room turnover, supply retrieval, and disposal of used materials consume substantial staff time and directly affect OR efficiency Portney and Demirci (2024). These tasks are repetitive and physically demanding, and do not require highly trained personnel. Automating these tasks with robots rather than relying on an already strained workforce is a promising avenue to improve turnover times. The postoperative phase provides a practical setting for automation: the patient has left, most staff have stepped away, and the environment is comparatively controlled Kernbach et al. (2026); Wachs (2026). Humanoid robots are attractive for such tasks because they can, in principle, operate within spaces designed for humans without major modifications.

At the same time, modern ORs are becoming increasingly instrumented. Ceiling- and wall-mounted cameras have been used to recognize surgical phases, localize staff and equipment, and construct digital twins (DTs) of the OR Zhang et al. (2026a); Perez et al. (2025); Özsoy et al. (2026); Wang et al. (2026). Yet this ambient sensing infrastructure has primarily been used to inform clinical teams rather than directly support robotic autonomy. We ask whether the instrumented OR itself can instead become part of the robot’s perceptual infrastructure, providing persistent room-scale context that complements the robot’s local, egocentric view.

This question is particularly relevant for humanoid autonomy in the OR, where two limitations make robot-centric operation difficult. First, autonomous task planning requires an accurate representation of the current environment, but an onboard camera provides only a moving and frequently occluded view of a cluttered room. Upon entering the room to complete an assigned task, a robot may therefore need to explore the environment before it can decide where and how to act. Second, humanoid execution remains imperfect: navigation can terminate short of a target, and grasps can fail. A plan generated from the initial scene state therefore becomes unreliable when execution deviates from expectation. Foundation-model agents can decompose open-ended instructions into robot skills Huh et al. (2026), but reliable physical autonomy also requires broader access to the world state and feedback about executed actions.

We address these limitations with ActOR, an ambient AI-based agentic orchestration framework for humanoid autonomy in the OR (Fig. 1). ActOR fuses observations from a wall-mounted ambient camera and the robot’s head-mounted camera into a shared object-level DT, combining room-scale awareness with near-field observations for manipulation. A large language model (LLM) agent plans over the DT using a library of pre-programmed skills, without task-specific training. During execution, the DT is updated and the outcome is fed back to the agent, which retries, changes its approach, or replans. We evaluate ActOR on postoperative support tasks in two simulated ORs reconstructed from real rooms and on a Unitree G1 humanoid in a physical mock OR. Our contributions are:

A shared scene representation integrating room-scale and egocentric sensing for robot orientation and task planning in ORs.

A shared scene representation integrating room-scale and egocentric sensing for robot orientation and task planning in ORs.

A closed-loop execution mechanism that feeds skill outcomes and scene updates back to an LLM planner for recovery and replanning.

Simulation ablations of ambient perception and execution feedback, together with physical validation in a mock OR.

1. A shared scene representation integrating room-scale and egocentric sensing for robot orientation and task planning in ORs.

2. A closed-loop execution mechanism that feeds skill outcomes and scene updates back to an LLM planner for recovery and replanning.

3. Simulation ablations of ambient perception and execution feedback, together with physical validation in a mock OR.

title: DiMuRe: Diagnosis-Guided Multilevel Recovery for Robotic Task Execution
authors: Renkai Yi,Yuwei Wu,Haoyu Zhang,Penghao Dai,Zhi Gao,Jin Chen,Che Sun
comment: including appendices
abstract:
Disturbances can invalidate the conditions required by a robot’s next action
even when much of its task program remains useful. A recovery system must
therefore choose a response suited to the current state.
We present DiMuRe (diagnosis-guided multilevel recovery), a framework for
robot-use agents that uses phase-specific evidence and method preconditions
to select program reuse or predefined recovery skills, including bounded
vision-language-action (VLA) grasping. After the original program exits, a
multimodal large language model (MLLM) can generate corrective code from images
and execution feedback. Local verification checks the outcome of each recovery
attempt. We also introduce LIBERO-Disturb, a benchmark for robustness and
recovery under mid-execution disturbances, supporting program-based agents
and VLA policies. On 801 scheduled disturbed Encore development cases, Local
DiMuRe (program reuse and recovery skills) achieves 77.65% complete-task
success, compared with 58.68% for the original program under the same
physical-step allowance. Full DiMuRe achieves 81.90% with terminal replanning,
an additional step allowance, and early handoff. Local DiMuRe also uses fewer
physical steps per scheduled episode than the original program.
introduction:
When a target object moves during manipulation, a previously valid grasp
command may fail even though much of the task program remains useful.
Robot-use agents express perception, motion, and feedback through executable
programs [12, 21], which can already include
checks and retries. Recovery therefore requires determining which parts of
the existing behavior still apply. If the object has only shifted in position,
translating a recorded grasp segment may suffice. If the grasp assumptions
no longer hold, a different recovery procedure may be needed.

Each recovery option has limits. Program reuse preserves task-specific
motions but depends on the available segments and how they can be adapted.
Predefined recovery skills, including bounded vision-language-action (VLA)
grasping, handle particular failures when their preconditions are met.
A multimodal large language model (MLLM) can compose new action sequences
from visual observations and execution feedback, at the cost of additional
inference and verification. Choosing among these options requires more than
a failure alarm. The system needs evidence that a response is applicable
and must then check whether it restores the state needed to continue the task.
Obtaining this evidence also takes time, so the decision must account for
the cost of further sensing and reasoning.

To study these choices, an evaluation must introduce controlled disturbances
during execution. Specifying a disturbance does not guarantee that it was
applied, had its intended physical effect, or prevented task completion.
Recording these outcomes separately makes it possible to assess both the
original program’s resilience and the benefit of added recovery.

To address these challenges, we make two contributions:

DiMuRe uses phase-specific diagnostic evidence to select among
program reuse, predefined recovery skills, and MLLM-assisted replanning.
It checks each method’s preconditions and verifies the result of recovery
before deciding how to continue.

LIBERO-Disturb is a benchmark for mid-execution disturbance
robustness and recovery in robotic manipulation. It separates disturbance
injection and task evaluation from the tested system, supporting both
program-based robot-use agents and VLA policies.

1. DiMuRe uses phase-specific diagnostic evidence to select among
program reuse, predefined recovery skills, and MLLM-assisted replanning.
It checks each method’s preconditions and verifies the result of recovery
before deciding how to continue.

2. LIBERO-Disturb is a benchmark for mid-execution disturbance
robustness and recovery in robotic manipulation. It separates disturbance
injection and task evaluation from the tested system, supporting both
program-based robot-use agents and VLA policies.

title: Online iLQR-MPC with Whole-Body Control for Robust Humanoid Locomotion
authors: Xiang Li,Linlin Ou,Ruihan Wu,Xinyi Yu
abstract: Humanoid locomotion requires deciding where to step and how to distribute contact forces. However, a disturbance can invalidate the nominal plan, requiring coordinated revision under constraints that switch with every footfall. To solve this online, the proposed approach employs the single-rigid-body model, which retains attitude dynamics and the full contact wrench. An iterative linear-quadratic-regulator MPC (iLQR-MPC) then jointly optimizes contact forces and footstep locations in a single receding-horizon problem, without a separate step planner. Specifically, contact and motion constraints are incorporated into the backward pass through augmented-Lagrangian and relaxed-barrier penalties. A whole-body controller subsequently maps the plan to joint torques at 500​Hz500\,\mathrm{Hz} while preserving contact feasibility. The model-based formulation makes disturbance responses interpretable through explicit costs and constraints, and requires no platform-specific policy training. In MuJoCo simulations, the iLQR-MPC replans at 100​Hz100\,\mathrm{Hz} (mean solve time 8.9​ms8.9\,\mathrm{ms}); the Unitree G1 sustains steady-state walking and recovers from impulsive 245​N245\,\mathrm{N} forward and 175​N175\,\mathrm{N} lateral pushes.
introduction:
Humanoid robots must maintain dynamic balance, track footholds, and respect hard constraints (joint limits, torque bounds, and friction cones) on a floating base with dozens of degrees of freedom (DoF) and hybrid dynamics that switch at every contact event. The dominant paradigm pairs a simplified-model MPC with a whole-body controller (WBC), from the Atlas humanoid [1] to recent quadrupeds [2]; a recent survey identifies it as the standard framework [3]. Reinforcement learning offers an alternative through sim-to-real transfer [4], but requires per-platform retraining and gives no formal guarantee on constraint satisfaction.

Within model-based control, competing tasks must be resolved. A weighted-sum objective cannot guarantee safety-critical constraints when they conflict with secondary goals; for a walking humanoid, a violation means a fall. Task-priority control instead enforces tasks in priority order through null-space projection [5, 6], extended to inequality constraints via hierarchical quadratic programming (HQP) [7] and validated on torque-controlled humanoids [8]. Because WBC acts on the instantaneous state alone, it is reactive; MPC adds lookahead by planning contact forces over a receding horizon, but full-order nonlinear MPC is intractable at real-time rates. The standard approach therefore pairs a reduced-model MPC at 50–100 Hz, which plans ground reaction forces and CoM trajectories, with a WBC at 500–1000 Hz mapping the plan to joint torques. Linear MPC based on the zero-moment point (ZMP) [9] and nonlinear contact-implicit MPC [10] have been deployed this way.

External pushes test these constraint margins. Push recovery uses three strategies [11]: ankle (ZMP modulation), hip (angular-momentum regulation), and stepping (footstep adjustment). Stepping is the last recourse because it redefines the support base [12]. Online gait adaptation has followed two directions. The first modifies step timing [13, 14], relying on reduced-order dynamics, chiefly the linear inverted pendulum, for tractability. The second promotes footstep location to a state variable within the MPC, coupled with a foot-velocity control, so footholds and contact forces are co-optimized: Romualdi et al. [15] introduced this on the position-controlled iCub, and Ding et al. [16] applied the same idea within an orientation-aware MPC.

Despite these advances, the standard MPC+WBC pipeline faces two challenges. The first concerns constraint handling in DDP-style nonlinear MPC: most deployed formulations linearize the dynamics and simplify the contact constraints to preserve convexity, so under large disturbances the executed motion can violate friction-cone, unilateral, or ZMP conditions that the plan satisfies. Nonlinear solvers such as differential dynamic programming (DDP) and its Gauss–Newton variant, the iterative linear-quadratic regulator (iLQR) [17], avoid this, and have been demonstrated across multi-contact DDP [18], hybrid contact-implicit iLQR-MPC [19, 20], and reduced-order-guided contact-implicit MPC for humanoids [21]. DDP exploits the temporal structure of the problem, but its weakness is inequality constraints: an SQP step carries them as QP inequalities, whereas augmented Lagrangian and relaxed-barrier penalties fold them into the stage cost. Within DDP, augmented Lagrangian (AL) penalties drive feasibility through adaptive multiplier updates [22], while relaxed barriers (ReB) replace the logarithmic barrier with a quadratic extension that keeps the backward-pass Hessian bounded [23]. Li and Wensing [24] combined the two, assigning AL to switching equality constraints and ReB to inequalities; AL-DDP has since been applied to biped gait generation with centroidal dynamics, but in an offline planning formulation [25]. HS-DDP itself runs offline on a 2D planar quadruped; to our knowledge, no bipedal humanoid controller has run the AL+ReB pairing inside an online receding-horizon MPC, where the narrower stability margin makes the constraint handling harder.
The second challenge is structural: a reduced-model plan is a reference, not a feasible whole-body motion. The single-rigid-body (SRB) model omits limb momentum [28] and joint-level limits, and returns a resultant wrench per foot rather than joint torques; completing the plan in joint space is left to the execution layer. Prior work resolves this in one of three ways: tracking the MPC force references at high priority [8] can produce infeasible joint commands; tracking motion references [2] forgoes force-level planning; and optimizing the full whole-body dynamics directly [26] remains costly. A whole-body QP that co-optimizes contact-force increments and task-space acceleration corrections reconciles the plan with the full-body dynamics under all constraints [27, 7]. The WBC is bounded by the plan it receives: it reshapes the contact wrench and the base acceleration, but it cannot move a footstep, so any adaptation the MPC does not plan is left to the ankle and hip strategies within the support polygon the plan already fixed.

The proposed controller addresses both challenges (Fig. 1) with an iLQR-MPC and a whole-body controller; a reference-planning module upstream converts a velocity command into a CoM reference, nominal footholds, and a contact schedule. The contributions of this paper are as follows.

Joint footstep and contact-force planning. The controller jointly optimizes contact forces and footstep locations in a single receding-horizon iLQR-MPC on the single-rigid-body model. Both are re-optimized at every replan, so a push is answered by moving the next footstep and redistributing the stance wrench in the same solve, without a separate step planner.

Online constraint handling. Augmented-Lagrangian and relaxed-barrier penalties place the contact and motion constraints in the backward pass, which keeps the joint optimization practical at replan rate.

Interpretable, model-based control. Every stage is defined by explicit models, costs, and constraints, from the centroidal dynamics in the MPC to the null-space kinematics and floating-base QP in the whole-body layer. A disturbance response can therefore be traced to specific model terms, and no platform-specific policy training is required.

title: Grasping and Stabilizing Tumbling Objects with Rotating-Base Multi-Arm Space Manipulators
authors: Farhad Aghili
abstract: This paper presents an innovative guidance and control method for a space manipulator that actively maneuvers its base to hold a tumbling object stationary relative to the base during proximity operations. This simplifies motion planning, reduces collision risk, and enables impact-free capture using single- or multi-arm configurations, with or without predefined grasping interfaces. The proposed approach involves two phases. In the pre-grasping phase, a synchronization control aligns the target’s center of mass (CoM) with the system’s instantaneous center of rotation (ICR), virtually rigidizing the target–servicer system to keep the object stationary for reliable grasping. In the post grasping phase, a control strategy based on Hamiltonian dynamics and optimal control stabilizes the combined system by minimizing time, fuel, or energy, while respecting base torque limits and multiple grasping constraints. For structured targets, applied forces and torques stay within their bounds; for unstructured ones, friction constraints prevent slipping. A case study demonstrates the method’s effectiveness in enabling both the subsequent grasping and de-tumbling phases.
introduction:
Space manipulator systems (SMSs), also known as chasers or servicers, are designed to perform on-orbit servicing (OOS) tasks such as satellite maintenance, orbital debris removal, and the assembly and upkeep of orbital infrastructure [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8].
Typical SMSs consist of a servicing satellite have one or more robotic manipulators, each is equipped with a specialized end-effector or grappling mechanism for capturing and manipulating client satellites or other orbital targets. Topologically, an SMS can be modeled as a kinematic chain with two free-moving ends: the base (i.e., the servicing spacecraft) and the end-effector. Due to the dynamic coupling between the manipulator joints and the motion of both the base and the end-effector, control strategies for SMSs are generally categorized into two main approaches:
(i) free floating arm control, where the base is allowed to drift and rotate passively; and
(ii) coordinated control, which stabilizes the base either partially or fully using internal momentum exchange devices (e.g., reaction wheels or control moment gyroscopes) and, when necessary, thrusters. A third control mode that entails the simultaneous coordinated maneuvering of both ends is also feasible in addition to these traditional control methods. Since the target can remain stationary relative to the base throughout the entire proximity operation, this approach offers several advantages for the robotic capture and manipulation of tumbling objects, thereby enhancing mission safety and operational simplicity. This paper presents a comprehensive investigation into such control strategies for space robotic systems.

The success of forthcoming space exploration and utilization missions relies critically on advances in on orbit robotic manipulation and capture capabilities [2, 9, 10]. Capture targets may be cooperative or non cooperative, collaborative or non collaborative, with ground observations indicating that many resident space objects are tumbling, which makes autonomous capture particularly challenging. While robotic manipulators have successfully captured cooperative satellites in orbit [11, 12, 5], autonomous capture of tumbling targets remains unachieved due to mission constraints, stringent performance requirements, and technological limitations [13].
Autonomous robotic capture and manipulation of a tumbling satellite is commonly decomposed into three phases: pre capture, contact, and post capture [2, 14]. During pre capture, trajectory planning and control aim to intercept the target grapple fixture with minimal relative velocity to limit impact forces [15, 16]. Numerous optimal and vision based motion planning approaches, including online and adaptive methods for free flying robots, have been proposed for this phase [17, 18]. The contact phase spans initial contact to secure grasping, for which force motion and impedance control strategies have been developed to ensure safe interaction [19, 20, 21, 22], including self learning soft grasp approaches based on variable stiffness [23]. In the post capture phase, the end effector secures the target while the manipulator actively damps and stabilizes residual motion. Control and path planning methods for detumbling and stabilization have been widely studied [4, 6, 24, 25]. Most existing approaches assume that the servicing manipulator system base attitude must be stabilized, either through coordinated control or reactionless manipulation exploiting the null space of internal momentum devices [26, 27, 22, 28, 16, 29, 30].

Effective autonomous capture of tumbling targets requires tightly integrated planning and control that accommodate operational, system, and safety constraints, including time criticality, actuator limits, and collision avoidance. Prior to proximity operations, the servicing spacecraft uses thrusters to translate the system center of mass (CoM), bringing the target within the manipulator workspace. During proximity operations, the system typically operates in either full free floating or partial free floating mode. In full free floating mode, the system CoM remains stationary and the spacecraft passively responds to manipulator motion, whereas in partial free floating mode the spacecraft attitude is actively regulated using momentum devices to maintain functions such as antenna pointing. While extensive research has addressed planning and control for individual phases, namely pre capture, contact, and post capture, their seamless integration under multiple constraints remains a major challenge. Collision risk is particularly acute during approach and must be considered in both pre and post capture trajectory planning [31, 32]. Moreover, smooth phase transitions are essential due to persistent relative motion after capture, motivating the use of impedance control [19]. To mitigate these challenges, the servicing robot base can be dynamically controlled to translate and rotate so as to null the relative motion between the tumbling target and the spacecraft base.

This work introduces a novel guidance and control strategy for robotic grasping and manipulation of tumbling space objects, based on the concept of virtual rigidization between the target and the robot base through alignment of the Instantaneous Center of Rotation (ICR) with the Center of Mass (CoM). This strategy eliminates relative velocity between the space robot’s base and the target even when the latter exhibits multi-axis tumbling, in contrast to methods that rely on matching the target’s rotation axis and spin rate under pure spin [14]. The post-capture phase further incorporates friction constraints and an optimal control formulation, enabling robotic grasping and detumbling of non-cooperative targets with minimal time, energy, or fuel consumption, depending on the controller’s parameter selection. As illustrated in Fig. 1, a synchronization control scheme aligns the SMS’s ICR with the target’s CoM, causing the combined target–robot system to behave as a single rigid body. This effectively renders the tumbling target stationary relative to the robot base during grasping. During the post-grasping detumbling phase (Fig. 2), the robotic arms remain fixed while coordinated torque commands are applied to the base and joints to dampen the system’s motion in a time-optimal manner, subject to actuation limits and grasping constraints.
This approach allows the entire robotic operation, both pre- and post-grasping phases, to be treated as grasping a stationary target, thereby minimizing dynamic effects and impact at the moment of capture without the need for impedance control or complex collision avoidance, while also enabling friction-based grasping of tumbling objects using multi-arm robots. The paper is structured as follows: Sections II-A and II-B present the coordinated planning and control strategy for achieving zero relative velocity during approach and grasping by aligning the ICR and CoM. Section III formulates the grasping forces and moments in relation to base torques. Section III-B describes the optimal control strategy under force and torque constraints, Section III-D addresses friction-based grasping during detumbling, and Section IV presents the validation results.

title: Online Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability Onboard the Robot Control Loop: A Real-Time GPU Solver for Safety-Critical Autonomy
authors: Kevin Weekly,Alexandre M. Bayen
abstract:
Hamilton–Jacobi (HJ) reachability provides certified backward
reachable tubes (BRTs) for safety-critical robotic systems, but the
level-set computation scales exponentially in the state dimension and
has historically been performed offline. As autonomy stacks
(ADAS/AV, humanoid robotics, and vision–language–action models)
increasingly rely on black-box, probabilistic policies, a deterministic
safety layer with formal guarantees is an essential complement. We
present a CUDA implementation of the canonical WENO5 + TVD-RK3 +
Lax–Friedrichs level-set Hamilton–Jacobi–Isaacs solver for 2D, 3D,
and 4D dynamics that is fast enough to run inside a robot’s control
loop. In 32-bit floating point (FP32) on a single workstation GPU
(NVIDIA RTX 4000 Ada), it computes the 3D Air3D BRT at 112112\,Hz, a 4D
pursuit–evasion BRT at 6161\,Hz, and a 2D wind-affected drifter BRT
at 7474–147147\,Hz, 5.95.9–17.5×17.5\times faster than the JAX reference
hj_reachability at matched precision and 1.71.7–16×16\times
faster than a torch.compile reimplementation of the same
scheme. In 64-bit floating point (FP64) it agrees with
hj_reachability on eight benchmark cases, reproduces Mitchell’s
Air3D BRT to within 0.04%0.04\% of the reference cell count, and runs
2.02.0–4.6×4.6\times faster. On an embedded NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor it
computes Air3D at 6666\,Hz (N=41N{=}41) and the 2D drifter at 5454\,Hz,
3.83.8–8.9×8.9\times faster than hj_reachability on the same
device. As a multi-agent application, an in-kernel label-propagation
extension recovers the KK-agent capture-basin Voronoi tessellation
from a single combined HJ solve, independent of fleet size; it runs at
4.04.0\,ms per tick in a closed-loop wildfire-response simulation of six
quadcopters under time-varying, non-uniform wind.
introduction:
The next generation of autonomous robotics — advanced driver-assistance
and self-driving vehicles (ADAS/AV), humanoid platforms, and
vision–language–action (VLA) policies — pushes decision-making
into large, learned, fundamentally probabilistically determined models whose worst-case
behavior is case-dependent and whose safety properties cannot be certified by
inspection. A deterministic, model-based safety layer with formal
guarantees is therefore not optional but a structural enabler of these
stacks: it is the mechanism by which a black-box upstream policy can
be trusted in safety-critical deployment, and the only available
complement that gives the overall system the worst-case behavior the
upstream model cannot. Hamilton–Jacobi (HJ) reachability is the
strongest available primitive for that role. The backward reachable
tube (BRT) is the exact set of states from which a constraint
violation cannot be avoided against the worst-case
disturbance [29, 32, 4].
Three properties of the BRT make it the right object for safety, and
keeping them distinct avoids a common confusion. First, depending on
how it is computed, the BRT—or, more precisely, its boundary—delimits
the set of states from which, regardless of the control, the
worst-case disturbance can force the system into the target set (here,
the unsafe set). Second, from any state outside the tube there always
exists a control that keeps the system safe over the horizon. Third, on
the boundary of the tube at least one control must be applied to
stay safe: absent it, the disturbance can drive the system into the tube
and ultimately into the unsafe set.
A robot whose current state lies inside the BRT must either accept a
failure outcome or apply the value-function-derived optimal control
to escape, and so the BRT answers the most fundamental question a
safety-critical autonomy stack can ask [17, 21].
A BRT-based safety filter can sit downstream of a learned planner and
either certify its proposed action or override it with a provably
safe one [21, 17], giving the deployed
ADAS/AV, humanoid, or VLA stack a deterministic floor of behaviour
that the upstream learned policy is not by itself required to provide.

The well-known drawback is that the level-set computation that
delivers a guaranteed-fidelity BRT scales exponentially in the state
dimension. The historical response has been to compute the BRT once
offline and then use it as a fixed lookup in the control
loop [34, 20, 45]. This is a
critical limitation for next-generation autonomy: in any setting
where the disturbance model, the obstacle set, or the dynamics are
not known a priori — the operating regime of every real ADAS
stack, every legged platform on unmodeled terrain, and every VLA
policy in an unfamiliar environment — a stale offline BRT is a
stale safety guarantee.

With the implementation presented in this article, we demonstrate that the boundary between offline and online
BRT computation has moved. On a single workstation GPU (NVIDIA
RTX 4000 Ada), the canonical Mitchell Air3D 3D pursuit–evasion
BRT [32] solves in 99\,ms at 32-bit floating point (FP32) with the same
numerical scheme used by the Stanford Autonomous Systems Laboratory (ASL) JAX reference
hj_reachability [45], a 4D pursuit–evasion
BRT at 314≈10631^{4}\approx 10^{6} cells solves in 1616\,ms, and the 2D
drift-affected vehicle BRT solves at 7474–147147\,Hz at WENO5 fidelity.
These rates place the level-set solver inside the inner control loop
of a robot, and shift the design question from how to live with a
single BRT precomputed for an entire mission to how to use a BRT that
is recomputed at every control tick.

Concretely, our solver implements the standard level-set HJI recipe on
CUDA—fifth-order WENO (WENO5) reconstruction of the spatial gradient,
total-variation-diminishing third-order Runge–Kutta (TVD-RK3) time
integration, and a Lax–Friedrichs numerical Hamiltonian—with one
fused kernel per RK3 stage (reconstruction, Hamiltonian, stage
combine, and BRT clamp in-register), a division-lean WENO5
reconstruction, a host-static CFL step, and an FP32 precision mode
that is the relevant regime for embedded robotic deployment. At
matched 64-bit floating point (FP64)
arithmetic (the academic-standard precision for verification studies)
our solver agrees with hj_reachability on eight canonical
benchmarking cases at 2.02.0–4.6×4.6\times the speed on matched hardware,
reproduces Mitchell’s Air3D BRT [32] to within 0.04%0.04\% of the
reference cell count at N=51N{=}51, and is 1.31.3–1.4×1.4\times faster
than a torch.compile [2] reimplementation
of the identical scheme, a maximally-tuned tensor-compiler baseline.
In FP32 mode the solver is
2121–33×33\times faster than its own FP64 path with sub-grid BRT-set
deviation, and 5.95.9–17.5×17.5\times faster than the JAX reference at
matched FP32 on the same hardware. To verify that these rates are
not specific to a desktop-class GPU, we re-run the solver on an
NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor embedded developer kit
and measure 2727–6666\,Hz on the 3D Air3D and 2D drifter cases
(3.83.8–8.9×8.9\times faster than hj_reachability on the same
device), with the closed-loop fleet solve drawing approximately 3131\,W
of total system input power. As a multi-agent
application we extend the 2D solver with an in-kernel
label-propagation kernel, in the spirit of competitive fast
marching [38], that recovers the KK-agent capture-basin
Voronoi tessellation from a single combined HJ solve whose cost is
independent of fleet size, with
99.5%99.5\% label agreement with a per-agent argmin reference.
We demonstrate the latter on a closed-loop wildfire-response fleet of
six quadcopters defending a 20×2020\times 20\,km region under
time-varying, non-uniform wind.

The rest of this article is organized as follows.
Section II reviews the HJ reachability formulation
and the level-set discretization recipe we use.
Section III positions our solver against the
classical-fidelity offline tools and the learned-value online
approximators at the two ends of the existing literature.
Section IV describes the CUDA implementation, the FP32
precision mode, and the boundary and obstacle postprocessors.
Section V describes the verification protocol
against hj_reachability, and Section VI
reports cross-library agreement, the equi-accuracy comparison, and
the FP32 real-time envelope.
Section VII presents the multi-agent
wildfire-response Voronoi demonstration.
Section VIII discusses the dimensional ceiling,
the FP32 fidelity floor, embedded-platform performance on Jetson AGX
Thor, and future work. Section IX concludes.

title: VARP: A Visual Adaptive Rearrangement Planner for Non-Monotone Object Rearrangement Planning
authors: Hanwen Ren,Meng Zheng,Zhongpai Gao,Anwesa Choudhuri,Benjamin Planche,Terrence Chen,Ziyan Wu
abstract: Object rearrangement planning in cluttered environments is often non-monotone, requiring objects to be temporarily relocated before reaching their final destinations. Although search-based planners can solve such tasks, they incur substantial computational cost and require expensive replanning when the environment changes. We propose the Visual Adaptive Rearrangement Planner (VARP), which learns non-monotone rearrangement directly from visual state representations generated from expert demonstrations. VARP predicts pick-and-place actions from the current and goal visual state representations, and incorporates an Action Refinement Strategy (ARS) to improve action feasibility and a Progress Enforcement Strategy (PES) to mitigate progress stagnation. By continuously updating actions from the latest visual state representations, VARP adapts online to disturbances without replanning from scratch or performing online combinatorial search. In challenging rearrangement benchmarks, VARP achieves a 98.3% success rate with only 0.4 s planning time per task, 97.5% success under execution-time disturbances, and 94.5% under continuous severe disturbances, while generalizing effectively to unseen object counts. These results demonstrate that VARP provides a scalable and robust solution for non-monotone object rearrangement.
introduction:
Object rearrangement planning is a fundamental capability for robotic manipulation, with applications in warehouse automation, household assistance, manufacturing, and logistics [1]. Given an initial object arrangement and a desired target configuration, the robot must determine a sequence of prehensile pick-and-place actions that transform the scene while avoiding collisions and satisfying task constraints [2]. In cluttered environments, achieving the target arrangement often requires non-monotone planning, where objects must be temporarily relocated to an intermediate buffer region before they can be placed at their final destinations. Such non-monotone rearrangement problems are known to be NP-hard in general [3], making the task particularly challenging as scene complexity increases.

Classical rearrangement planners typically formulate the problem as a search over object relocation sequences and rely on task-and-motion planning, sampling-based methods [4], or tree search algorithms [5] to identify feasible solutions. While these approaches can produce high-quality plans, they often incur substantial computational cost due to repeated collision checking, dependency reasoning, and motion planning. Furthermore, when the environment changes during execution, planners frequently require expensive replanning procedures to recover from disturbances, limiting their applicability in dynamic settings.

Recent advances in imitation learning and vision-based manipulation have motivated the use of learning-based policies for rearrangement tasks[6]. By learning an observation-to-action mapping directly from expert demonstrations, neural policies can amortize planning effort and generate actions with significantly lower inference latency [7]. However, CNN-based or Transformer-based policies approximate the observation-to-action mapping from finite data and may produce errors under perceptual uncertainty or distribution shift. Unlike search-based planners which explicitly reason about state transitions and action feasibility, existing learning-based approaches often struggle in cluttered non-monotone environments, where small prediction errors may lead to infeasible actions, self-relocations, or repetitive behaviors that prevent task completion [8]. Achieving the efficiency of learned policies while retaining the robustness of classical planning thus remains an open challenge.

To this end, we propose a Visual Adaptive Rearrangement Planner (VARP) for non-monotone object rearrangement planning. VARP combines a goal-conditioned visual policy that efficiently predicts rearrangement actions from visual state representations with two lightweight inference-time reasoning mechanisms that improve action feasibility and long-horizon execution reliability. Executed in a closed-loop manner, VARP continuously updates its decisions based on the latest scene configuration, enabling robust adaptation to execution-time disturbances without expensive online replanning or combinatorial search. Overall, the main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

We propose VARP, a visual adaptive rearrangement planner that integrates a learning-based goal-conditioned visual policy with lightweight inference-time reasoning for efficient and reliable non-monotone object rearrangement planning.

title: MABEL: An Open Anthropomorphic Mobile Bimanual Platform for Teleoperation and Learning
authors: Qilong Cheng,Rooholla Khorrambakht,Mohamed Yassine Kabouri,Quang Nam Nguyen,Luca Macesanu,Haoran Zhou,Yipeng Wang,Ludovic Righetti
comment: . Project page:this https URL
abstract:
As robot learning moves beyond the tabletop, many tasks require mobility, adjustable reach, active perception, and bimanual dexterity.
Commercial platforms combining these capabilities are costly, while affordable open-source alternatives cover only a subset and require software integration.
We present MABEL, an open-source anthropomorphic mobile bimanual robot with 56 degrees of freedom (DOF) and a US$8.1k parts cost.
It combines two 7-DOF arms with 17-DOF hands, a pitching torso, a lift, a 3-DOF neck, and a holonomic base.
Back-drivable arms and torso support compliant interaction, with fingertip reach from floor level to 2.23 m2.23\text{\,}\mathrm{m}.
The head and torso roughly triple modeled camera coverage relative to a torso-fixed camera.
Apple Vision Pro head and hand tracking enables whole-body teleoperation without handheld controllers, with 137 ms137\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{s} mean glass-to-glass stereo video latency over the robot’s Wi-Fi hotspot.
We demonstrate an end-to-end imitation learning pipeline, from teleoperated data collection to policy deployment, using a shared command interface and whole-body controller.
introduction:
Recent advances in learning from demonstrations [1, 2, 3, 4] have enabled increasingly complex household tasks involving mobile and bimanual dexterous manipulation.
Moving such learning off the tabletop now depends as much on capable embodiments as on better policies.
Collecting the data requires a robot with enough degrees of freedom (DOF) to move, reach across heights, perceive actively, and often manipulate dexterously.
Its actuators must also provide the torque to carry payloads and the back-drivability or torque feedback needed for compliant, contact-rich interaction.
Commercial platforms do offer robots that combine these capabilities, but at the cost of US$69k–$120k [5, 6, 7], a substantial barrier to adoption for most research laboratories.
Open-source platforms cost far less, but they often give up capability.
Many rely on position-controlled servos and 1-DOF grippers [1, 3, 8, 9], some trade mobility for stronger arms on a fixed base [10], and few offer active gaze or adjustable height [11, 12].
Many labs instead assemble custom systems from commercial arms, mobile bases, and lifts, leaving each to integrate its own teleoperation, simulation, and data-recording software.

Base: Holo. = holonomic, Nonholo. = nonholonomic; arms: DOF×\timescount; hand, neck: DOF; body: lift, torso, or both.
Shading:

We present MABEL, a Mobile Anthropomorphic Bimanual Embodiment for Learning: an open-source, full-stack platform that meets these requirements at a parts cost of US$8,056 (Fig. 1).
Back-drivable 7-DOF arms adapted from OpenArm [15] and a pitching torso support compliant contact.
The torso and a lift extend fingertip reach from the floor to 2.23 m2.23\text{\,}\mathrm{m}, a 3-DOF neck provides active perception, and a three-module swerve base provides omnidirectional mobility.
The end-effector is modular and can be swapped with 17-DOF ORCA hands [16] or a gripper depending on the research needs (Table I, Fig. 2).
With an Apple Vision Pro, the robot becomes the operator’s avatar: head and hand tracking alone is retargeted into whole-body motion, and the robot’s stereo view returns to the headset at 137 ms137\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{s} glass-to-glass latency (Sec. IV).
Teleoperation, simulation, and learned policies share one command interface and whole-body controller, so demonstrations are recorded through the control path that later executes the policy (Fig. 3, Sec. V).
On hardware, we characterize repeatability, odometry, and latency, demonstrate teleoperated household tasks including compliant interaction, and train and deploy a whole-body Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) policy to validate the learning pipeline (Sec. VI).
All designs, software, and the digital twin are released, and the robot goes from parts to running in about two weeks (Sec. III).
Our contributions are:

Affordable open hardware: a US$8.1k fully open-source mobile bimanual platform integrating compliant actuation, dexterity, mobility, active perception, and floor-to-overhead reach.

Whole-body teleoperation: a controller-free interface that retargets sparse head and hand tracking into whole-body motion with stereo feedback.

Unified control and learning stack: one compliant whole-body controller shared by teleoperation, simulation, data collection, and learned policies, validated end to end with an ACT policy.

title: FEIJOA: Task-Driven Grounding and Execution for Mobile Manipulation
authors: Aditya Agarwal,William Shen,Sahit Chintalapudi,Lucy Cai,Nishanth Kumar,Aidan Curtis,Travis Manderson,Tomás Lozano-Pérez,Leslie Pack Kaelbling
abstract:
A mobile manipulator asked to “put the toys away in the toy box” must decide which objects are toys and which container the user means, then find base poses, grasps, and placements it can execute.
Because a scene representation is built before the instruction is known, it may lack the attributes, affordances, or concepts needed to resolve the task.
We present Feijoa, a language-model agent that grounds the instruction at test time. It queries a grounding tool over a posed RGB-D scan, inspects the returned candidates, and refines its queries until they resolve the instruction.
An embodiment-aware harness checks each skill’s preconditions, samples base poses from which the target is reachable, and verifies the skill’s effect from observations before and after execution.
On 103 open-ended grounding queries, Feijoa resolves 94.2% exactly, compared with 68.0% for the best prebuilt representation.
Over 50 real-world trials on Spot, it completes 35 tasks; 17 of these successes follow recovery from a failed tool call or verification check. Of the 15 failed trials, 13 were caused by the robot’s physical skills, and only 2 by grounding or the agent’s reasoning.
introduction:
Robots operating in homes and offices must execute long-horizon tasks from open-ended natural language instructions.
Consider asking a robot to “Clean up the room so the plush toys are all on the same table”.
To complete this task, the robot must identify all the plush toys among everything else in the room, determine which table the user likely wants the toys placed on (one table already has four plush toys on it), navigate to base poses from which it can grasp and stably place the toys onto the table, and monitor its progress and recover from failures in execution.
More generally, this requires open-ended grounding that depends on the task, the state of the environment, and common-sense reasoning. Acting on what is grounded requires finding base poses, grasps, and placements that are collision-free and feasible for the robot’s embodiment.

Many existing approaches construct task-agnostic semantic scene representations before the instruction is known. These include open-vocabulary 3D object maps [1], 3D scene graphs encoding spatial and semantic relationships between objects [2, 3, 4, 5], and 3D feature fields [6, 7, 8].
These representations make large environments efficient to index, since the expensive perception is done once, before any query.
However, they reduce the scene to a collection of embeddings or captions, and are therefore incomplete with respect to any specific instruction: they may lack the fine-grained attributes, affordances, and concepts it requires (e.g., “most colorful object”, “plush toy with a bow tie”, “cleanest table with shelves above it”).
We argue that for open-ended mobile manipulation, grounding must be task-driven and computed against raw observations at test time: which objects to find, and what relationships to resolve between them, depend on the instruction.

We introduce Feijoa, a language-model agent for long-horizon mobile manipulation that decides what to ground and how to act (Figure 2).
The agent has access to tools that ground objects, update and mark off subgoals in its task plan, estimate the cost of navigating between objects, and execute robot skills such as navigation, picking, placing, pushing, and wiping.
At each turn, the agent chooses among these tools based on the current observations and robot state, its task plan, and the history of its reasoning and tool results.
Our embodiment-aware harness constructs this context for each turn, dispatches every tool call, and records its result for the agent’s next decision.
For a robot skill, the harness also checks feasibility before execution and verifies the effects afterwards.

We evaluate Feijoa’s grounding performance, ablate key design decisions in the harness, and deploy it in the real world on a Spot quadruped with an arm and an RB-Y1 bimanual humanoid with a wheeled base.
Over 103 grounding queries that reference objects by category, attribute, spatial relation, membership in a set, or that require reasoning beyond appearance (e.g., negation, affordance, comparison), Feijoa finds every target object with no false positives on 94.2% of them.
Feijoa significantly outperforms the best baseline, a text-captioned 3D scene graph at 68.0%, and our grounding tool without the agent at 47.6%.
We demonstrate that each design decision in our harness matters by ablating effect verification, feasibility-aware sampling, and cost estimation.
Finally, we run 50 real-world trials on Spot over short, medium, and long horizon tasks, in which the agent made 1,045 tool calls in total and executed up to 12 manipulation skills per trial, excluding navigation.
Feijoa succeeds on 35/50 trials, 17 of them after recovering from a failed tool call or verification check.
Of the 15 failed trials, 13 were caused by the robot’s physical skills, and only 2 by grounding or the agent’s reasoning.

Overall, we make three contributions: (1) task-driven grounding, in which a language-model agent decides what and how to query our grounding tool and judges its results against the instruction;
(2) an embodiment-aware agent harness that checks a skill’s preconditions and samples feasible parameters before execution, and verifies the effects afterwards;
and (3) 50 real-world mobile manipulation trials on Spot with an analysis of how the agent recovers from failed tool calls and where the system fails.

title: A Practical Causal Framework for Autonomous Mobile Robots: From Simulation to Real-World Human Environments
authors: Luca Castri,Gloria Beraldo,Nicola Bellotto
comment: Accepted in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
abstract: Causal inference has emerged as a powerful paradigm enabling robots to make safe, efficient decisions by reasoning about the “why” behind events. However, its real-world application is hindered by the difficulty of collecting causal data, especially in human-populated environments where training takes time, while users expect immediate operation. To this end, we tackle the challenge of transferring simulation-learnt causal relations to the real world with minimal effort. While retaining the invariant high-level causal structure, we empirically demonstrate the system adapts efficiently to real-world situations by updating only the causal model parameters with a limited set of new observations. Our results show that the parameter update enables rapid sim-to-real transfer. The framework runs efficiently onboard of a mobile robot and significantly outperforms a non-causal baselines navigating successfully and safely in complex human-shared scenarios.
introduction:
Deploying autonomous mobile robots in human-populated environments (e.g., warehouses, hospitals, airports, malls) requires safe and efficient interaction with humans. Understanding how robot actions causally affect their surroundings enables better action selection, motivating methods that reason about causal relationships in the environment and human-robot interactions.
Accordingly, the robotics community has increasingly embraced causal approaches in various fields Hellström (2021), including robot manipulation Lee et al. (2021); Cannizzaro et al. (2025); Castri et al. (2024c), explainable robotics and HRI Diehl and Ramirez-Amaro (2022); Love et al. (2024), spatial interactions Castri et al. (2024b), planning Cannizzaro and Kunze (2023), and robot understanding Edström et al. (2023).
However, transitioning these algorithmic frameworks from theoretical formulation to real-world deployment remains a challenge. Even in purely robotic scenarios, this process is hindered by the need for extensive and time-consuming data collection Zhao et al. (2020). This difficulty is amplified in human-populated settings, where long-term data collection is often impractical.

Despite these constraints, users typically expect robots to be immediately functional. To meet this operational demand, a robust strategy must leverage simulation for extensive data collection and subsequent causal discovery, while enabling rapid adaptation to real-world dynamics. This necessitates a modular, end-to-end causal inference framework—spanning from raw sensor data acquisition and structure learning directly to online reasoning. Crucially, such a framework must be capable of efficient sim-to-real transfer, retaining the high-level logic learnt in simulation while seamlessly updating its parameters to the physical environment.

Prior work Castri et al. (2026) laid the groundwork for our approach with a modular, causality-enhanced decision-making framework supporting both causal discovery and reasoning. However, the authors evaluated task execution efficiency and human safety only in simulation, leaving real-world deployment and validation unaddressed. This paper bridges the gap between simulated and real applications by proposing an improved framework with a data-efficient adaptation process that tunes the initial simulation-learnt causal model to work equally well on a physical mobile robot in human environments (Fig. 1).
We validate this approach in two real-world scenarios – a poster session and a social event – proving that the causal framework operates as expected onboard of a robot for solving challenging navigation tasks, outperforming a non-causal alternative while maintaining low inference time.
Our main contributions include:

A new data-efficient sim-to-real transfer that exploits structural causal invariance to adapt the framework via rapid parameter update on limited real-world data.

The first real-world deployment and validation of an end-to-end causality-based framework applied to robot navigation tasks in human environments, made publicly available11
1
https://lcastri.github.io/causal-sim2real/ for reproducibility and future applications.

An experimental evaluation across challenging simulated and real-world group encounters, focusing on task success, operational safety and inference time.

title: Physical Experience Builds Continual Spatial World Models
authors: Yuhang Sun
abstract:
World models are increasingly used to support prediction and planning in
embodied agents, but the knowledge is usually established before
deployment and then carried into later encounters. Continual operation
faces a different problem. A familiar environment may change, and the
agent must use previous experience without allowing old expectations to
override current physical evidence. This study asks what repeated
physical experience must contribute for a spatial world model to become
progressively more useful rather than simply more persistent. A
physics-grounded dynamic maze separates recurring spatial change from
the continuous consequences of action. Cross-episode Spatial Change
Memory learns relations among environmental transformations, while
state-action-outcome experience refines predictions of motion.
Structured experience progressively reduces the need for future route
correction and transfers to spatial transitions not encountered during
learning. The advantage disappears when past changes contain no
information about future ones. Continuous navigation further shows that
predictive memory changes behavior when a previous decision becomes
invalid but leaves behavior unchanged when the decision remains correct.
Physical tests expose a complementary limit: correct topology does not
guarantee correct action prediction, and accumulated physical experience
reduces this mismatch within the modeled dynamics. The results
characterize continual world knowledge as experience that improves
future prediction and action beyond stored episodes while remaining
revisable by the physical outcomes it is intended to predict.
introduction:
The ability to predict the consequences of action has shaped model-based
learning from its earliest formulations. Dyna used observed transitions
both to improve a model and to plan with it [1], and PILCO later
showed that data-efficient control could be obtained from learned
probabilistic dynamics [2]. Deep world models extended the same
principle to high-dimensional observations: recurrent latent models,
PlaNet, Dreamer, MuZero, and more recent general-purpose world-model
agents demonstrated that compact predictive states can support planning,
imagined rollouts, and policy learning [3-7]. These systems
established the practical value of internal predictive models.
Deployment, however, changes the question. A robot does not encounter a
single stationary environment once. It returns to places whose
accessibility, geometry, and dynamics may evolve, so a model that was
adequate yesterday can become incomplete without any failure in the
planner itself.

Spatial navigation makes this problem especially transparent.
Cognitive-map experiments suggested that animals can represent spatial
relations beyond fixed stimulus-response associations [8], and
place- and grid-cell studies established neural correlates of location
and movement across experience [9,10]. Robotics developed analogous
capabilities through probabilistic mapping and localization [11,12],
structured neural memory [13], topological memory [14],
long-horizon scene memory [15], and learned topological navigation
[16]. A complementary planning literature asked how computation from
earlier problems could be reused after the environment changes. D* Lite
and Lifelong Planning A* retain information from earlier searches
[17,18], while Experience Graphs reuse successful motions to bias
subsequent planning [19]. These contributions show that memory and
previous computation can make navigation more efficient. They also
delimit the question addressed here: route reuse, incremental
replanning, and episodic storage are not by themselves evidence that a
world model has learned how a changing environment behaves.

Continual learning has largely focused on retaining competence while new
data arrive, including regularization, replay, and architectural
mechanisms for limiting catastrophic forgetting [23,24]. Online
model-based reinforcement learning has begun to address a related
requirement by updating predictive dynamics during continued interaction
[25]. For spatial world models, the unresolved issue is more
specific. A robot may detect a familiar blockage and replan successfully
on every visit, yet the tenth visit can require nearly the same new
observation and correction as the first. Repeated success can therefore
coexist with little accumulation of reusable spatial knowledge.
Conversely, a large episode archive may help only when the current
situation closely matches a stored one. A stronger test is whether
experience acquired elsewhere changes prediction on a held-out encounter
and reduces the amount of correction needed later. This shifts attention
from memory of previous states to regularities in how spatial states
transform across encounters.

Embodiment adds a second source of incompleteness. A route can be
topologically valid and still fail during execution because rolling
inertia, dissipation, contact, or actuator response changes the
consequence of a command. Physics-aware control and system
identification have long treated these effects as essential to reliable
behavior [20,21], and robotic world-model formulations increasingly
emphasize action-conditioned prediction in the physical environment
[22]. The point is not that navigation has ignored dynamics. Rather,
spatial memory and action dynamics are commonly represented at different
levels of the system: one determines where a transition exists, while
another determines whether the body can realize it from the current
state. The resulting internal map may be spatially correct yet
insufficient to predict the outcome of action.

A deliberately small tilted circular maze is used here to separate these
questions experimentally. Gate states can change between encounters,
while a rolling ball is governed by inertia, dissipation, compliant
contact, and finite actuator lag. Spatial Change Memory (SCM) pools
evidence about recurring relations among changes instead of caching
complete routes. A complementary state-action model accumulates physical
transitions and updates predictions of action consequences. The study
rests on two testable assumptions. First, repeated environmental changes
may contain transferable statistical structure; when that structure is
removed, additional history should not improve prediction. Second, over
the operating range considered here, the dominant physical consequences
of action can be represented by an interpretable low-dimensional
dynamics model. The experiments therefore combine a zero-information
change control, a spatial transition withheld entirely from training,
matched decision-changing and decision-preserving navigation episodes,
and controlled physical-model mismatch. The aim is not to claim a
general solution to lifelong robotics, but to identify when repeated
interaction produces knowledge that is reusable across encounters and
still corrigible by the physical world. Figure 1
summarizes the experimental logic: repeated navigation and reactive
updating (Figure 1(a,b)), cross-episode Spatial Change
Memory (Figure 1(c)), and the structured-versus-random
predictability boundary used as a falsifiable control
(Figure 1(d)).

title: Self-governed access control in open robot swarms using a blockchain-based DAO
authors: Raina Zakir,Alexandre Pacheco,Andreagiovanni Reina,Marco Dorigo,Volker Strobel
abstract: Robot swarms harness simple, local interactions among many individually limited robots to produce complex, coordinated collective behavior, making them valuable across domains from agriculture to disaster response. We envision the next frontier for such swarms as open swarms, in which robots join or leave the swarm dynamically at runtime. The ability to dynamically adjust swarm size has been shown to be beneficial, for instance by reducing inconsistencies and network partitioning, especially under sparse connectivity or in complex environments, ultimately improving task performance. For practical deployment, however, open swarms requires governance, particularly protection against Byzantine behavior (i.e., faulty or malicious robots), since allowing robots to join freely also makes the swarm easier to infiltrate. Blockchain technology has recently been incorporated into robot swarms, offering secure, decentralized coordination and improved resilience, though largely in closed settings with a fixed, predetermined membership. In this work, we extend these benefits to open swarms by introducing robot swarms governed by a blockchain-based decentralized autonomous organization (DAO), in which the swarm regulates itself using autonomous rules encoded in smart contracts. We outline several DAO-based governance mechanisms for robot swarms, depending on the needs of the application, and present a proof-of-concept implementation of a simple DAO that regulates swarm membership and prevents Byzantine infiltration. Our simulation results and real-robot validations show that DAO-governed access control and robot removal can maintain proper swarm functioning while keeping the number of Byzantine robots within acceptable limits.

title: h-NESDF: An Infinitely Differentiable Signed Distance Between Two Sets with Robotic Applications
authors: Vinicius Mariano Gonçalves,Pedro Antonio de Souza Campos Rodrigues
abstract: Computing distances between sets is important in many robotic applications, such as motion planning and control. In many applications, derivatives of the distance are needed as well. It is well known that the Euclidean distance is not always differentiable, which create issues to algorithms that need a derivative. In this paper, we introduce NESDF, the Normal Euclidean Signed Distance Function between two general (with mild regularity assumptions but possibly non-convex) sets. This metric is still not differentiable, but it allows us to introduce a generalization, hh-NESDF, which has a smoothing parameter hh such that the metric is infinitely differentiable for all h>0h>0 and that reduces to the NESDF when hh goes to 00. The metric is amenable to GPU parallelization, and thus can be computed efficiently. We show extensive simulation results to evaluate its viability in motion planning.
introduction:
Distance computations are central to robot motion planning, collision detection, and control. Their integration into gradient-based planners and feedback controllers often requires more than accurate distance values: the underlying functions must also provide sufficiently regular derivatives. Control Barrier Functions (CBFs), for example, rely on gradients, and some formulations require higher-order derivatives of distance-like functions to enforce safety constraints [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. Insufficient regularity can lead to excessively large control inputs [8] or noisy control signals [9]. Motion planners such as CHOMP [10] similarly use distance gradients to update trajectories and resolve collisions during optimization. In this setting, signed distance-like functions are particularly useful because their negative values encode overlap and provide information about infeasible configurations.

However, Euclidean distance functions are generally not differentiable at every configuration [11]. A common source of nonsmoothness is a change in the geometric features that determine the closest points. Such transitions often involve nonunique witness points, namely, pairs of points, one on each object, that attain the minimum distance. This can produce abrupt changes in the distance gradient as the relative pose of the objects varies.

Several works have investigated differentiable alternatives to Euclidean distance functions for robotic applications. The approach in [8] introduced an infinitely differentiable, unsigned distance-like function between convex sets and applied it to second-order kinematic control. The method generalized von Neumann’s alternating projection algorithm into an iterative distance computation, but remained cumbersome to evaluate and did not guarantee a zero value when the sets overlapped. Subsequently, [9] introduced a substantially simpler formulation that correctly vanishes upon overlap, while retaining the convexity assumption and unsigned nature of the function. The work in [12] developed a differentiable distance-like function between a point and an object represented as a set of discrete points, and used it to construct safe and smooth guiding vector fields that avoid collision with obstacles represented as point clouds. Signed differentiable distance metric between convex sets were also developed in [6, 13], using different smoothing techniques and demonstrating applications to CBF-based control.
Related constructions also arise outside robotics, particularly in surface reconstruction. For example, [14] reconstructs a smooth approximation of a point-to-set signed distance field from sampled surface data. Similarly, [15] proposes an explicit differentiable level-set formulation that approximates the signed distance to a geometry.
The methods discussed above either assume convexity for both extended objects or address point-to-set distances. More recently, [16] introduced a smooth signed distance metric for nonconvex objects aiming to use it within a contact simulation framework. Table I shows comparisons between different differentiable distance approaches.

In this work, we propose a signed, infinitely differentiable distance-like function between two possibly nonconvex objects. We first introduce the Normal Euclidean Signed Distance Function (NESDF), a potentially nonsmooth function whose sign characterizes separation, contact, and interior overlap. We then apply a smoothing procedure to obtain the hh-NESDF, which is infinitely differentiable with respect to smoothly parameterized rigid motions. Its sampled approximation is amenable to GPU parallelization. Figure 1 shows an example of the hh-NESDF computed for two LL shapes as one of them rotates, with three different values of hh, one of them being as h→+0h\rightarrow+0, that is, the non-differentiable case.

Our construction differs from the proposed metric in [16] in several respects, bringing some benefits. One distinction concerns the use of the gradient of the metric in a gradient-ascent procedure for resolving overlap between two objects, useful, for example, in motion planning. In some deeply overlapping configurations, the metric in [16] produces an ascent direction that increases geometric overlap, whereas ours produces the correct behavior. These distinctions are examined in detail throughout the paper.

The contributions of this paper are then:

NESDF, the Normal Euclidean Signed Distance Function, a novel signed distance metric between two general, possibly non-convex sets in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. We establish that this metric has the expected behavior of being positive when the two objects do not overlap and negative when they overlap. This metric is also amenable for a smoothfication procedure.

NESDF, the Normal Euclidean Signed Distance Function, a novel signed distance metric between two general, possibly non-convex sets in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. We establish that this metric has the expected behavior of being positive when the two objects do not overlap and negative when they overlap. This metric is also amenable for a smoothfication procedure.

hh-NESDF, a smoothed version of NESDF that is infinitely differentiable, with smoothing parameter hh that controls the smoothing. We show that when h→+0h\rightarrow+0, NESDF is recovered. This metric can be implemented in an approximated manner using sampled point clouds and normal vectors, and parallelized on a GPU. This metric brings benefits when compared to other comparable approaches, as [16].

We present extensive computational experiments assessing hh-NESDF efficiency and usefulness in motion planning .

title: CoReMatch: Recurrent Continuous Coordinate Refinement for Real-Time Robotic Feature Matching
authors: Robert J. Wang,Charles Ling,Boyu Wang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: Accepted by CoRL 2026
abstract: Feature matching underpins many robotic perception tasks, including visual localization, mapping, SLAM, and autonomous navigation. Existing semi-dense matchers predict confidence on fixed grids, limiting correspondences to predefined locations and requiring costly high-resolution grids for precise localization. We present CoReMatch (Coordinate Refinement Match), a recurrent framework that refines correspondences directly in continuous coordinate space rather than predicting discrete confidence maps. CoReMatch progressively improves correspondence estimates by propagating information across iterations. At the coarse stage, a Deep Aggregated Transformer captures global context and iteratively updates correspondence coordinates, while a lightweight regression head further sharpens their localization. Experiments on indoor and outdoor benchmarks show that CoReMatch strikes a strong balance between accuracy and efficiency, outperforming Efficient LoFTR in accuracy while running more than 10×10\times faster on embedded edge hardware. These results demonstrate that recurrent coordinate refinement offers an efficient and scalable approach to real-time feature matching for robotic perception. Code is available at edge-cv/CoReMatch.
introduction:
Image feature matching establishes pixel-level correspondences between images and is a core component of robotic perception. It supports visual localization, mapping, pose estimation, and navigation in systems such as SLAM, VIO, and autonomous aerial robots. In real-time applications, matches must be computed under tight latency, memory, and power constraints, as unreliable correspondences can directly degrade trajectory estimation, map consistency, and control stability.
Classical matching pipelines rely on keypoint detection and descriptor matching, but often struggle with large viewpoint changes, motion blur, illumination variations, and low-texture regions. Learning-based methods improve robustness by combining dense visual features with global context. In particular, semi-dense matchers [24, 35, 4, 11, 18, 25, 29, 33] replace explicit keypoint detection with coarse dense matching, followed by local refinement of high-confidence correspondences.

Despite their effectiveness, existing semi-dense matchers typically predict discrete confidence maps over spatial grids. Precise localization is therefore constrained by the resolution of the prediction grid, often requiring higher-resolution inputs to achieve accurate correspondences. However, the computational and memory costs of Transformer-based architectures increase substantially with input resolution. Although recent methods reduce theoretical FLOPs through linear or aggregated attention, practical runtime on embedded platforms can still be dominated by memory movement and feature aggregation. Consequently, modest increases in image resolution can lead to disproportionate latency growth. For example, as shown in Tab. 7, Efficient LoFTR [33] requires 311 ms to process a 640×640640\times 640 image pair, while increasing the resolution to 960×960960\times 960 results in a 4.5×4.5\times runtime increase for only a 1.5×1.5\times increase in input resolution. At 1152×11521152\times 1152, it requires more than two seconds to process an image pair on an NVIDIA AGX Orin. This scaling behavior presents a significant challenge for real-time and on-device robotic perception, motivating more resolution-efficient approaches to correspondence estimation.

Recent dense matching methods [8, 9] obtain subpixel correspondences through continuous regression and iterative refinement. However, they commonly rely on correlation volumes and multi-scale warping, which introduce substantial computational and memory overhead. These limitations motivate a central question: Can semi-dense matching produce accurate subpixel correspondences without high-resolution prediction grids or costly correlation-volume refinement?

In this work, we answer this question with CoReMatch (Coordinate Refinement Match), an efficient semi-dense feature matching framework designed for real-time robotic perception. Unlike existing semi-dense methods that formulate matching as discrete confidence prediction over feature grids, CoReMatch reformulates correspondence estimation as a recurrent continuous coordinate refinement problem. CoReMatch directly refines correspondences in coordinate space through persistent hidden-state updates, significantly reducing computational and memory overhead while preserving accurate sub-pixel localization.
Specifically, CoReMatch adopts a two-stage recurrent refinement framework. At the coarse level, a Deep Aggregated Transformer (DAT) iteratively predicts and refines correspondences through direct coordinate updates while maintaining a persistent hidden state across iterations. This design enables efficient global geometric reasoning without explicit dense correlation-volume construction. The recurrent refinement process shares parameters across iterations, allowing the number of refinement steps to be dynamically adjusted at runtime based on hardware constraints or convergence behavior.
At the fine level, a lightweight convolutional network performs local dense regression within small full-resolution windows for efficient sub-pixel refinement. By combining recurrent coordinate-space refinement with sparse computation, CoReMatch bridges the gap between efficient semi-dense matching and accurate dense correspondence estimation.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:

A recurrent continuous refinement framework for efficient semi-dense feature matching. We formulate semi-dense matching as a recurrent continuous coordinate refinement problem, enabling accurate sub-pixel correspondence estimation without constructing a dense correlation volume. CoReMatch enables efficient geometric reasoning while reducing reliance on high-resolution feature maps. As a result, CoReMatch achieves higher accuracy at a lower input resolution (448×\times448) than Efficient LoFTR at substantially higher resolutions.

State-of-the-art accuracy–efficiency trade-offs with strong robotic generalization.
We evaluate CoReMatch on multiple indoor and outdoor correspondence benchmarks, including MegaDepth [14], ScanNet [5], and HPatches [1]. CoReMatch consistently outperforms state-of-the-art semi-dense methods while achieving over 10×10\times faster inference on embedded edge devices. Beyond benchmarks, CoReMatch improves robustness in downstream SLAM and VIO systems and demonstrates strong generalization to unseen environments and cross-modality RGB–infrared matching.
