title: Self-Consistent Neural Control: Learning Trajectories for Implicit Equilibrium
authors: Hengyi Zhou,Haobo Fang,Xiaonan Huang,Dezhong Tong,M. Khalid Jawed
abstract: One big challenge in physical AI is interacting with systems whose states are defined by implicit equilibrium. Learning in these systems is difficult because their responses can be multistable, path-dependent, and sensitive over long horizons. Adjoint learning provides an efficient way to optimize trajectories without unrolling iterative equilibrium solvers, but its gradient relies on the frozen-tangent approximation, which neglects higher-order sensitivity terms and can become inaccurate when the local equilibrium varies rapidly. In this work, we introduce Self-Consistent Neural Control (SCNC), optimizing trajectories along which sensitivity variations are explicitly controlled. We derive a mathematical bound on the resulting gradient error and develop a practical finite-difference approximation. We validate the framework on deformable objects, which are representative of implicit equilibrium systems, ranging from simple quadratic energy models such as elastic rods to complex systems including thin-walled tubes, measuring tapes, and Slinky-like structures. Compared with the adjoint learning and the gradient-free iCEM baselines, SCNC achieves faster convergence and more stable optimization by reducing switching to undesirable equilibrium branches, doubling the stable optimization rate over adjoint learning (83.3% vs. 41.7%) and reducing the average loss by more than 1.5 orders of magnitude on thin-walled tubes, where sensitivity variations are pronounced.
introduction:
Physical AI aims to enable robots to perceive, reason, and interact with the physical world.
For robots that manipulate compliant objects and structures, many interactions can be modeled through mechanical equilibrium rather than explicit state-transition equations.
The system state is therefore obtained by solving an equilibrium problem subject to control-dependent boundary conditions.
Efficient learning and control through such implicit models are important for complex robotic interactions and have attracted growing interest (Yin et al. 2021; Tong et al. 2026).

Despite this progress, learning and long-horizon control through implicit equilibrium systems remain challenging, particularly when the equilibrium response varies strongly with the control input.
Multiple stable equilibria may coexist, and the equilibrium branch reached by the system can depend on its deformation history (Tong et al. 2026).
Deformable-object manipulation provides representative examples.
As shown in Fig. 1, elastic rods provide a relatively well-behaved, bending-dominated case, although the attained equilibrium branch can still depend on the deformation path.
Measuring tapes and thin-walled tubes are more instability-prone: increasing curvature can induce cross-sectional deformation, kinking, and abrupt equilibrium changes through the Brazier effect (Pastrana et al. 2025) (Fig. 1(B)–(C)).
More complex structures, such as Slinky-like systems, exhibit strongly coupled bending, stretching, and large geometric reconfiguration (Fig. 1(D)).
Although these systems differ mechanically, they illustrate a more general computational challenge: the local sensitivity of an implicit state to control can vary rapidly along the optimization trajectory.

Existing approaches differentiate such systems by unrolling iterative solvers, differentiating explicit learned surrogates, or applying implicit differentiation to converged equilibria or fixed points (Hu et al. 2020; Sanchez-Gonzalez et al. 2020; Bai et al. 2019).
Explicit surrogates provide direct gradients but require representative training data and may accumulate model error over long horizons (Sanchez-Gonzalez et al. 2020; Janner et al. 2019).
Implicit models are commonly evaluated through iterative solvers such as Newton–CG or fixed-point iteration.
Differentiating through these iterations requires unrolling and backpropagating through the full solution process (Williams and Peng 1990), resulting in deeply nested computational graphs and substantial computational and memory costs.
These limitations motivate methods that differentiate directly through the converged implicit condition without unrolling the internal solver iterations.

Recently, adjoint learning was proposed to retain the implicit forward solve while avoiding costly solver unrolling (Tong et al. 2026).
Rather than differentiating through the internal iterations of the equilibrium solver, it constructs proxy dynamics whose gradients are determined by the sensitivity of the converged equilibrium state to controllable quantities.
To improve computational efficiency over long horizons, adjoint learning further adopts a frozen-tangent approximation, in which higher-order variations of the implicit-state sensitivity along the trajectory are neglected (Tong et al. 2026).

The accuracy of this approximation, however, relies on the implicit-state sensitivity varying sufficiently slowly along the optimization trajectory. This condition can fail in strongly nonlinear regimes, where small changes in control may produce large variations in the local sensitivity or drive the system toward different solution branches (Mróz and Haftka 1994; Geng et al. 2021). The neglected higher-order sensitivity variations can then introduce substantial gradient errors, producing poor search directions and driving optimization toward highly sensitive or undesirable regions of the implicit solution landscape. This exposes a fundamental inconsistency: the gradient approximation assumes locally smooth implicit-state sensitivity, yet the optimization trajectory itself is unconstrained from entering regions where this assumption becomes invalid.

We address this inconsistency with Self-Consistent Neural Control (SCNC), a framework for learning control policies in implicit equilibrium systems with both smooth and rapidly varying equilibrium sensitivities (Fig. 2). SCNC is self-consistent in the sense that it regularizes the optimization trajectory to satisfy the local smoothness condition on which its own gradient approximation relies. Rather than assuming that higher-order sensitivity variations are negligible, SCNC explicitly controls their magnitude along the trajectory. We derive a bound relating these variations to the resulting gradient error, making gradient validity a consequence of the optimization process rather than an external assumption. We further develop a practical finite-difference formulation that estimates these sensitivity variations using neighboring converged implicit states to avoid high computational cost.

We validate SCNC across a range of implicit equilibrium systems, including elastic rods, thin-walled tubes, measuring tapes, and Slinky-like structures with neural-network-based energy models. The benchmarks span both smooth bending-dominated responses and strongly instability-prone regimes, with validation in simulation and real robotic manipulation experiments. Compared with adjoint learning and the gradient-free iCEM baseline, SCNC achieves lower task loss and higher optimization success rates while retaining computational efficiency comparable to adjoint learning.

In summary, the main contributions of this work are:

We characterize theoretically and numerically how rapidly varying implicit-state sensitivities can introduce substantial errors under the frozen-tangent approximation, leading to unreliable gradients along the optimization trajectory.

We develop Self-Consistent Neural Control (SCNC), derive a bound relating higher-order implicit-state sensitivity variations to gradient error, and introduce a practical finite-difference formulation that estimates and regularizes these variations along the optimization trajectory.

We validate SCNC across smooth and instability-prone implicit equilibrium systems, including elastic rods, thin-walled tubes, measuring tapes, and Slinky-like structures, demonstrating improved task performance and optimization robustness over adjoint learning and the gradient-free iCEM baseline in both simulation and real-world experiments.

1. We characterize theoretically and numerically how rapidly varying implicit-state sensitivities can introduce substantial errors under the frozen-tangent approximation, leading to unreliable gradients along the optimization trajectory.

2. We develop Self-Consistent Neural Control (SCNC), derive a bound relating higher-order implicit-state sensitivity variations to gradient error, and introduce a practical finite-difference formulation that estimates and regularizes these variations along the optimization trajectory.

3. We validate SCNC across smooth and instability-prone implicit equilibrium systems, including elastic rods, thin-walled tubes, measuring tapes, and Slinky-like structures, demonstrating improved task performance and optimization robustness over adjoint learning and the gradient-free iCEM baseline in both simulation and real-world experiments.

title: RoboScope Kit: Unified Interfaces for Fast and Scalable Embodied-AI Evaluation
authors: Deng-Ke Wu,Yifan Jin,Yida Yang,Lei Qian,Zhaoye Zhou,Hongru Zhang,Kai Ye,Shuyuan Hu,Yiran Mao,Zewei Ye,Bo Zhao
comment: . Project page:this https URLCode:this https URL
abstract:
Simulation benchmarks are the standard way to compare robot policies, but each benchmark brings its
own evaluator, observation layout, and action convention, and evaluation is slow: 500 RoboTwin Easy
episodes with one simulator and one model on one GPU take 359.7 minutes. Profiling the official
StarVLA evaluator shows that simulation occupies CPU cores while the GPU averages 14.3% utilization.
RoboScope Kit wraps each model once in a Python class called a Policy, and each benchmark once in an
adapter around the benchmark’s own evaluator, so the benchmark’s rules and scoring stay unchanged. Scheduling runs simulator workers and Policy replicas as separate pools,
sizes both from measured probes, and shards work deterministically across GPU instances; runtime
optimization renders only the observations an action-chunk Policy reads. Adapters cover six benchmark families. On LIBERO-Long with a StarVLA
checkpoint on one 48 GiB RTX 4090, the concurrency search selects twelve simulator workers sharing three
Policy replicas, which evaluate 500 episodes 4.45×\times faster than the official StarVLA evaluation
with equivalent success rates, 2.78×\times faster than RLinf, and 1.52×\times faster than vla-eval
at its tuned configuration. With CUDA MPS, which lets the replicas run their kernels concurrently,
the search selects sixteen workers sharing four replicas, 6.16×\times faster than StarVLA,
3.85×\times faster than RLinf, and 2.10×\times faster than vla-eval. On RoboTwin Easy, four GPUs with
chunk-boundary observation complete the 500 episodes in 14.4 minutes, 25.04×\times faster than the
single-GPU baseline, with identical success outcomes and terminal steps.
introduction:
Simulation benchmarks evaluate complementary aspects of robot behavior: knowledge transfer in
LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023), bimanual manipulation in RoboTwin (Chen et al., 2025),
language-conditioned task sequences in CALVIN (Mees et al., 2022), and household manipulation in
RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2024). Each benchmark brings its own evaluator, observation layout, action
convention, and episode bookkeeping, and each policy family brings its own preprocessing and
inference loop. Connecting several policies to several benchmarks repeats this integration for every
pair. Execution cost compounds the problem: with a StarVLA checkpoint, the official evaluation of
500 LIBERO-Long episodes takes about 50 minutes on one GPU, and running 500 RoboTwin Easy episodes
with one simulator and one model on one GPU takes 359.7 minutes. Comparing checkpoints, seeds, or training stages multiplies these costs, and a shared evaluation
layer can remove much of this repeated work.

Profiling the official evaluators shows where this time goes (Section 2.2).
Simulation occupies CPU cores while one loaded model leaves the GPU mostly idle, so simulators and
models are best scaled separately. On RoboTwin, an action-chunk Policy reads one of every 16 rendered
observations, so the others need not be rendered. RoboScope Kit addresses the repeated integration with
one interface and the execution cost with two acceleration mechanisms, scheduling and runtime
optimization.

RoboScope Kit wraps each model once as a Policy, a class that loads the
checkpoint and keeps the model’s own preprocessing, and each benchmark once as an adapter
around the benchmark’s own evaluator. The Policy also declares what RoboScope Kit may rely on: the
observations it reads, the chunk length it returns, and how often it needs a new observation.
It keeps each episode’s state separate, so one loaded model can serve many simulators at once. Simulator workers, Policy replicas, scheduling, and
result collection run as separate components, so the number of simulators KK and the number of
loaded models gg vary independently. The concurrency search chooses KK and gg for each workload
and host from short probes. Runtime optimization in the Simulation Runtime removes simulation work that
the Policy never consumes, such as rendering observations between action-chunk boundaries. Beyond one host, RoboScope Kit partitions the work items deterministically across independent GPU
instances, each running its own workers and replicas, and merges their results.

This report makes three contributions:

A measurement of where evaluation time goes. On one RTX 4090, the official StarVLA
LIBERO-Long evaluator spends 55% of its time on simulation and per-step handling on CPU cores while
the GPU averages 14.3% utilization. Adding simulators to one model saturates it at 45.7% utilization, and a
second Policy replica raises utilization to 87.7%. On RoboTwin, the official evaluator renders three
cameras at every control step, yet the StarVLA Policy reads one observation every 16 steps.

A shared evaluation interface. A model is wrapped once as a Policy class and
then runs on any benchmark that provides the inputs it needs, without changes to RoboScope Kit. Adapters cover six benchmark families.
With a StarVLA checkpoint, a fixed RoboScope Kit
configuration reproduces all 500 LIBERO-Long success outcomes of the official StarVLA evaluation.

Fast evaluation through scheduling and runtime optimization. Scheduling runs simulator
workers and Policy replicas as separate pools, so simulators and loaded models scale independently
and several simulators share each model; a time-bounded concurrency search sizes both pools for each
workload and host, and deterministic sharding extends an evaluation across GPU instances. For runtime
optimization, a Policy can declare that it needs a new observation only once per action chunk;
RoboScope Kit then renders once per chunk, and each worker reuses one SAPIEN engine and renderer across
its episodes. On one RTX 4090, the configuration chosen by the concurrency search evaluates 500
LIBERO-Long episodes in 485 s, against 2,990 s for the official StarVLA evaluation
(6.16×\times), with equivalent outcomes, and is 3.85×\times faster than RLinf and
2.10×\times faster than vla-eval. On RoboTwin Easy, scheduling
and runtime optimization together cut the time for 500 episodes from 359.7 minutes, with one
simulator and one model on one GPU, to 14.4 minutes on four GPUs (25.04×\times).

title: AIRoA-0: Long-Horizon, Precise, Cross-Embodiment Manipulation from Handheld Data
authors: Yueh-Hua Wu,Kei Ota,Hanlong Li,Hayata Yuasa,Jason Wang,Kengo Ikeuchi,Kensuke Chiyoma,Makoto Sugiura,Masafumi Takahashi,Masatoshi Tateno,Naoaki Kanazawa,Nicola Scianca,Petr Khrapchenkov,Satoshi Otsubo,Takehiko Ohkawa,Takuya Okubo,Tatsuya Matsushima,Yuki Noguchi,Yuma Shin,Zixuan Zhong

abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
Data recorded with handheld grippers grows with the number of people who
record it, not with the number of robots available: a person holds a gripper
in each hand and does the task, and no robot is needed. UMI [1]
introduced the approach; with YUBI [2], our open-source gripper of
this kind, we have recorded 16,151 hours of bimanual demonstrations, 10.65
million subtask segments in all, each with a task instruction and a subtask
instruction. AIRoA-0 (A-0) uses handheld demonstrations for pre-training and
post-training alike: no teleoperation, no reinforcement learning, no on-robot
corrections and no simulation.

The properties that let this data scale are the ones that make it hard to
learn from. Every demonstration is made by a person, so nothing in the data
shows a robot acting, failing or recovering. The policy sees only through the
cameras on the grippers, the one view that is the same in a person’s hand and
on a robot: with no head or scene camera, it never sees the workspace as a
whole and must follow a long task through two partial views that are often
consistent with more than one of its steps. Data that anyone can record is
the work of many operators, here across well over a hundred tasks, and a
single model has to learn from all of it. And people record wherever they
are, which is not where the robot will work. Deployment at an unseen site is
therefore the ordinary condition of this approach and the one under which it
must be judged: not one of the demonstrations A-0 learns from was recorded
at the site where it is evaluated.

A-0 works under all of these conditions at once. Given a single sentence of
instruction, it sorts more than a dozen small parts into their numbered
cells, deciding for each part which cell it belongs in, which hand should
take it, and whether it must first pass from one hand to the other. It opens
the zipper of a pencil case, which the two grippers must grasp almost side
by side; it folds a towel; it replaces the mop pads and the brush of a robot
vacuum. These are long tasks that
demand precise contact, and the robot performs them with the grippers that
people record with. On the ten tasks of our evaluation, A-0 averages a
success rate of 78%, against 27% for the strongest of four other
vision-language-action models post-trained on the same task demonstrations:
each of them with its best setting on every task, A-0 with one recipe
for all ten. And although nothing in its data shows a robot meeting a
disturbance, A-0 acts on what it sees: when a person pushes the bins aside
as it brings a part to them, it moves over to the correct bin in one continuous
motion (Figure 4). Because those grippers mount on different arms, A-0
is embodiment-agnostic: the same weights run on robots such as a bimanual
Franka, TX-G2, OpenArm and UR (Section 2.3).

A-0 is built as one system that spans every layer between the gripper in a
person’s hand and the motion of the robot (Figure 6), and
each of these difficulties is met at the layer where it arises. State and
action are defined at the grippers themselves, so the same numbers describe a
person holding them and a robot carrying them, on one arm as on another.
Pre-training tells a single model, through language at two levels, both the
task and the step in progress, and a visual evidence budget [3] teaches
it, with no annotation of where to look, which regions of each wrist view
matter for the task. Post-training adds a prediction of the stage a long task
has reached and a memory of recent motion, and the inference harness smooths
the predicted stage and decodes actions as a continuous stream on a
non-uniform noise schedule that we propose.

With this report we are releasing the full dataset of 16,151 hours of
handheld-gripper demonstrations with task and subtask instructions, together
with the pre-trained weights of A-0 and its post-training recipe. Together with the YUBI gripper’s hardware design
and collection software, which are already public, they open the path
from a gripper in a person’s hand to a policy on a robot: the gripper is built
from the open design, the task is recorded by hand, and the pre-trained model
is post-trained on it with the one recipe that serves every task in this
report, in under four hours on a single node of eight H200 GPUs.

Our contributions are:

A-0, a bimanual manipulation system learned from 16,151 hours of
handheld data, with no robot data collected at any stage.

A-0, a bimanual manipulation system learned from 16,151 hours of
handheld data, with no robot data collected at any stage.

An open release of the path from a handheld gripper to a robot
policy: the dataset, to our knowledge the largest open dataset of
handheld-gripper demonstrations with task and subtask instructions; the
pre-trained weights; and the post-training recipe, alongside the public
YUBI hardware design and collection software.

Long, precise tasks carried out from a single instruction, through
two wrist cameras, at a site where none of the training data was
recorded.

An embodiment-agnostic system: it runs on robots that take the
recording gripper as their end effector, such as a bimanual Franka,
TX-G2, OpenArm and UR.

title: Robot-Matched Soft Fingers for UMI Data Collection: Lessons from 100 Hours of Pick and Place
authors: Kobi Kelemen,Tomasz Niedziałkowski,Marcin Paszczak,Victoriano Montesinos
comment: . Accepted as a poster at the CoRL 2026 UMI Arena Workshop (Track 3). Project page:this https URL
abstract: Training robot policies for multi-task pick and place requires demonstrations on many objects, which handheld Universal Manipulation Interfaces (UMIs) can collect quickly and cheaply. However, existing UMIs depend on external base stations, use rigid fingers that give no signal about contact forces, or use parallel-jaw fingers that limit grip strength. We present a battery-powered handheld interface, built on YUBI, whose soft, angled fingers wrap around objects, deform visibly under load as a visual proxy for force, and match the grippers of the robot. With it, we collect a 99.7-hour dataset over 53 objects, train π0.5\pi_{0.5} policies on 49 of them, and hold out the other 4 as unseen objects. We find that a top camera raises success by 13 points even when only about half of the data includes it, and that mid-training on our multi-task data raises success after fine-tuning on unseen objects from 35% to 57%. Finger design, dataset, and data processing code: lute-corp.github.io/soft-yubi-site
introduction:
General robot policies for multi-task pick and place must handle a wide variety of objects, so they need to be trained on demonstrations with many of them.

The Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) [4] enables collecting such multi-task datasets quickly and cheaply, without a robot in the loop. Follow-up work mostly changes how the handheld gripper is tracked: with a tracking camera [14], a phone [12], a 360∘ camera [11], head-mounted SLAM [9], self-tracking trackers [6], or VR controllers [7], while EgoMI [13] also captures the operator’s head motion. However, these interfaces either require external base stations [3], use rigid fingers that give the policy no signal about contact forces [7, 9], or use parallel-jaw fingers [4, 14, 12, 6] that touch the object at only two surfaces, which limits grip strength and the range of graspable shapes and breaks the one-to-one mapping to robots with angled grippers [14]. KIWI [11] also uses deformable fingers, but evaluates only capture: its grippers do not match a robot gripper, and it trains no policies.

To address these limitations, we introduce a portable data collection system (Fig. 1) built on YUBI [7]. It needs no base stations and runs from a portable battery and laptop, so it can be used anywhere. Its soft, angled fingers wrap around objects, match our robots’ grippers, and deform visibly under load, giving the policy a visual proxy for force.

Our contributions are (1) a portable handheld data collection interface for pick and place, built on YUBI with robot-matched soft fingers; (2) a 99.7-hour dataset over 53 objects, to be released with our finger design and simplified data processing code; and (3) an evaluation of the value of a top camera and of how multi-task mid-training helps policies learn unseen objects.

title: DreamX: Video Diffusion Model is a Universal Latent Action Learner
authors: Jisoo Kim,Chaehyun Kim,Junsu Kim,Jiho Park,Seongchan Kim,Eunbeen Hong,Soowon Son,Fu-En Yang,Seungryong Kim
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: Project Page:this https URL
abstract: Learning a universal action representation from video requires modeling dynamics that are consistent across different executions of the same action yet invariant to changes in embodiment and appearance. Existing latent action models infer actions from visual transitions, but their representations often entangle the underlying action with irrelevant visual variations, limiting transfer across embodiments. We introduce DreamX, which repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model as a universal latent action learner. Our approach extracts compact latent actions from the video model’s rich spatiotemporal features, compressing each latent video frame by 𝟑𝟎𝟎×\bm{300\times} (1,200→𝟒\bm{1{,}200\rightarrow 4} tokens). In addition, by leveraging the video model’s generative prior, these latent actions capture action-relevant dynamics disentangled from visual appearance. The resulting latent space serves as a shared action interface across embodiments (human and robot), environments, and action parameterizations. On LARY-Bench, DreamX achieves state-of-the-art performance among latent action models. Moreover, actions encoded in one setting remain effective in another: the latent space supports any-to-any video transfer and zero-shot action transfer across diverse embodiments and environments. Furthermore, this shared interface also enables policy learning in a compact latent action space, reducing the computational cost of video-diffusion-based policies.
introduction:
Generalist robot policies, including vision-language-action (VLA) models (Kim et al., 2024; Bjorck et al., 2025; Intelligence et al., 2025) and world action models (WAMs) (Kim et al., 2026b; Ye et al., 2026), benefit from diverse robot demonstrations, but collecting such data at scale remains costly.
Human egocentric videos offer a promising alternative as a scalable source of diverse manipulation behaviors, and recent works leverage these videos for policy learning (Li et al., 2025; Kareer et al., 2025).
However, action supervision remains tied to the embodiment that produces it.
Human videos lack robot action labels, and even robot demonstrations use different control spaces across embodiments.
The same behavior can therefore correspond to different low-level actions, making action labels difficult to share directly across embodiments.
Overcoming this mismatch calls for a common action representation that preserves shared motion and effects across embodiments.

Latent action models (LAMs) offer a promising route toward learning such a representation from video.
Although humans and robots have different bodies and control spaces, their actions can all be observed as changes in a visual scene.
LAMs typically use dedicated encoders to compress these changes into compact representations, called latent actions (Ye et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025c; Bu et al., 2025b), where these encoders are trained using a decoder that reconstructs future frames solely from the current frame and latent actions. However, reconstruction accuracy alone does not ensure that latent actions isolate the underlying action. The learned representations can also encode domain-specific visual information, such as viewpoint and scene appearance, whenever it helps reconstruction (Nikulin et al., 2025). Capturing action-relevant structure shared across embodiments while separating it from domain-specific visual factors therefore remains a challenge.

Pretrained video diffusion models provide a promising foundation for addressing this challenge.
First, through large-scale video generation, they learn rich spatiotemporal representations that capture motion, correspondence, geometry, and semantic structure (Nam et al., 2026; Wiedemer et al., 2025; Son et al., 2025).
Such representations encode how scenes, objects, and agents evolve over time, making them a natural source of action-relevant dynamics.
Second, these models possess a generative prior that enables future-frame synthesis conditioned on an initial frame and an additional signal.
With scene appearance supplied by the initial frame, additional conditioning can guide how the scene evolves. Together, these priors motivate extracting latent actions directly from pretrained spatiotemporal representations and supervising their learning with a pretrained generative decoder.

We introduce DreamX, a framework for learning universal latent actions across embodiments using a pretrained video diffusion model. We pass learnable query tokens alongside the video tokens through the model’s spatiotemporal attention, allowing the queries to gather action-relevant information across frames.
The queries condense frame-to-frame changes represented by 1,200 frame tokens into just 4 latent-action tokens, yielding a 𝟑𝟎𝟎×\mathbf{300\times} reduction in token count. These latent actions replace text conditioning in the same model to reconstruct future frames from the initial frame. With scene appearance supplied by the initial frame and visual detail by the pretrained generative prior, the reconstruction objective encourages latent actions to capture the motion needed to explain the observed future.

Trained on heterogeneous human and robot videos, DreamX achieves state-of-the-art performance among latent action models on LARYBench (Nie et al., 2026) and enables any-to-any video transfer and human-to-robot action transfer without paired training data. As a downstream application, we also show that the learned latent actions can serve as prediction targets for an observation-conditioned robot policy, without requiring future-video generation during execution. Together, these results suggest that DreamX learns a shared, transferable latent action space that supports motion transfer across embodiments and can also serve as a basis for downstream policy learning.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

We introduce DreamX, a framework that uses the spatiotemporal and generative priors of a pretrained video diffusion model to learn universal latent actions. The resulting representations achieve state-of-the-art performance among latent action models on LARYBench.

We demonstrate that the learned latent space supports any-to-any video transfer and human-to-robot action transfer without paired source–target training data. We further show the use of compact latent-action codes as prediction targets for downstream policy learning.

1. We introduce DreamX, a framework that uses the spatiotemporal and generative priors of a pretrained video diffusion model to learn universal latent actions. The resulting representations achieve state-of-the-art performance among latent action models on LARYBench.

2. We demonstrate that the learned latent space supports any-to-any video transfer and human-to-robot action transfer without paired source–target training data. We further show the use of compact latent-action codes as prediction targets for downstream policy learning.

title: Visibility-Aware Reference Generation for Benchmarking Visual 3D Reconstruction in Vegetation-Rich Environments
authors: Zhipeng Zhong,Matthew Coombes,Cunjia Liu
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Reliable evaluation of visual 3D reconstruction and depth estimation in vegetation-rich outdoor environments is limited by the scarcity of geometric ground-truth data and the cost of complete scanner surveys. We present a LiDAR-based reference-generation pipeline for evaluating the zero-shot performance of feed-forward visual-geometry models alongside conventional structure-from-motion (SfM) methods.
The pipeline reuses camera images, LiDAR scans, and reference poses from existing multi-sensor localization datasets to generate per-view depth maps and visible reference point clouds. To address visibility errors in accumulated LiDAR scans, we introduce the Large-Depth-Gap Visibility Score (LDGVS) for point-wise visibility filtering and automatic scale selection in Hidden Point Removal (HPR).
Experiments on TartanAirV2 and TartanGround show that, compared with Poisson surface reconstruction, which is an approach suited to completed scan surveys, the combined HPR and LDGVS filtering retains approximately three times the point density at comparable absolute relative error. We also apply the pipeline to the BotanicGarden dataset to systematically compare depth estimation and 3D reconstruction methods. Feed-forward methods produce dense depth predictions efficiently, but their 3D reconstructions can contain duplicated structures. Conventional SfM generally produces more coherent geometry, but its reconstructions remain sparse and more prone to failure in challenging vegetated scenes. The benchmark toolkit and datasets will be released.
introduction:
Visual depth estimation and 3D reconstruction are essential capabilities for agricultural and other field robots, providing dense geometric information from lightweight, low-cost cameras. Many studies [1, 2, 3, 4]
have sought to improve visual geometric methods in vegetation-rich outdoor environments, including forests, orchards, crop fields, and botanical gardens.
However, agricultural applications continue to rely predominantly on conventional geometry-based SLAM [5, 6] or SfM [7, 8], while the feed-forward methods [8, 9, 10] have been less widely adopted. This pattern contrasts with general-purpose 3D-reconstruction and depth-estimation benchmarks [11, 12, 13, 14, 15], where feed-forward models are increasingly prominent[16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22].
This motivates us to evaluate their zero-shot performance in vegetation-rich outdoor environments.

However, benchmarking in these environments remains challenging because publicly available datasets with suitable ground-truth (GT) geometry are scarce and acquiring such data is time-consuming and labor-intensive. A standard approach is to use high-accuracy terrestrial laser scanners to capture complete and dense scans of the environment[14, 15]. This process, however, requires professional surveying expertise and substantial manual effort for data acquisition, scan registration, and outlier removal. These requirements make complete surveys particularly costly in extensive and structurally complex vegetation-rich outdoor environments. A few studies have used laser scanners
[8, 23, 24] to
obtain GT geometry in such environments, but the resulting datasets are often limited in scale and not fully publicly available.

To address this gap, we investigate repurposing mobile LiDAR measurements from existing multi-sensor localization datasets as geometric references. Mobile LiDAR enables data collection over large areas, and a growing number of datasets provide camera images, LiDAR scans, and reference trajectories in agricultural and other vegetation-rich outdoor environments, as summarized in Table I. Although these datasets contain large-scale observations of complex scenes, they were developed primarily for localization and mapping rather than for benchmarking visual depth estimation or 3D reconstruction. Consequently, they do not directly provide camera-aligned reference depth or visibility-filtered 3D geometry. Previous studies have demonstrated the use of LiDAR-derived references for depth estimation and 3D reconstruction in urban and road environments [25, 11, 26, 27, 28, 29], but extending this approach to vegetation-rich environments remains challenging. The difficulty arises because mobile LiDAR measurements are sparse and nonuniform and may be affected by motion distortion. Accumulating multiple scans improves point density but can introduce visibility errors caused by incomplete observations, occlusions, and camera–LiDAR parallax.

These limitations raise a central question: how can mobile LiDAR data be converted into reliable camera-view geometric references for benchmarking visual depth estimation and 3D reconstruction in vegetation-rich environments? We therefore develop a reference-generation pipeline and apply it to the representative BotanicGarden[30] dataset, where the generated references are used to compare feed-forward visual-geometry models with conventional SfM methods.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose a pipeline that converts camera, LiDAR, and reference-pose data from existing localization datasets into per-view depth and visible point-cloud references.

We introduce the Large-Depth-Gap Visibility Score (LDGVS) for point-cloud visibility filtering and automatic Hidden Point Removal (HPR) scale selection, providing greater reference density than Poisson surface reconstruction at comparable absolute relative error.

With the proposed pipeline, we construct a BotanicGarden benchmark comparing feed-forward visual-geometry models with conventional SfM methods in geometric quality, metric scale, cross-frame consistency, robustness, and efficiency.

abstract:
We propose PadLoc, a training-free localization back-end that places
a moving sensor within a known floor plan. Floor plans are cheap, persistent, and
robust to appearance change, but recent learned-depth methods localize against
them by filtering per-frame depth through dense (x,y,θ)(x,y,\theta) pose grids.
PadLoc keeps the swappable depth front-end and replaces the dense grid back-end
with sparse geometric matching: dominant wall orientations define a small
pose-candidate set, masked normalized cross-correlation scores observed free
space against the plan, and a moving-pose Gaussian-mixture Bayes filter plus
consensus readout decodes the trajectory. Holding each competitor’s depth fixed,
PadLoc matches or beats UnLoc’s
forward filter and the F3Loc filter at every Gibson trajectory length, and
UnLoc’s offline refinement from T=35T{=}35 on; it exceeds Z-FLoc’s published
results with a shared MapAnything front-end. On Bonn
LiLocBench, PadLoc improves pooled SR@1 m over UnLoc by 2323–3232 pp under wheel
odometry and 3535–4343 pp with ground-truth motion; with full-FOV
LiDAR plus wheel odometry the same readout reaches
100 %100\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} SR@1 m at 9 cm to 10 cm9\text{\,}\mathrm{cm}10\text{\,}\mathrm{cm} median error on
the static sequence. On the Hilti-Trimble Localization Challenge PadLoc
localizes a camera-only fisheye rig on construction floors hundreds of metres
across at 0.900.90–0.980.98 online SR@2 m on three of five sessions; adding
learned wall isolation, applied to every session, covers all five at 0.670.67–0.920.92
with the localizer unchanged throughout.
PadLoc thus matches or outperforms dense grid back-ends
while preserving sensor modularity and a compact state that does not grow with
trajectory length.
introduction:
Localizing a moving sensor against a 2D floor plan is attractive: floor
plans already exist, are compact, and avoid dense 3D mapping. Recent systems
such as F3Loc [7] and UnLoc [30] pair learned
per-column depth with a dense Bayes-filter recursion over an (x,y,θ)(x,y,\theta)
grid—robust, but the posterior is large and persistent, and the design
is tied to one depth front-end.

PadLoc keeps the swappable depth front-end and changes only the localizer.
The front-end may be learned; the localizer itself has no trained parameters.
Dominant wall orientations form a small heading set, weighted masked
NCC [24] scores each sliding window, and the whole
NCC field over translations is kept, not only its argmax. The
top-KK local maxima feed a moving-pose Gaussian-mixture Bayes filter (GM-BF),
and a consensus readout reuses the raw NCC fields to select the absolute
trajectory anchor.

This separation lets us hold each competitor’s depth fixed and compare only the
localizer. On Gibson, PadLoc matches or outperforms the UnLoc and F3Loc forward
filters at every trajectory length under a frozen readout, and UnLoc’s offline
refinement from T=35T{=}35 on; it exceeds Z-FLoc’s published
results [27], with the largest gains at short horizons. The same matcher transfers unchanged
to Bonn LiLocBench with LiDAR, wheel odometry, VO, and RGB-D front-ends,
beating UnLoc on shared monocular depth, and scales to construction-size
buildings on the Hilti-Trimble Localization Challenge from a camera-only
fisheye front-end once the fusion window is matched to the reconstruction
batch.

We make three contributions.

A training-free masked-NCC matcher. Floor-plan localization
cast as registration with partial overlap: an interior mask and an observation
mask separate observed free space from unexplored cells, and rotation is
reduced to dominant wall-orientation candidates.

A sparse multi-hypothesis decoder, online at bounded lag.
Top-KK NCC peaks become a compact posterior decoded by a moving-pose GM-BF
and a consensus readout kept as a running sum. A single fixed lag bounds
both heading and translation evidence; the mixture is 𝒪⁡(K)\mathcal{O}(K), the
consensus state does not grow with the trajectory, and the
𝒪⁡(N​log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(N\log N) matching kernel scales to building-sized plans and runs
on a phone.

Matched-depth and cross-building evidence. Holding each
competitor’s depth fixed, PadLoc matches or improves over the F3Loc and
UnLoc forward filters and Z-FLoc’s published results, and
transfers across buildings. Knobs that depend on the
front-end (fusion window, motion noise, cell size, blur)
are set by stated rules, never per scene, and then carried from apartment scale (Bonn) to
construction scale (Hilti) with a new MapAnything fisheye front-end.

title: Sparse Anchors for Visual Multi-Session Registration in Changing Environments
authors: Yunus Talha Erzurumlu,Niklas Trekel,Saurabh Gupta,Nico Koltermann,Olga Vysotska,Jens Behley,Louis Wiesmann,Cyrill Stachniss
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Repeated robotic monitoring requires localization across visits to the
same environment, even if the environment changes.
Such changes can substantially reduce persistent visual content, and
repetitive structures can lead to incorrect cross-session correspondences.
In this paper, we address visual multi-session registration of a new data
recording (the query session) to a previously reconstructed reference map.
Under substantial visual and structural changes, cross-session
localization may be possible only for parts of the trajectory.
In our approach, we therefore rely on a sparse set of reliable absolute pose constraints and
combine them with within-session relative-pose information to register the
complete trajectory to the reference map.
We first estimate absolute alignment hypotheses through visual place recognition,
local feature matching, and geometric verification.
We then use sequence consensus to reject hypotheses that are inconsistent with
a common query-to-reference alignment and retain the remaining poses as
absolute anchors.
These anchors are refined through featuremetric alignment against a Gaussian
feature field and combined with within-session relative-pose constraints in a
robust pose-graph optimization.
We evaluate our approach on 15 cross-session experiments from the challenging
HILTI26 construction-site dataset, covering substantial scene changes and
difficult-to-match environments.
Our method achieves 94.4% recall within 1 m and 100.0% within 5 m,
outperforming independent image localization, which peaks at 65.3% and
70.7%, respectively, as well as direct registration of independently
reconstructed Structure-from-Motion geometry.
Our results show that sparse, reliable absolute anchors can provide accurate
and complete trajectory registration even when reliable cross-session
correspondences are available only for part of the query session.
introduction:
Most robotic systems operating repeatedly in the same environment must reliably
localize in a previously built map despite scene changes.
Reliable cross-session localization and registration are therefore important for
long-term autonomy, repeated inspection and monitoring, as well as persistent
mapping [17, 37, 13].
This becomes particularly challenging when changes are structural rather than purely
appearance-level, since parts of the previously mapped geometry may no longer exist,
while new structures may alter or occlude previously visible content.

Construction sites are a particularly demanding instance of this problem.
Their geometry and appearance evolve as walls, installations, temporary
structures, and surface finishes are added, removed, or modified, while
repetitive and low-texture structures create additional perceptual
ambiguity [32], further compounded by the frequent lack of GNSS
availability in indoor construction environments.
Construction progress monitoring requires repeated observations to compare the current
as-built state against earlier observations or the planned state
 [34].
Autonomous mobile robots can acquire such observations, but comparing visits requires
reliable localization in a common coordinate frame.

In this work, we address visual multi-session registration in challenging,
GNSS-denied, and changing environments.
Given a previously reconstructed reference map, together with
its posed reference observations, for example computed with any SLAM system,
we seek to register the query session, a visual sequence acquired at a different time.
The sequence of body poses associated with the noisy query observations forms the
query trajectory, which we seek to recover in the reference map coordinate frame.
This is difficult because substantial geometric and appearance changes reduce the
persistent visual content available for cross-session correspondences, while repetitive
structures can produce plausible correspondences between physically distinct locations,
as shown in Fig. 1.

Existing strategies often use image-based localization against an earlier
map [27] or direct registration of independently reconstructed 3D maps.
Image-based localization becomes unreliable when persistent visual content is limited
or perceptually ambiguous, while 3D point-cloud registration degrades as spatial and
temporal changes accumulate [32].

The main contribution of this paper is a visual multi-session registration approach for
changing environments, where scene changes and perceptual aliasing can make reliable
cross-session correspondences available only for parts of the trajectory.
Our approach combines conservative cross-session anchor selection, retaining only
absolute pose hypotheses that are geometrically verified and consistent with the query
trajectory, with featuremetric pose refinement for precise image-to-map alignment.
These sparse absolute anchors are then combined with within-session relative-pose
constraints to recover the complete query trajectory even when reliable cross-session
correspondences are only sparsely available.

We make three key claims: our approach
(i) provides more accurate and complete multi-session registration than the baselines;
(ii) improves the reliability of cross-session constraints under scene change and
perceptual aliasing through conservative filtering and sequence consensus; and
(iii) improves fine image-to-map alignment through featuremetric refinement of the
verified absolute anchors.
We will publicly release our implementation upon publication.

title: DRAP: Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity for Continual Learning in Physical AI
authors: Oswaldo Ludwig
abstract: Continual learning in physical AI differs from conventional continual learning because small per-step policy errors can accumulate over a trajectory. Each deviation may move the agent outside the training distribution, increase subsequent prediction errors, and ultimately cause closed-loop task failure. This work introduces Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity (DRAP), a replay-free method that estimates the historical importance of adaptable model tensors from sample-level action gradients weighted by local trajectory-amplification risk. A ridge-regularized local linear model is fitted to expert state-action transitions, and the largest singular value of its state-transition matrix provides a policy-independent, Lyapunov-inspired estimate of one-step perturbation amplification. After each task, risk-weighted squared gradients are accumulated in a tensor-level importance memory. During subsequent tasks, DRAP uses normalized cumulative importance to scale the effective AdamW learning rate of each tensor, immediately reducing the plasticity of components that supported previous behavior at dynamically sensitive trajectory points. We instantiate DRAP on a fixed KappaTune-selected subnetwork of OpenVLA and evaluate replay-free sequential adaptation across the LIBERO Spatial, Object, and Goal suites. Compared with standard AdamW fine-tuning and EWC, the results show substantially improved retention of previously learned behaviors while preserving strong new-suite acquisition.
introduction:
Continual learning in physical AI differs from conventional continual learning because small changes in a policy can alter future observations and amplify into closed-loop task failure. In embodied control, an action error changes the next physical state, modifies the next observation, and may place the policy outside the training distribution. Subsequent errors can therefore compound over the remainder of the trajectory [1, 2].

Vision-language-action (VLA) models combine visual perception, language grounding, and low-level control within a single pretrained policy. OpenVLA provides an open 7B VLA with tokenized actions and a pretrained vision-language backbone [3]. OpenVLA-OFT later demonstrated that continuous actions, action chunking, and optimized decoding can substantially improve success and inference efficiency [4]. These advances strengthen task acquisition, but do not remove the continual-learning problem: sequential fine-tuning can overwrite behavior required by earlier manipulation skills.

Existing continual-learning strategies offer complementary trade-offs. Replay remains a strong baseline but requires storing or regenerating previous observations. Expansion and routing methods isolate tasks but add modules or routing mechanisms. Parameter-regularization methods preserve a previous solution but can restrict acquisition. Direct update-suppression methods reduce future plasticity according to past update history, but can become too restrictive for large heterogeneous models.

This work develops a replay-free mechanism based on a physical observation: parameters supporting correct behavior at dynamically sensitive trajectory regions should become less plastic in later tasks.

Unlike reference-based consolidation methods, the proposed Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity (DRAP) does not penalize parameter displacement from a previously stored checkpoint. Instead, similar to CLASSP [5], it uses accumulated historical importance to directly regulate future plasticity. Protection is therefore active from the first update of each subsequent learning stage and does not require storing reference copies of the adaptable parameters.

This work contributes a local policy-independent dynamics-risk estimator derived from expert state-action trajectories. The resulting risk scores weight the historical importance of adaptable tensors, which is then used to regulate their future plasticity through tensor-specific AdamW learning rates. This mechanism suppresses the actual optimizer step rather than merely scaling raw gradients.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on continual learning for vision-language-action models and on importance-based plasticity control. Section III describes the sequential LIBERO evaluation protocol. Section IV motivates the dynamics-risk signal from the compounding-error perspective of imitation learning, and Section V formalizes the replay-free continual learning problem. Section VI presents the DRAP method, including the KappaTune-based subnetwork selection, the local dynamics-risk estimator, the risk-weighted tensor importance, and the tensor-specific learning-rate control. Section VII reports the experimental results, including ablations of KappaTune selection and of dynamics-risk weighting. Finally, Section VIII concludes and outlines directions for future work.

title: For You, Not for Everyone: Bystander-Aware Delivery of Critical Feedback in Robot Tutoring
authors: Atikkhan Faridkhan Nilgar,Manuel Dietrich,Kristof Van Laerhoven
comment: Submitted for Review
abstract:
Robots in shared settings may expose information intended for an individual user to nearby bystanders. Robot tutoring makes this concern particularly salient: critical feedback is directed at an individual learner, yet bystanders may overhear or see it. To address this, we compared context-invariant and context-adaptive robot behaviors in a between-subjects study with 40 participants. Following an initial phase without a bystander, a bystander entered the setting. Participants then received two scripted critical feedback messages concerning their pronunciation and handwriting, independent of their actual performance. With the context-invariant behavior, the robot tutor delivered both messages aloud. With the context-adaptive behavior, the robot tutor scanned for the bystander, turned its body and display away after detecting them, gave a spoken attention cue, and presented the same feedback messages silently on its display.
Participants rated the robot tutor higher in perceived privacy awareness and perceived social competence in the context-adaptive condition than in the context-invariant condition, while evidence for reduced experienced embarrassment was inconclusive. These findings inform the design and evaluation of robots that respond to bystander presence by adapting how they communicate potentially sensitive information.
introduction:
Social robots are increasingly being studied for use in schools, healthcare facilities, and homes (Belpaeme et al., 2018; Jayaraman et al., 2024; Levinson et al., 2024). In these settings, interactions with robots do not necessarily take place in isolation. Other people may be present without being directly involved in the interaction, creating opportunities for bystanders to observe or overhear exchanges between a robot and its user. Prior work on indirect human–robot interaction (HRI) and incidental encounters has therefore identified bystanders as an important consideration for HRI research (Tsui et al., 2010; Rosenthal-von Der Pütten et al., 2020).

The presence of bystanders becomes particularly relevant when an interaction involves sensitive or potentially private information. When a robot communicates information intended for its user aloud, being overheard by others may be experienced as a privacy violation (Dietrich et al., 2026). Similar concerns have been identified in research on smart environments. For example, users of shared smart speakers have reported concerns about housemates overhearing phone conversations conducted through the devices (Huang et al., 2020). Likewise, prior work has examined situations in which visitors may inadvertently see information displayed for a particular user and has called for adaptive systems that account for who is present (Marky et al., 2020).

Privacy research in HRI, however, has predominantly focused on how, when, and where robots collect, process, and store information (Lutz et al., 2019). Comparatively less attention has been paid to privacy risks arising from the robot’s social communication itself, that is, how information is communicated when other people are present. Existing work has examined how robots manage information shared across conversations (Tang et al., 2022) and proposed that robots adapt their communication to the presence of others (Reinhardt and Misra, 2025).

In this work, we investigate this question in the context of robot tutoring in social settings. Robot-assisted language learning, for example, has been studied in shared learning environments, including primary-school classrooms in which interactions take place under teacher guidance (Maijala and Mutta, 2024). In such settings, feedback from a robot may be received in the presence of other people. When that feedback is critical, learners may therefore be concerned not only about the criticism itself but also about others becoming aware of it.
We investigate whether adapting a robot tutor’s communication in the presence of a bystander affects users’ perceptions of its privacy awareness and social competence, as well as their experienced embarrassment.

In a between-subjects study, 40 participants interacted with an Ohbot robot used as a language tutor. Each interaction consisted of a bystander-absent phase followed by a bystander-present phase. During the second phase, the robot delivered two scripted critical feedback messages concerning the participant’s pronunciation and handwriting. The messages were independent of participants’ actual performance, allowing the feedback content to remain constant across conditions. In the context-invariant condition, the robot delivered the critical feedback aloud despite the bystander’s presence. In the context-adaptive condition, the robot scanned for and detected the bystander, turned its body and display away from them, provided the participant with a spoken attention cue, and then presented the same feedback messages silently on its display (Figure 1). Thus, the conditions differed in whether the robot adapted the modality and presentation of its feedback to the changed social context, while the feedback content itself remained constant.

Our work makes the following contributions:

An implemented approach to bystander-aware robot communication that detects a bystander and adapts the robot’s orientation and communication modality when delivering potentially sensitive feedback.

An empirical evaluation of this approach in robot tutoring, examining perceived privacy awareness, perceived social competence, experienced embarrassment, and users’ interpretations of the robot’s behavior.

1. An implemented approach to bystander-aware robot communication that detects a bystander and adapts the robot’s orientation and communication modality when delivering potentially sensitive feedback.

2. An empirical evaluation of this approach in robot tutoring, examining perceived privacy awareness, perceived social competence, experienced embarrassment, and users’ interpretations of the robot’s behavior.

title: iMED: A Multi-Endoscope Dataset for Surgical 3D Perception
authors: Sierra Bonilla,Fengyi Jiang,Chinedu Nwoye,Jingpei Lu,Kailey Reardon,Humphrey W. Chow,Francisco Vasconcelos,Sophia Bano,Adam Schmidt,Omid Mohareri
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: Published at ECCV 2026. including supplementary material. Code and dataset:this https URL
abstract:
We introduce iMED, the first synchronized multi-endoscope dataset for robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery (RAMIS), designed to address a fundamental limitation in surgical vision benchmarking: the absence of independent held-out viewpoints. Existing surgical datasets capture single-trajectory sequences from a single endoscope, making it impossible to distinguish geometric generalization from photometric interpolation along a narrow forward-facing path. iMED provides 340 sequences (≈\approx170K synchronized timepoints with 4 views per timepoint) recorded simultaneously from two independent stereo endoscopes across ex vivo, postmortem, and live surgical settings, spanning 14 specimens with diverse anatomical regions and motion regimes. The dataset includes calibrated camera intrinsics, ArUco-based frame-wise pose estimates with uncertainty quantification, instrument segmentation masks, and rich clinical metadata.
Using a train-on-one-endoscope, test-on-another evaluation protocol, we benchmark 23 state-of-the-art methods across rigid and deformable novel view synthesis, pose estimation, feature matching, and monocular depth estimation. Our experiments show that methods relying primarily on photometric supervision degrade substantially under this held-out-endoscope setting, while methods with explicit geometric regularization are more robust across views in our benchmark.
Notably, large-scale foundation models transfer surprisingly well to surgical imagery, often outperforming domain-specific models, suggesting pitfalls in current fine-tuning protocols. iMED establishes a new evaluation protocol for geometric generalization in surgical vision. Dataloader and dataset links can be found at
github.com/surgical-vision/imed.
introduction:
Non-rigid scenes with constrained camera motion are among the most challenging regimes for image-based 3D perception tasks (i.e. pose estimation, feature matching, optical flow, depth estimation, and novel view synthesis (NVS)). Although challenging, such conditions often arise in real-world robotic applications like digital human modeling of clothed bodies [7], submarine exploration [10], and robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery (RAMIS) [54]. Among these, RAMIS represents an extreme regime. Cameras operate inside the body under severe viewpoint constraints, typically following narrow, forward-facing trajectories through deformable tissue with strong specularities and transient phenomena (smoke, bleeding, topology changes). These conditions compress multiple failure modes for 3D perception methods, making RAMIS an informative stress test for visual geometry in real-world robotic systems.

Computer vision benchmarks have historically advanced 3D perception through standardized evaluation protocols [20]. In rigid environments, datasets capturing scenes from many surrounding viewpoints with known camera poses enabled progress in multi-view reconstruction and mapping [1, 31, 12, 75]. Dynamic-scene benchmarks later extended these ideas to time-varying NVS and reconstruction [51, 45, 46, 28], typically relying on wide-baseline or 360∘/180∘ capture where cameras observe scenes from diverse directions. Surgical vision datasets have enabled progress in reconstruction, camera tracking, and tool analysis [3, 54, 23, 22]. Unlike the surrounding-view capture in general benchmarks, endoscopic cameras follow narrow forward-facing paths through tissue, producing sequences with significant image overlap and limited viewpoint diversity.

In NVS and 3D scene representation, models are typically evaluated using images at held-out camera poses and reporting metrics such as PSNR and SSIM against held-out views [5, 56, 24, 73, 30]. These metrics quantify photometric fidelity and have become standard quantitative benchmarks. However, they are proxies for reconstruction quality rather than direct measures of geometric consistency: high PSNR/SSIM can reflect local interpolation between nearby viewpoints, without uniquely determining whether the model has learned the underlying 3D structure [68]. This limitation is amplified when train and test poses lie along the same forward-facing trajectory, where test views are typically sampled from nearby frames in time so differ only slightly in view. A complementary evaluation is to test generalization under larger viewpoint shifts. In classic multi-camera dynamic-scene benchmarks, this protocol is well established: models are trained on a subset of cameras and evaluated on held-out cameras [28, 8, 34].

To address this limitation in surgical vision, we introduce iMED, the first multi-endoscope dataset for RAMIS, providing synchronized recordings from two physically independent stereo endoscopes, four camera streams with overlapping fields of view, enabling cross-trajectory geometric validation (see Fig. 1). The dataset comprises 340 sequences totaling ∼\sim170K synchronized timepoints (4 frames×\times60 FPS) across diverse surgical scenarios: 10 ex vivo organ specimens (chicken, porcine, and bovine; ≈\approx7 sequences each), 3 human cadaver subjects (≈\approx6 anatomical sites per subject, ≈\approx7 sequences per site), and 1 live porcine subject (10 anatomical sites, ≈\approx7 sequences per site). Data collection was performed in a USDA-licensed clinical lab using one porcine model and three human cadaver models sourced from a willed body program. Each 10-15 second sequence captures varied conditions including static scenes, respiratory motion, tool-tissue interactions with 20 common robotic instruments (see both Tab. 2 and Suppl.Tab.7, contact-based tissue deformations, lighting variations, and specularities. All sequences include comprehensive metadata: anatomical regions labeled by clinical specialists with surgical robotics expertise, robot tool types, powered instrument usage (e.g., electrocautery), and motion categories (e.g., camera sweep, robot tool-tissue interaction, calibration). All frames include inferred filtered instrument segmentation masks generated by [9]. Refer to Tab. 2 for label provenance. To filter sequences towards specific applications (e.g. deformable vs. rigid), refer to Suppl.Tab.10. Recordings include intrinsic calibrations and frame-wise ArUco-based [18] camera poses refined through reprojection-error optimization with uncertainty estimates.

Using iMED, we evaluate 23 SOTA algorithms across tasks central to 3D perception: rigid NVS, deformable (online & not) NVS, camera pose estimation, feature matching, and depth estimation.
Our analysis suggests that, under this held-out-endoscope protocol, methods relying primarily on photometric supervision degrade under physically independent viewpoints, while methods with explicit geometric regularization are more robust across views. Depth supervision has representation-dependent effects, and large multi-domain foundation models often transfer well to surgical imagery compared with surgical-only training or aggressive fine-tuning. We define train-on-one-endoscope, test-on-another evaluation protocols that eliminate trajectory overlap and measure geometric generalization across physically independent cameras, a standard in multi-view human capture datasets that is absent from surgical benchmarks. Motivated by the lack of independent test views in surgical datasets, we introduce iMED and make the following contributions:

A train-on-one-endoscope, test-on-another evaluation protocol providing held-out viewpoints with large baseline and viewing-direction differences, as a better proxy for geometric generalization beyond photometric interpolation

A train-on-one-endoscope, test-on-another evaluation protocol providing held-out viewpoints with large baseline and viewing-direction differences, as a better proxy for geometric generalization beyond photometric interpolation

A synchronized multi-endoscope dataset for RAMIS with 340 sequences (≈\approx170K timepoints with 4 images per timepoint) across ex vivo, in vivo postmortem, and in vivo settings (See Fig. 3)

Calibrated multi-view images and structured annotations (cam intrinsics, reference trajectories, anatomical labels, motion categories, instrument masks)

A benchmark of 23 methods across NVS, pose estimation, feature matching, and monocular depth estimation that exposes previously unobserved behaviors: models trained using only image supervision perform poorly on new viewpoints, methods with explicit 3D regularization generalize more reliably, and foundation models often transfer better than surgical-only training

title: Cycle WAM: Coupling Action and Video through Cycle Consistency
authors: Qinglin Yang,Jiepeng Wang,Yuxing Huang,Haibin Huang,Kai Xu,Chi Zhang,Ruizhen Hu,Xuelong Li
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Recent advances in video modeling have driven substantial progress in world
action models (WAMs).
Existing approaches exploit pretrained video priors by decoding actions
from latent representations or inferring them from generated videos.
The underlying link is causal: robot actions produce changes in the scene,
and video observations of these changes provide evidence for inferring the
actions that produced them. However, existing training formulations do not
by themselves ensure that actions and their predicted visual consequences
are consistent, potentially limiting the use of pretrained capabilities.
We treat video and action as paired modalities linked by this causal
relationship and learn their correspondence through a unified training
framework designed to better exploit pretrained video priors.
Cycle WAM first augments video–action co-training with bidirectional
conversion to reinforce cross-modal correspondence and recover forward and
inverse dynamics. It then introduces a differentiable cycle-reconstruction
objective to further couple the two mappings.
The resulting model supports both forward and inverse dynamics, with the
potential to improve performance through more effective use of pretrained
video priors.
Cycle WAM achieves state-of-the-art performance among comparable methods
on LIBERO-Pro and substantially improves DreamZero on DROID. Comparisons with UWM characterize its inverse-dynamics performance and show
sharper visual detail in the displayed forward-dynamics predictions.
introduction:
General-purpose manipulation requires robots to connect desired changes in
the scene with executable actions. Pretrained video models offer rich priors over such changes, motivating world action models (WAMs) that learn visual dynamics and action generation together [20, 43, 19]. We study how learning the
correspondence between video and action can more fully realize the potential
of pretrained video models for action-conditioned forward dynamics,
inverse dynamics, and policy execution. Within the broader AI Flow
framework [2], this work focuses on video–action learning
for embodied intelligence.

Early action-conditioned visual models supported model-predictive control
[13, 14], while visual planning
translated predicted states into commands through learned inverse models or
tracking controllers [31]. These approaches use predicted visual outcomes to guide action selection, providing a foundation for exploiting richer video priors in robot control.

Recent policies exploit stronger visual priors by conditioning controllers
on generated video plans [11, 4] or learning actions
alongside future visual representations [37, 8, 48].
These routes transfer visual knowledge, but a plausible future and an action that realizes it remain distinct prediction targets.
Building on these advances, unified world action models jointly model robot actions and future visual observations. UWM uses separate diffusion timesteps for video and action to support forward and inverse dynamics [54]. DreamZero adapts a pretrained video backbone for joint video–action generation [43].

The connection between video and action is rooted in the causal structure
of an interaction. Given the current scene, robot actions produce changes
that become visible in subsequent observations. Conversely, these visual
changes provide evidence about which actions could have produced them,
enabling inverse dynamics inference even when the underlying action is not
uniquely determined. A shared backbone does not by itself ensure consistency between predicted actions and their visual consequences. Our goal is to strengthen this correspondence so that pretrained video knowledge can support both predicting action outcomes and inferring actions from video.

We therefore view video and action as complementary modalities describing
the same underlying interaction. Bidirectional conversion and cycle
consistency encourage the model’s internal representations to capture how
actions relate to visual changes, helping it make fuller use of pretrained
video priors without introducing an explicit intermediate representation.

We introduce Cycle WAM, a unified training framework for learning
this correspondence (Fig. ). Building on video–action co-training,
Bidirectional Conversion trains the model to convert between video
and action, strengthening their correspondence and recovering forward and
inverse dynamics. We further introduce a Cycle mechanism that reconstructs
the input modality after conversion to the other modality, reinforcing the
relationship learned through bidirectional conversion.
By learning to convert between video and action and reconstruct the input
modality, the model is encouraged to preserve information about the
interaction that the two modalities share. Our theoretical analysis clarifies how bidirectional conversion and cycle consistency complement each other in learning the correspondence between video and action.
