title: Just Between Us? Exploring a Wearable-Mediated Channel for Discreet Human-Agent Interaction in a Shared Game Setting
authors: Atikkhan Faridkhan Nilgar,Manuel Dietrich,Kristof Van Laerhoven
comment: Accepted in 25th International Conference on Mobile and Ubiquitous Multimedia (MUM) 2026
abstract:
In shared settings, social robots may need to exchange information with an individual while limiting how readily co-present others can access or interpret that information.
Publicly observable speech and gestures do not necessarily
support this need. We therefore investigate a wearable-mediated channel for
discreet interaction, combining in-ear audio messages with
deliberate rightward head tilts as responses. To examine its feasibility
and participants’ experiences, we studied 20 pairs
(40 participants) playing a card game with a screen-based
conversational agent representing a social robot. A researcher
controlled this robot character in a Wizard-of-Oz setup.
Each pair played with and without the channel: one participant
wore the device (wearer), while the other (non-wearer) learned
about it after gameplay. The channel provided information
that could help the wearer or robot character choose an
opponent they could defeat. This exchange and the resulting opponent selection occurred as intended in 39 of 40 channel-mediated turns. Wearers reported low perceived
pressure/tension in both conditions, with no statistically
significant difference, and favorable immediate usability after
use. However, retrospective interviews revealed differing
accounts of noticing among non-wearers and contrasting
perceptions of teamwork and unfairness. These findings support the exchange’s feasibility
within this game and highlight awareness and fairness as
considerations for future designs.
introduction:
Social interactions involving multiple people are common in everyday life. As social robots become increasingly integrated into society, they need to interact effectively in multi-party or group settings (Nigro et al., 2025; Sebo et al., 2020). Robots typically communicate in these settings through speech, gestures, or body movements that everyone present can observe. Although this overt communication can support transparency and mutual understanding, it may be unsuitable when information is intended for only an individual, particularly when that information is privacy-sensitive (Nilgar et al., 2024; Nilgar et al., 2025; Dietrich et al., 2023; Tang et al., 2022; Zand et al., 2025). For example, a healthcare robot may need to coordinate with a patient, healthcare provider, or caregiver without unnecessarily exposing patient information to others who are present (Jayaraman et al., 2024). This creates a need for an interaction channel that can direct task-relevant information to a person and receive a response while limiting how readily co-present others can access or interpret the exchange.

Humans address related communication needs through combinations of explicit and implicit verbal and gestural cues (Shah and Breazeal, 2010). Robots can likewise use nonverbal cues such as gaze or body orientation to direct attention (Admoni and Scassellati, 2017; Mutlu et al., 2009a; Mutlu et al., 2009b). Although these cues can indicate an intended recipient, they remain publicly observable and potentially interpretable by others attending to the robot.

In this work, we use discreet interaction to
describe a bidirectional exchange between an agent and a human within a shared activity. The exchange
provides differential information access by making message
content available to that person while making their response
less readily interpretable to co-present others. We treat discretion as a graded, observer-dependent design goal; it does not imply invisibility, confidentiality, or guaranteed privacy (Pohl et al., 2019; Uhde et al., 2023). Wearable devices provide one possible basis for implementing such an exchange. Figure 1 illustrates two hypothetical domestic scenarios in which such an exchange may be embedded within an ongoing shared activity. Ear-worn devices can selectively deliver in-ear audio to an individual while incorporating inertial sensors capable of sensing head movements (Kawsar et al., 2018; Min et al., 2018; Li et al., 2022).

To investigate such an exchange, we created a bidirectional, wearable-mediated channel combining in-ear audio with a deliberate rightward head-tilt response using eSense11
1
            
            
            
          https://www.esense.io/.

We evaluated the channel using a screen-based conversational
agent representing a social robot, referred to as the robot
character. Our empirical focus is wearable-mediated interaction
with this conversational agent during a shared activity.
The evaluation required a setting in which exchanged information
could influence subsequent actions while another person
remained an active participant.

We therefore developed a customized three-player card game inspired by rock–paper–scissors. Prior studies have used familiar competitive games to investigate social responses to a robot’s fair or unfair behavior (Short et al., 2010; Litoiu et al., 2015). Here, the game served a different purpose: participants played in a triadic setting, and the competitive choices gave task-relevant consequences to the information exchanged between the wearer (participant who used the channel) and the robot character. The non-wearer (participant not informed about the channel) was therefore not a passive observer but a co-present participant with opportunities to notice or infer the channel’s use.

In-ear audio carried messages from the robot character to the wearer. In the reverse direction, detection or non-detection of a qualifying rightward head tilt from the wearer determined the displayed response state and, consequently, the robot character’s next action. Channel-mediated turns were embedded within the game’s normal turn structure, and the information exchanged could affect the wearer’s or the robot character’s subsequent opponent selection. The two turn types assigned the wearer and robot character distinct roles within the prescribed information–response–action sequence, reflecting the procedural interdependence described in human–autonomy teaming research (O’Neill et al., 2022; Traeger et al., 2020; Takko et al., 2021).

To evaluate the wearable-mediated channel in the shared game, we pose the following research questions:

RQ1: What does the game indicate about the formative, context-bound feasibility of discreet interaction through the wearable-mediated channel?

RQ1: What does the game indicate about the formative, context-bound feasibility of discreet interaction through the wearable-mediated channel?

RQ2: How do wearers perceive pressure/tension when playing the game with versus without discreet interaction through the wearable-mediated channel?

RQ3: How do wearers perceive the wearable-mediated channel’s usability after using it for discreet interaction in the game?

We use feasibility in a formative, context-bound sense: whether the prescribed exchange could be enacted through the wearable-mediated channel and what wearer and non-wearer accounts reveal about the conditions that supported or constrained it. We treat perceived pressure/tension and immediate usability as separate wearer-reported outcomes. Alongside these research questions, exploratory interviews examined wearers’ accounts of channel use, non-wearers’ pre-disclosure retrospective accounts of noticing or inference, and both groups’ post-disclosure interpretations. We also examined participants’ suggestions for alternative interaction techniques, modalities, and application contexts to inform future research on discreet interaction in shared settings.

This study makes three contributions: (I) We describe discreet interaction in terms of
bidirectional exchange and differential information access
within a shared ongoing activity.
(II) We instantiate this concept through a wearable-mediated channel and a controlled three-player card game in which a non-wearer remains an active participant. (III) We provide a formative characterization of protocol consistency, wearers’ immediate experience, and wearer and non-wearer interpretations of differential information access via a wearable-mediated channel.

2. RQ2: How do wearers perceive pressure/tension when playing the game with versus without discreet interaction through the wearable-mediated channel?

3. RQ3: How do wearers perceive the wearable-mediated channel’s usability after using it for discreet interaction in the game?

title: Aero-VPA: Few-Step Flow-Matching Control over Non-Reconstructive JEPA Latents for Agile Flight on Edge Hardware
authors: Yeonseok Lee
subjects: Logic in Computer Science (cs.LO); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)

abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generalize across tasks, but their autoregressive decoders need sequential forward passes in proportion to the action horizon, each bounded below on embedded aerial platforms by streaming billions of parameters from memory. We present Aero-VPA, a lightweight Vision-Predictor-Action architecture for 3D navigation on edge hardware. A compact RGB-D Vision Transformer and a five-head ensemble predictor, trained without pixel reconstruction, forecast the next latent state; a Conditional Flow Matching solver generates a velocity and yaw-rate chunk in two Euler steps, so each decision takes five sequential network evaluations; and the ensemble dispersion drives an uncertainty fallback. Version 1 specified the architecture, deployment and protocol without results. This version reports the first closed-loop evaluation: PX4 software-in-the-loop simulation of quadrotor missions in procedurally generated forests. Behaviour cloning failed on all 60 missions despite open-loop errors of 0.02–0.04 m/s: the policy copies its last command, a copycat form of causal confusion. DAgger with a privileged, safety-gated supervisor gave the first successes but plateaued at 11.1–21.1% across six checkpoints. A map-free runtime shield with a 15 s depth memory, barrier constraints, a cap on motion outside the 73° field of view and backoff along the flown path raised the first DAgger policy’s success on 180 paired missions from 21.1% to 52.2% (95% CI [45.0, 59.4]; exact McNemar p=1.2×10−10p=1.2\times 10^{-10}) and cut its crashes from 72.2% to 22.2%, while timeouts rose from 2.8% to 23.3%. All six checkpoints gained 30.0–34.4 percentage points, at mean speeds of 1.16–1.36 m/s. The code (https://github.com/ylee-sling/Aero-VPA), the trained policy (72.6 MB, https://huggingface.co/ylee-sling/aero-vpa) and the full benchmark dataset are public.
introduction:
Navigating cluttered three-dimensional environments at speed requires a micro aerial vehicle (MAV) to convert onboard sensing into motor commands within a fraction of the time it needs to reach the nearest obstacle. Modular pipelines that chain visual-inertial odometry, volumetric mapping, and trajectory optimization [1, 2, 3, 4] remain the dominant engineering solution, but each stage adds latency and couples the system to the accuracy of an explicit map; learned sensorimotor policies have accordingly been shown to fly faster and more robustly in the wild [5] and to reach champion-level performance in drone racing [6, 7]. In parallel, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [8, 9, 10] have demonstrated broad semantic generalization by casting control as sequence modeling. Most VLAs, however, emit actions through an autoregressive language-model decoder: an HH-step chunk of dad_{a}-dimensional actions discretized into qq tokens per component requires N=q​H​daN=qHd_{a} dependent forward passes. At batch size one, every pass must stream the decoder weights from memory, so the latency is bounded below by N​|WLLM|​b/B​WN|W_{\mathrm{LLM}}|b/BW, where |WLLM||W_{\mathrm{LLM}}| is the number of parameters, bb the bytes per parameter, and B​WBW the memory bandwidth. On an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano 8 GB, whose LPDDR5 interface provides 68 GB/s in its original configuration and 102 GB/s in the JetPack 6.2 “Super” configurations [11], a 3B-parameter model in 16-bit precision (6 GB, three quarters of the device memory) needs at least 88 ms per pass at 68 GB/s. A single four-component velocity command (q=1q=1, H=1H=1, da=4d_{a}=4) then takes at least 0.35 s (at most 2.8 Hz), and a 16-step chunk at least 5.6 s, during which a vehicle flying at 5 m/s travels 28 m. These bounds are optimistic: they ignore compute, attention over the context, and memory shared with perception and middleware.

The Vision-Predictor-Action (VPA) framework [12] removes the language decoder from the control loop. A compact encoder maps observations into a latent space learned by a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) [13, 14, 15], which predicts future embeddings rather than future pixels and is therefore not required to model task-irrelevant appearance; a predictor forecasts the latent consequence of the selected skill; and a Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) solver [16, 17, 18] transports Gaussian noise to an entire action chunk by integrating a learned ordinary differential equation (ODE). Denoising diffusion policies [19] generate chunks by iterative denoising, commonly with 10 to 100 network evaluations per chunk; the CFM sampler is instead a deterministic ODE map from a sampled initial condition, and straight transport paths admit accurate integration in very few steps; the number of sequential network evaluations per decision is K+3K+3 for KK integration steps, independent of the horizon HH [12]. A reference implementation with fewer than 20M trainable parameters ran a decision step in 10.5–14.2 ms on an Apple M4 and succeeded in 40.0% of LIBERO-10 manipulation episodes [12]. Flight, however, differs from tabletop manipulation in three respects that this paper addresses: the platform is underactuated and cannot pause in free space, so the controller needs a safe action whenever its predictions become unreliable; commands must be streamed to a flight controller at a fixed rate under strict failsafe timing [20]; and the compute budget is that of an embedded module rather than a workstation.

Aero-VPA is an autonomous navigation framework incorporating a JEPA-based latent world model. The JEPA predictor serves as the latent dynamics world model predicting forward state transitions, while a flow-matching policy acts as the downstream controller. This paper formalizes Aero-VPA, a specialization of VPA to aerial navigation whose long-term goal is agile flight on edge hardware, specifies the protocol by which it is evaluated, and reports its first closed-loop evaluation. The architecture has three parts: a high-level generative actor, the primitive selector πϕh\pi^{h}_{\phi} and the CFM solver vθv_{\theta}; a lightweight latent dynamics world model that conditions the actor, the JEPA encoder EψE_{\psi} and the five-head ensemble predictor PωP_{\omega}, whose ensemble mean enters the actor’s conditioning and whose dispersion drives an uncertainty fallback, and which is not used for planning; and, added in this version, a deterministic low-level runtime safety shield.

Version 1 of this preprint reported no experiments. In PX4 software-in-the-loop (SITL) simulation, the policy trained by behaviour cloning (BC) on about 5.5 million frames of a privileged expert matched the expert almost perfectly offline—on held-out expert frames, the median error of its first velocity knot was 0.02 m/s—but succeeded in none of 60 missions. Input-swap tests (Section 6.2) show why. The command follows the last dispatched setpoint a¯t\bar{a}_{t}, which is part of the proprioceptive input StS_{t}: replacing a¯t\bar{a}_{t} by that of another frame changed the command by 0.85 m/s and moved it to within 0.31 m/s of the other frame’s label (medians; two frames’ labels differ by a median of 1.13 m/s), whereas replacing the image or the goal changed it by 0.01 m/s. On expert data, a¯t\bar{a}_{t} lies within about 0.02 m/s of the next label, so repeating it is nearly optimal offline and useless in closed loop, where nothing corrects the drift. This is the copycat problem of behaviour cloning [21], a form of causal confusion [22]. Withholding a¯t\bar{a}_{t} moved the shortcut to the measured velocity. DAgger [23], stage (iii) of the training procedure (Section 3.8), produced the first successes, but neither a second round nor four round-3 recipes aimed at the shortcut (input removal, state dropout, keyframe weighting) improved on the first round, and the DAgger policies still copied a¯t\bar{a}_{t} on expert frames.

The front camera sees 73° horizontally, and in simulation the vehicle responded to a velocity setpoint after a dead time of 0.24 s with a first-order lag of 0.5 s. Across our evaluations, 26.2–36.4% of the policies’ decisions were blind—the commanded direction lay outside the field of view, or the depth there was invalid—compared with 3.7% for the expert on its own held-out flights. The braking envelope of the learned safety layer (Section 3.6) checks only the current frame, and with the identified response its stopping guarantee does not apply. A runtime safety layer therefore has to remember what the camera has seen, and it must not itself move blindly: in a pilot of our first shield version, 10 of its 11 crashes happened while the shield was flying the vehicle, and 8 of its 10 collisions were with obstacles beside or behind the camera.

title: ReSMap: Recasting Satellite Priors for Robust and Accurate Online HD Map Construction
authors: Kyungmin Kim,Sumin Lee,Sungoh Jeong,DoHyun Lim,Seonghyun Park,Soonmin Hwang
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)

abstract:
Despite recent advances in camera-based online HD map construction, these systems remain susceptible to sensor failures due to their reliance on onboard cameras.
In contrast, satellite images remain available independently of real-time sensing conditions as they are cached offline. Existing methods utilizing satellite images, however, primarily leverage them under nominal conditions, without explicitly addressing them as redundancy when a sensor degrades. To address this gap, we propose ReSMap, a redundancy-aware camera-satellite fusion framework for robust online HD map construction. Our framework explicitly leverages satellite images as a complementary source to improve robustness against camera failures.
A Predict-then-Fuse (PTF) module fuses camera and satellite BEV features by using each branch’s own prediction confidence as a per-pixel reliability weight, with no learned router. An Object-Centric Cooperative Multi-modal Query (OCMQ) decoder then extends this per-modality separation to the query level: each modality cross-attends only to its own BEV, and per-modality updates are merged through a learned per-token gate.
Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on nuScenes across all splits and range settings. More importantly, it also sets the new state-of-the-art under camera-failure scenarios, demonstrating that satellite images serve not only as a strong prior but as practical redundancy for robust online HD mapping.

introduction:
For safe autonomous driving, an accurate and reliable understanding of the surrounding road geometry and map elements is critical. Online HD map construction aims to predict vectorized road elements around the ego vehicle from real-time camera observations, for regions where an up-to-date HD map is not available. With the advent of query-based vectorized map construction [1], several methods have been proposed to improve the online HD map construction performance [2, 3, 4]. However, relying solely on onboard sensors has two key limitations.
First, in real-world deployment, they can become partially or completely unavailable due to hardware faults, occlusion, or temporary signal loss.
Second, they provide increasingly sparse and unreliable evidence as distance increases, making distant-region map prediction particularly challenging.

Beyond camera-only designs, several works have explored auxiliary modalities to enhance map prediction.
Some methods utilize additional LiDAR sensors [5, 6, 7], while others propose utilizing pre-existing low-resolution SD maps to understand coarse road topology [8, 9, 10].
However, LiDAR is still coupled to the onboard sensor stack, while SD maps lack the dense lane-level geometry required for fine-grained HD map prediction.
Satellite images offer another promising auxiliary modality: they provide top-down visual observations of the surrounding road layout while remaining available independently of real-time sensing conditions through offline caching [11, 12, 13].

Nevertheless, existing models using such auxiliary modalities still treat them as supplementary cues for improving accuracy under clean conditions, implicitly relying on the unrealistic assumption that sensor observations remain stable and informative.
As a result, they neither fully exploit auxiliary modalities as spatial priors under clean conditions nor use them as reliable redundancy when sensor observations are degraded or missing.

In this paper, we recast satellite images as an offline redundancy modality. Under normal conditions, they should complement onboard sensing by providing additional spatial evidence where sensor observations are uncertain or incomplete. Under sensor degradation, they must serve as an independent redundancy when onboard observations become unreliable or missing.

Our framework effectively exploits satellite images as both an explicit spatial prior under normal conditions and a redundancy source when sensors degrade. The model consists of two main architectural designs. i) Predict-then-Fuse (PTF) fuses camera and satellite BEV features using the prediction confidence estimated from each branch.
ii) Object-Centric Cooperative Multi-modal Query (OCMQ) decoder keeps a single shared object-query pool while computing modality-conditioned updates inside each decoder layer, and merges them through a learned per-token gate.

Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of our design. Our model achieves state-of-the-art HD map construction performance across diverse evaluation settings and consistently outperforms existing methods utilizing external modalities under sensor degradation, demonstrating its ability to fully utilize satellite images as both spatial prior and failure-time redundancy.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

We formulate geo-aligned satellite images as an offline-cached redundancy modality for onboard camera sensing in online HD map construction.

We introduce two architectural designs: a Predict-then-Fuse (PTF) interface for confidence-aware BEV fusion, and an Object-Centric Cooperative Multi-modal Query (OCMQ) decoder that preserves complementary map evidence through camera, satellite, and fused query streams.

We achieve state-of-the-art mapping performance under clean conditions across all evaluation settings, with the gap over prior work widening as the perception range grows.

We retain accuracy under camera failure where existing baselines suffer significant drops, by reallocating our model’s dependence onto the satellite stream when the camera signal becomes unreliable.

1. We formulate geo-aligned satellite images as an offline-cached redundancy modality for onboard camera sensing in online HD map construction.

2. We introduce two architectural designs: a Predict-then-Fuse (PTF) interface for confidence-aware BEV fusion, and an Object-Centric Cooperative Multi-modal Query (OCMQ) decoder that preserves complementary map evidence through camera, satellite, and fused query streams.

3. We achieve state-of-the-art mapping performance under clean conditions across all evaluation settings, with the gap over prior work widening as the perception range grows.

4. We retain accuracy under camera failure where existing baselines suffer significant drops, by reallocating our model’s dependence onto the satellite stream when the camera signal becomes unreliable.

title: Computing Invariant Reachable Sets through Sum-of-Squares Programming
authors: Mohamed Khalid M Jaffar
subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY); Robotics (cs.RO); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
comment: . Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Control Systems Technology. Code:this http URL
abstract: Funnels, time-varying invariant sets around nominal trajectories, certify that a closed-loop system tracks its plan, and can be composed into verified motion plans. Their computation by sum-of-squares (SOS) programming is well established in formulation but not in practice: the result depends on implementation choices such as the initial guess, Lyapunov function normalization, and termination rule, which the literature documents only briefly. This paper presents a self-contained treatment of SOS-based funnel computation, implemented in the open-source package computeSOSFunnels. We propose a minimum-volume formulation with inlet and outlet constraints under which funnels with coinciding nominal endpoints compose by construction. Numerical experiments on a unicycle, with timing studies on a cart-pole and a 12-state quadrotor, characterize the pipeline: infeasible initial guesses are partly decidable before solving, the certificate shows no violations among 39,000 boundary samples per funnel under the true dynamics, and constructing the semidefinite program, not solving it, dominates computation time.
introduction:
Autonomous systems that act near people and obstacles need more than a nominal motion plan: they need a guarantee that the closed-loop system stays near that plan despite deviations from it. Funnels provide such a guarantee. A funnel is a time-varying set around a nominal trajectory that every closed-loop trajectory starting in its inlet remains inside until it exits through its outlet. Because the guarantee is set-based, when funnels compose, that is, when the outlet of one funnel lies in the inlet of the next, the guarantees chain, and a sequence of funnels becomes a verified motion plan [1]. This composability makes funnels a natural primitive for feedback motion planning [2, 3, 4].

Computing funnels for a general dynamical system is the bottleneck. For nonlinear systems, a standard approach is to search for time-varying Lyapunov functions with sum-of-squares (SOS) programming, which turns invariance conditions into semidefinite programs (SDPs) [5, 6, 7]. The resulting problem is bilinear (non-convex) in the Lyapunov function and the SOS multipliers, so it is solved by alternating between convex subproblems, and its solution depends on design choices the formulation leaves open — the initial guess, termination rule, normalization that fixes the scale of the Lyapunov function, and the polynomial approximation of the dynamics. These choices decide whether the method returns a useful funnel or an infeasible program, yet the literature typically documents them only briefly, and the theory, which draws on real algebraic geometry and semidefinite optimization is spread across several papers. This paper is written to be self-contained, so that a reader new to SOS programming can follow it from theory to formulation to implementation.

SOS funnels and their use in planning: Tedrake et al. [2] presented LQR-trees that grow a tree of trajectories, each stabilized by a time-varying linear quadratic regulator (TVLQR), and verify a funnel around each with SOS programming. Tobenkin et al. [7] developed the underlying funnel computation framework, including the time-sampled verification and the Riccati-based initial guess adopted in this work. Majumdar et al. [8] extended the search to the controller itself, maximizing the set of states driven into a goal region. Majumdar and Tedrake [3] reversed the objective, computing minimum-volume outer approximations of the states reachable from a given initial set; our formulation is closest to theirs. Funnels have since served as primitives for online replanning in dynamic environments [9].

Alternatives to SOS-based funnels: Funnel synthesis for systems with Lipschitz nonlinearities can be posed as a numerical optimal control problem with matrix inequality constraints [10]. Hamilton–Jacobi reachability analysis yields tracking-error bounds for planning with reduced-order models [11], and Bernstein polynomial bounds give fast funnel computation for polynomial systems [12]. Contraction metrics certify tracking tubes through differential conditions rather than Lyapunov sublevel sets [13]. These methods trade the generality of polynomial certificates for scalability or tighter structure. SOS methods face their own scalability limit, since the SDP size grows combinatorially with state dimension and polynomial degree; diagonally dominant relaxations [14] and related techniques [15] trade conservatism for tractability.

Gap: The SOS formulation for computing funnels is well established, but its practical implementation is not. Where reference implementations exist, the accompanying papers do not fully characterize how the computation behaves: which initial guesses yield feasible programs, when to stop the alternation procedure, how well a polynomial approximate certificate holds for the true dynamics, and where the computation time goes. This paper addresses that gap. Its contributions are:

computeSOSFunnels11
1
github.com/khalid2696/computeSOSFunnels, an open-source, end-to-end implementation of the computation pipeline, from trajectory optimization and TVLQR synthesis to polynomial approximation and invariance certification. It automatically generates Taylor approximations of arbitrary user-specified degree from symbolic system dynamics.

An empirical characterization of the pipeline in practice: feasibility of initial guesses, part of which is decidable before any SDP is solved; validity of the certificate under the true dynamics; and computational cost, including a closed-form count of the SDP size.

A minimum-volume funnel formulation with both inlet and outlet constraints. As in [3], the funnel contains a given inlet set; in addition, its outlet lies within a user-specified terminal set nested inside the inlet set. So funnels with coinciding nominal endpoints compose, avoiding runtime set-containment checks whose cost accumulates during motion planning.

title: Say the Same, Act Differently: Diagnosing and Steering Text-Action Divergence in Reasoning VLAs

abstract:
Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) models pair physical control with natural-language rationales that supervisors can read to monitor embodied safety.
Prior attacks on VLA reasoning corrupt the rationale itself and leave visible evidence in the text.
We show that visual perturbations can instead alter the physical action while keeping the generated rationale word-for-word identical.
At the shared text/action interface of Alpamayo for driving and InstructVLA for manipulation, our text-neutral action-subspace (TNAS) diagnostic shows that the locally most action-sensitive direction is nearly orthogonal to the active text-loss gradients, with 1.87%1.87\% and 5.28%5.28\% norm overlap.
At equal hidden-state perturbation norms across both models, interventions along this text-neutral residual shift actions 4.64×4.64\times to 47.8×47.8\times more than text-gradient perturbations, whereas text-gradient perturbations induce 21.2×21.2\times to 277×277\times more text drift.
Steering visual perturbations along this direction reaches the same decoupling from the image.
Across 154154 obstacle-annotated driving scenes in Alpamayo, TNAS-guided attacks induce a new collision under a word-for-word identical rationale in 52.6%52.6\% of scenes under full-image perturbations and 35.1%35.1\% under a localized forward-camera patch, compared with 4.55%4.55\% for unguided action attacks.
Relative to a text-preserving baseline, TNAS guidance raises exact rationale preservation from 83.0%83.0\% to 89.5%89.5\% and cuts teacher-forced text drift by 68.4%68.4\% at a comparable collision rate.
In InstructVLA, TNAS guidance cuts text drift by 40.5%40.5\% and preserves the exact response on 85.0%85.0\% of examples alongside a 1.731.73-unit action-chunk shift.
An unchanged rationale therefore cannot certify a safe action, so monitors for reasoning VLAs must verify the predicted action channel directly.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models translate visual observations and language instructions into embodied actions.
Reasoning VLAs additionally produce natural-language scene descriptions, rationales, or plans alongside continuous action predictions [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].
Unlike latent representations or raw motor commands, this language channel gives human supervisors an explicit, readable account of what the model perceives and intends to do.
A supervisor can inspect that account for a missed obstacle, an incorrect target object, or an intention that conflicts with the instruction, potentially before the action is executed.
The same idea drives chain-of-thought monitoring for language agents [6, 7], and for embodied models the stakes are even higher because an erroneous physical motion can cause collisions or physical damage.
Whether this interface can be trusted for safety hinges on one question: can the action become unsafe without any change in what the model says?

Recent attacks on reasoning VLAs redirect behavior by changing the reasoning itself.
TRAP steers chain-of-thought and downstream actions toward an adversary’s target with adversarial patches [8], while Trinh et al. [9] corrupt the intermediate reasoning trace directly, for example by substituting object names.
Both leave evidence in the channel a monitor reads. Because the reasoning text has changed, an incorrect object reference or an instruction-inconsistent plan is visible to a supervisor.
In contrast, as illustrated in Figure 1, we study rationale-preserving action divergence, where a perturbed input changes the predicted action while leaving the generated rationale word-for-word identical to the clean run.
When a perturbed driving input produces a colliding plan under the exact same rationale as the clean input, a monitor restricted to that rationale receives identical evidence in both cases.

This failure mode is rooted in how reasoning and action share a representation.
In the reasoning VLAs studied here, action prediction reads continuous hidden states that also produce the text [4, 5].
Because the rationale is a discrete, many-to-one readout of those continuous states, many distinct hidden states can map to the same generated text.
Under ordinary inputs the text and action co-vary, which makes rationales informative in typical operation.
For a rationale monitor to certify safety, however, any unsafe change in the action must also change the rationale.
Prior reasoning-hijacking attacks show that altering the text alters the action, leaving open the converse question: does the shared hidden state contain action-sensitive variation that leaves the text readout unchanged, and can visual inputs reach it?

We answer this question with the text-neutral action-subspace (TNAS) diagnostic and a corresponding input-level attack.
At the shared text–action interface, TNAS identifies the locally most action-sensitive direction in the hidden state, measures its overlap with the active text-loss gradients, and projects out that text-gradient component to isolate a text-neutral action direction (dTNASd_{\mathrm{TNAS}}).
We first perturb the clean hidden state directly along dTNASd_{\mathrm{TNAS}} and control directions, under both fixed text-drift budgets and equal perturbation norms, to verify that this local direction shifts the predicted action while leaving the token distribution nearly unchanged.
We then align image perturbations with dTNASd_{\mathrm{TNAS}} during input-level optimization to steer the model toward silent action divergence under paired free generation.

Contributions.

Rationale-preserving action divergence through visual inputs.
We demonstrate that visual perturbations can substantially alter a reasoning VLA’s action while preserving the exact generated rationale.
In Alpamayo, TNAS-guided perturbations introduce a geometric collision absent from the clean plan while leaving the rationale word-for-word unchanged in 52.6%52.6\% of annotated scenes under full-image perturbations and 35.1%35.1\% under a localized forward-camera patch, and in InstructVLA, they preserve the exact response in 85.0%85.0\% of examples with a mean action-chunk shift of 1.731.73 normalized units.

A local geometric mechanism for text–action decoupling.
We introduce TNAS and show that the action-sensitive direction at the shared interface overlaps the active text-loss span by only 1.87%1.87\% of its norm in Alpamayo and 5.28%5.28\% in InstructVLA.
Under equal perturbation norms across both models, perturbing the hidden state along the projected text-neutral direction shifts actions 4.64×4.64\times to 47.8×47.8\times more than text-gradient perturbations, whereas text-gradient perturbations induce 21.2×21.2\times to 277×277\times more teacher-forced KL.

Mechanism-guided attacks with stronger text preservation at the same level of action deviation.
Directly combining an action-deviation loss and a text-preservation penalty creates competing gradients that interfere with each other during optimization.

title: te-comp: A Complete MLIR Compiler Generating Self-Contained C Inference Engines for MCUs
authors: Van Chan Ngo
abstract:
Deploying deep learning on microcontrollers (MCUs) requires fitting both the
model weights and runtime activations within tens to hundreds of kilobytes of
SRAM and Flash. Existing approaches either use an interpreter with a
pre-written kernel library or combine a Python code generator with hand-written C kernels.
This incurs dispatch overhead and requires framework dependencies. None produces
self-contained, dependency-free C code specialized to a given model.
introduction:
Microcontrollers (MCUs) power billions of embedded devices, from wearable
health monitors and keyword-spotting earbuds to industrial sensors and
autonomous vehicles. Running deep learning inference directly on these devices
eliminates cloud round-trips, reduces latency to microseconds, and preserves
user privacy. However, MCUs operate under extreme resource constraints:
typical ARM Cortex-M4/M7 targets offer 128–512 KB of SRAM, 512 KB–4 MB
of Flash, and clock speeds of 160–400 MHz with no GPU, no virtual memory, and
no dynamic allocation. Existing deployment approaches fall into the following categories,
each with fundamental limitations.

Interpreter runtimes (TFLite Micro David et al. (2021),
ExecuTorch Meta AI (2024)) load a serialized model and dispatch
operations through a generic interpreter loop. This is portable but incurs
20–50 KB of SRAM overhead from dispatch tables, op resolvers, and runtime
buffer management. Latency suffers from indirect function calls on every
operator. Neither framework supports large language model (LLM) inference on
MCUs.

Library-based code generators (MCUNet Lin et al. (2020); Lin et al. (2021)) use a Python script to generate a model-specific dispatch
function that calls into a hand-written C kernel library (33 source files for
MCUNet). This achieves near-optimal latency through carefully tuned SMLAD-based
kernels, but adding a new operator requires writing new C files, and the
generated code depends on the entire kernel library at link time.

General-purpose ML compilers (Apache TVM Chen et al. (2018),
IREE Google (2023), Glow Rotem et al. (2019)) use compiler IRs to optimize
models, but none produces deployable bare-metal code for Cortex-M
microcontrollers. TVM’s Cortex-M support is immature and still requires a
runtime. IREE and Glow target GPUs and Cortex-A mobile processors.

None of these approaches produces self-contained, dependency-free C code
specialized to a specific input model. We believe that this is the right
abstraction for deployment: the output should be plain C code that firmware
engineers just drop into any existing project and call with simple APIs without an interpreter, kernel
library, or framework dependencies.

We present te-comp, the first complete MLIR-based compiler that achieves this goal.
Given a standard model in .tflite for int8 CNNs or .safetensors for transformers, it produces:

{model}_engine.c/.h: The complete inference
engine with all kernels as nested loops, weight arrays in
.rodata, and the activation arena in .bss.

inference_task.c / inference_api.h: Integration layer (FreeRTOS or bare-metal).

CMakeLists.txt: Drop-in CMake library.

Self-contained C code.
Given any input model, te-comp emits all C artifacts needed for deployment: the inference engine, RTOS
glue code, a public API header, and a CMake library target with zero
runtime dependencies. No other tool produces this complete output.

Self-contained C code.
Given any input model, te-comp emits all C artifacts needed for deployment: the inference engine, RTOS
glue code, a public API header, and a CMake library target with zero
runtime dependencies. No other tool produces this complete output.

LLM inference on Cortex-M7.
te-comp compiles an 8.3M-parameter GPT-Neo (TinyStories-v2) to a
self-contained C engine using 249 KB SRAM and 3.62 MB Flash
(measured on hardware), achieving ∼\sim1 token/s interactive
generation. No existing MCU framework supports this capability.

Outperforms MCUNet. On all 10 CNN benchmarks, te-comp outperforms for both
peak SRAM (avg 0.62×\times, up to 5.9×\times less) and Flash (avg
0.86×\times, up to 32% less).

Numerical accuracy. te-comp matches TFLite on 10 int8 models with 50-70+ layers by generating identical ground-truth
label accuracy.

1. {model}_engine.c/.h: The complete inference
engine with all kernels as nested loops, weight arrays in
.rodata, and the activation arena in .bss.

2. inference_task.c / inference_api.h: Integration layer (FreeRTOS or bare-metal).

3. CMakeLists.txt: Drop-in CMake library.
